items.t: 1 · What this notebook is
items.x: A personal study and revision notebook for Modern Indian History, built only from the material you provided: the Sarrthi IAS handout chapters (the "book") and the class slides with the teacher's board notes. Nothing is added from outside. Where the teacher's slide and the handout differ, the notebook says so in a note box instead of quietly choosing one. Each chapter follows the same pattern: sections in the order of the class, the teacher's ink in teacher boxes, traps in alert boxes, then a mind map, timeline, flow charts, tables, connections, recall sheet, quiz and flash cards. items.t: 1 · Basics first: power, state, sovereignty
items.x: The teacher opens with vocabulary. Every later chapter uses these words (power, state, sovereignty, centralisation), so this section is worth reading slowly once. Teacher: Source for this course = only the Sarrthi IAS handout (the "book"). After the batch is over, add the new NCERTs (go to the Sarrthi IAS Foundation YouTube channel for those). Feudal, non-modern and modern Feudal = old in time and regressive. Modern = usually new in time and progressive / better / more efficient. Old is not always feudal or backward. Old can be gold (the handout's example: Lata Mangeshkar). Raja Ram Mohun Roy, the Father of Modern India, wanted a return to the pure past of Vedantic traditions. Teacher's ladder: Feudal → Non-modern (the transition period) → Modern.  Feudal is old in time and regressive; non-modern is the transition period; modern is usually new and progressive. Power and its six forms Power = Economic + Political (decision-making) + Military + Social (influence over people, or awe in their hearts) + Intellectual/Technological + Spiritual. A rise or fall in one form of power drives a rise or fall in the others. Example from the handout: a social-media influencer's popularity raises his or her economic power, while a scandal can hurt a politician's political power.  Power and its six forms (W1 to W6), with the teacher's notes: Mao, "person-power fit", and the joint-family example. Teacher: Person-power fit. Think of a joint family. The strong personality of the grandparents holds all the power. After years a weak personality follows, and power gets decentralised. Teacher: Mao: power flows from the barrel of a gun (written beside Military). Teacher: Baba Ramdev example: social power turns into money power (Patanjali, plus coaching). One power rising lifts another. It is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality Power centralises itself in a strong personality. That personality can be a human or an institution. When the personality weakens, power leaves in one of two ways: vertically downwards (decentralisation) or by horizontal displacement (another personality replaces it). Teacher's example of horizontal displacement by an institution: Kodak → smartphones.  Rise and fall of super-powers: a wave between centralisation and decentralisation. Mughals strong till 1707, then regional powers, Marathas by the 1750s, Third Battle of Panipat 1761, then the EIC. Teacher: Reading the wave. Till 1707: strong Mughal emperors (all-India power). After 1707: decline of the Mughals, decentralisation of power to regional powers. Then the Maratha empire by the 1750s, broken at the Third Battle of Panipat, 1761, and then the EIC (circled in red) rises. The teacher draws a grandparent with four children as the Mughal picture. Beside it are the initials "SS, RS, AA", which I could not decode from the handwriting. Check your own notebook. Country, nation, state Country = territory (Desh). State = the organisation that rules or governs a country and its people (Rajya). To rule = to make laws, implement them and settle disputes (L, E, J) over domestic affairs. That is also called governance. Nation = the summation of people who are one (fraternity), equal (equality) and supreme (liberty). This is the definition given by the French Revolution (1789). The teacher links it to "We the People" in the Preamble = Nation (Rashtra).  Teacher's board: State = organisation that rules a territory (country) and its people (nation). Nation = people who are or feel one, equal and supreme. State rules a territory and its people. Country = the territory. Nation = the people. The State talks, trades or fights with the outside world, but it *rules* only its own country and people. State structure  Teacher's board: State structure. The symbolic sovereign (the President, Head of State) over Legislature, Executive and Judiciary, at Centre and Province. Teacher's tree: Symbolic sovereign (= President, Head of State) sits over the Legislature, Executive and Judiciary. This structure repeats at the Centre and at the Province. The Executive = the Council of Ministers, which works through military servants and civil servants. The handout says the primary purpose of any constitution is to create the State structure. A modern State structure has separation of power, a well-defined internal structure with clear goals and functions, and mechanisms that keep the whole structure stable from top to bottom. A non-modern State structure has no institutional separation of power and is prone to instability. Student confusion resolved (handout). NCERT says a Modern State has "centralised power exercised over a clearly defined territory". In class we say a Modern State has separation of power. Both are right. A State can be vertically centralised (a strong Union Government with authority over the provinces) and at the same time have horizontal separation of powers at the Union level: Parliament makes laws, the Prime Minister implements them, the Supreme Court resolves disputes. Like parents who centralise power over the home, yet divide it between mother and father. Teacher: The word "province" is better than "state" for the units of a federation, otherwise it causes confusion with State = the ruling organisation. "Republic of India" and the point of Modern Indian History  Teacher's board: "Republic of India" is the name of the State (organisation) ruling the territory and people of India since 26 January 1950. "Republic of India" = the name of the State (organisation) ruling the Territory and People of India since 26 January 1950. Key goal of the Constitution = to define and create this State (organisation). MIH = the history of the States that ruled the territory of India and its people, for example the Mughal State, the Maratha State, the Awadh State, and the Company State by the EIC. INM (Indian National Movement) = a people's movement. Its goal: end the British colonial State and establish the Nation State (the Republic of India). Teacher: Keep one picture: a State is an organisation. Every dynasty in this course is just one such organisation, and each can be studied by the same questions: who rules, over what territory, with what structure, and why did it weaken? Types of State   Type   What it means    --- ---    Military State   Set up and sustained by military power     Police State   Sustained by overuse of the police     Kingdom / Empire   Head of State decided by bloodline. Organisations and their motives   Organisation   Motive    --- ---    Family   Welfare of its members     Private company   Profit for shareholders     NGO   A social motive     Political party   Power over the State (the 1886 INC rule: take up only political issues, not social issues, so the INC is a political party, not an NGO)     State   Territory, and ideally the people's welfare (example: a Nation State)   The common man does not want to be an MP, MLA or minister. She wants security: physical, economic, socio-cultural and spiritual. Teacher: The State's motive is territory. The common man wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural: religion, language, art and so on). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises. If social power rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example given: 1971, Indira Gandhi, and the hit song of the time. Sovereignty Sovereignty = symbolic sovereignty + the power to make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes (legislative, executive, judicial power), over external and domestic sovereign functions.   Aspect   Meaning    --- ---    Symbolic sovereignty   Who is the head of the State     The three powers   Make laws, implement them and adjudicate disputes (L, E, J)     External sovereign functions   Defence, Communications and Foreign Affairs: war and diplomacy (including trade)     Domestic sovereign functions   Everything else: Home, Finance, Agriculture, Industry, Infrastructure, Health, Education, Transport and so on     "Rule" / "Govern"   Always means exercising those powers over domestic affairs   Sovereign functions are also called subjects or affairs. The 7th Schedule of the Constitution (COI 1950) divides the domestic affairs between the Centre and the provinces.  What is Sovereignty? Teacher's notes: symbolic sovereignty (real power = 0), the power to do L, E, J on external sovereign functions and on domestic affairs. Teacher: Symbolic sovereignty: real power = 0. (The head of State is only a symbol.) Second part: the power to do L, E, J on (a) external sovereign functions = D, C, FA and (b) internal / domestic affairs = Home, Finance, Education, Health. Teacher: Affairs = subjects = sovereign functions = the items in the 7th Schedule of the COI.  External functions: Defence goes to the Defence Minister (war). Communications and Foreign Affairs go to the MEA (diplomacy plus trade). Foreign Affairs has an economic and a political side. Teacher: External functions map to ministers like this. D (Defence) → Defence Minister → war. C (Communications) and FA (Foreign Affairs) → MEA → diplomacy + trade. Foreign Affairs has an economic and a political side. Separation of powers in a modern State  Teacher's board: modern State structure. Symbolic Head of State over L, E, J, at Centre and provinces. Neither over-centralisation nor an over-weak centre.  Teacher's board, "Today": a modern State has horizontal separation of powers (L, E, J) and vertical separation of powers (federalism). Modern State structure = symbolic Head of State over L, E and J, at the Centre and provinces. The aim is separation of power, with neither over-centralisation nor an over-weak centre. Horizontal SoP = L / E / J. Vertical SoP = federalism. Inside the executive too: Head of State, PM, Council of Ministers, then the military servants ("gun power") and the civil servants ("political power"). Teacher: notice the separation of powers here also, for example a DM and an SP (more than one civil servant) share district power. Teacher: Non-modern State (example: Mughal). An absolute monarch, extremely powerful, with ministers, aristocrats and mansabdars below him. The mark is excessive centralisation. Teacher: Feudal State. The king is powerless, and feudal lords, ministers or aristocrats are powerful. There is no centralisation of power in the king: a very weak central authority.  The non-modern (Mughal) and feudal states compared with the modern structure. Modern INM: the phases  Modern INM (1857 to 1947) in five phases: Moderates, Extremists, Revolutionaries, Gandhian Era, Many Voices of the Nation.   Phase   Years   Tag    --- --- ---    Moderates   1857–1905   "the Pen"     Extremists   1905–20   "the People"     Revolutionaries   1907–47   "the Gun"     Gandhian Era   1920–47   —     Many Voices of the Nation   —   Working class, women's empowerment, Dalit issues   How the teacher says to remember battles and wars  Teacher's method: remember every battle or war by its Geography/Place, Duration, Participants and Reason. A war is the sum of battles. War = Σ (the sum) of battles. For any named battle or war, hold four things: Geography / place, Duration (example: the Seven Years' War), Participants, and Reason (example: the Austrian War of Succession, 1740–48). Passages: how regions connect  Passages: natural (passes on land, straits on water) and man-made (bridges, tunnels, canals). Khyber Pass is India's entry from the North-West. Khyber Pass = India's entry pathway from the North-West. A passage can be natural: on land a pass (Khyber); on water a strait (Gibraltar; the Dardanelles linking the Black and Mediterranean Seas). items.t: 3 · Mughal take-over from the Lodis (Babur 26-30)
items.x: Who were the Mughals? Babur 26-30 was born in 1483 to Umar Shaikh Mirza, ruler of Fergana, a semi-autonomous State in present-day Uzbekistan, roughly half the size of modern Haryana. Fergana belonged to the Timurid Empire, and Babur 26-30 was a descendant of Timur (Tamerlane). "Mughal" is a Persian corruption of "Mongol". The Mughals were a Turko-Mongol dynasty.   Side   Ancestor   Empire    --- --- ---    Maternal   Genghis Khan (1206–27)   Mongol Empire (1206–1368)     Paternal   Timur (Tamerlane) (1370–1405)   Timurid Empire (1370–1507)     Self-identity   Timurids   Pride in Timur, who had captured Delhi in 1398   They took greater pride in the paternal ancestor, so they called themselves Timurids, not Mughals.  Khanates of the Mongol Empire, about 1300 (handout figure).  Map: lands of the Empire of Timur (campaigns 1379 to 1405). Delhi is marked as sacked in 1398-99.  Map: the Fergana Valley, Babur's homeland (Kokand, Andijan, Osh, Namangan, Fergana, Jodzend). Why Babur 26-30 turned to India Babur 26-30 came to power young but could not hold Fergana; by 1512 his Central Asian ambitions had collapsed. He held Kabul (captured 1504), but Kabul was economically poor. India was wealthy but politically fragile under the Lodi dynasty. With artillery support from the Ottoman Empire (expert gunners), Babur 26-30 began attacking the Delhi Sultanate from 1519.  Map: the conquests of Babur, 1516 to 1529 (Kabul 1504, Khyber Pass, Panipat 1526, Agra 1528, Gwalior and the east 1529). The teacher marks Kabul as economically poor. Teacher: Babur 26-30's map: Kabul = "eco" (poor). The Khyber Pass is underlined. The dates 1526 (Panipat), 1528 (Agra) and 1529 (Gwalior and the march east) are underlined. First Battle of Panipat (1526) Babur 26-30 entered India through the Khyber Pass and met Ibrahim Lodi, the last ruler of the Lodi dynasty (1451–1526), on the plains of Panipat. Babur 26-30's army was smaller (about 12,000 men), but his small bronze cannons were decisive, a technology the Lodis could not match. Lodi was killed, the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) ended and the Mughal Kingdom was born. This was still a kingdom, not yet an empire. It became an empire under Akbar 56-05 and reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07.  First Battle of Panipat 1526: Babur's edge (small bronze cannons, Ottoman gunners), the battle, and the outcome. Teacher writes: Tech Power.  First Battle of Panipat, 1526: Mughal miniature of Babur against Ibrahim Lodi. Teacher: Tech power. Babur 26-30's edge over a fragile Lodi Sultanate was technology, not numbers. The teacher underlines "small bronze cannons", "about 12,000" and "Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)". Why three great battles happened at Panipat Three of the most consequential battles in Indian history, 1526, 1556 and 1761, were all fought at Panipat. Geography chose Panipat; the commanders merely followed: Panipat lay close to the Khyber Pass, the primary invasion route from Central Asia. It sat in the narrow corridor between the Thar Desert (south) and the Himalayan foothills (north), a natural bottleneck. The Yamuna to the east acted as a defensive choke-point, ruling out flanking manoeuvres. The Kala Amb memorial in Haryana commemorates the 1761 Third Battle, not the 1526 one. Babur 26-30 in Fergana; Timurid descendant, loses Fergana by 1512 (warn) Kabul held from 1504; economically poor India: rich but politically fragile under the Lodis Ottoman gunners and small bronze cannons; attacks from 1519 First Battle of Panipat 1526; Babur 26-30 (about 12,000) defeats and kills Ibrahim Lodi (good) Delhi Sultanate ends; the Mughal Kingdom is born (a kingdom, not yet an empire)

items.t: 4 · Humayun 30-40 and Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45
items.x: Babur 26-30 died in 1530; his son Humayun 30-40 succeeded. Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 was an Afghan-Pathan, born Farid Khan in Bihar, c. 1486. He was no foreign invader: his ancestors migrated to India under the Lodis and settled as Jagirdars in Bihar. He won the title Sher Khan by killing a tiger single-handed while serving Bahar Khan Lohani (Governor of Bihar under the Lodis till 1526, then independent Sultan Md Lohani, who refused Mughal sovereignty). Sher Shah 40-45 defeated Humayun 30-40 at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540), founded the Suri dynasty (1540–55) and pushed the Mughals out of India entirely.  Humayun's loss and return: 1530 succession, 1539 Chausa, 1540 Kanauj, 1555 Sirhind, Jan 1556 death and Hemu seizes Delhi. Teacher: a gap or intermission in the Mughal movie. Teacher: Two defeats: Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540). The Suri interregnum 1540–55 is a gap / intermission in the Mughal movie. Sirhind (1555) is boxed. Sher Shah 40-45's three reforms The Suri dynasty lasted only fifteen years, but Sher Shah 40-45's administrative innovations outlasted it: Revenue. A standardised system of land measurement and revenue assessment, the precursor to Akbar 56-05's Zabti system. Each peasant got a Patta specifying his revenue obligation, and the State took a Qabuliyat, a written agreement, from the peasant. The two-document system gave both State and cultivator an enforceable record. Currency. The silver Rupiya, a coin of standardised weight and purity, the ancestor of the modern Indian rupee. Infrastructure. He upgraded the Grand Trunk Road from Peshawar to Sonargaon in Bengal, transforming communication and trade across the subcontinent. Patta and Qabuliyat. The Patta is a document given by the State to the ryot: land details, ryot's name, the LR to be paid. The Qabuliyat is proof that the ryot agreed to pay the LR; it is given by the ryot to the State. Sher Shah 40-45 was the first to introduce this bilateral / mutual agreement system. In ancient times a Patta existed but it was not two-sided: the State gave the Patta (Tamra Patra, a copper inscription). Sher Shah 40-45 died in 1545. The Suri dynasty held Delhi until 1555, when Humayun 30-40 recaptured the throne. Much of what Akbar 56-05 later systematised had its roots in Sher Shah 40-45's innovations. Humayun 30-40 returns, with Safavid help To retake his throne, Humayun 30-40 turned to the Safavid dynasty of Iran. The Safavids agreed at a political price: Humayun 30-40 had to adopt Shia practices and outward observances, cede Kandahar to Iran, and promote Persian culture in India. Whether this was genuine conversion is debated; Humayun 30-40 publicly assumed Shia forms as the price of the alliance. Lasting consequences: Persian language and art became embedded in Mughal court culture, and a distinct Irani group of Mansabdars later emerged in the Mughal administration.  Teacher's board: the Safavid dynasty of Persia's conditions for helping Humayun: convert to Shia, promote Persian culture, make Persians mansabdars (link: the Irani group). With 14,000 Iranian troops, Humayun 30-40 defeated the Suris at the Battle of Sirhind (Punjab, 1555). In January 1556 Humayun 30-40 fell from the stairs of his library, struck his head and died. Hemchandra Vikramaditya (Hemu), from Rewari in present-day Haryana, who had served as chief commander and minister of the Suris, seized Delhi and declared himself Samrat.

items.t: 5 · How the Mughal Kingdom was re-established (Panipat 1556)
items.x: On one side stood Hemu, controlling Delhi. On the other, the Mughal army under Bairam Khan: general, strategist and guardian to the thirteen-year-old Akbar 56-05. Hemu was defeated. The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) secured the Mughal State in India for the next 150 years.  Second Battle of Panipat 1556: Hemu (declares himself Samrat; teacher: a powerful military general and minister of the Suris, 1540-55), Bairam Khan defeats him, the Mughal State is secured for about 150 years. Babur 26-30 enters through the Khyber Pass; First Panipat 1526 Humayun 30-40 defeated by Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 (Chausa 1539, Kanauj 1540) (bad) Suri dynasty 1540–55; Mughals lose India Safavid alliance; 14,000 Iranian troops; Sirhind 1555 Humayun 30-40 dies Jan 1556; Hemu seizes Delhi (good) Second Panipat 1556: Bairam Khan defeats Hemu; Akbar 56-05's reign secured

items.t: 6 · How Akbar 56-05 built the Mughal State: the Mansabdari System
items.x: Babur 26-30 founded the Mughal Kingdom. Humayun 30-40 nearly lost it. Akbar 56-05, ruling for fifty years (1556–1605), built the machinery of the Mughal State: the Mansabdari System, a military-bureaucracy that decided how the State was administered, how its army was maintained and how the King kept control over a vast and diverse territory. What is a Mansabdar? Mansab = a post or rank. Mansabdar = the holder of the post. Every Mansabdar had a dual function: military and civil-administrative. The same man who commanded troops also governed territory. That is why it is called a military-bureaucracy.  Teacher's board: the Mughal Emperor over Mansabdars (= ministers and senior officers). A post = mansab; a DM or minister = mansabdar; DMship or ministership = mansab. Teacher: Posts in the State structure. "O" = a post = mansab. A DM or minister = mansabdar; DM-ship or minister-ship = mansab. Mansabdars = the ministers and senior officers of the Mughal State. Five questions the teacher sets for the topic: *What is a mansab? What is a mansabdar? Salary? Ranks? How to become a mansabdar?* Rank: Zat + Sawar Each Mansabdar carried two ranks: Zat = personal rank, governing seniority and status. Sawar = the number of horsemen he must maintain and provide to the King. Net rank = Zat + Sawar. Example: Zat 2,000 + Sawar 3,000 = net rank 5,000.  Mansabdari, Zat plus Sawar. Teacher's notes: no separation of power between civil and military; Zat = A (like today), Sawar = B (army), net = A+B; eligibility primary = hereditary, exception Birbal; Piyush and Anshu on a Zat-Sawar graph. Teacher: No separation of power between civil and military. Zat is like today's rank (A); Sawar = the army, i.e. the horsemen (B); net rank = A + B. Teacher: Eligibility. "Lineage, not merit" in most cases. The primary rule was hereditary, with the exception of Birbal, who was not from an aristocratic family. Teacher: Zat-Sawar graph. Most nobles lie on the rising line (more Zat, more Sawar). Outliers: the favourite of the emperor = "Anshu" and the distrusted = "Piyush". The teacher's two names sit at opposite corners of the graph (Piyush high on Zat, Anshu high on Sawar). Who could become a Mansabdar? Lineage, not merit. If your ancestors had been Mansabdars, you had the opportunity. Talent alone was not enough, not unlike pre-revolutionary France, where only sons of nobles could enter the nobility. This rigidity later became a serious weakness. How Mansabdars were paid: Jagir, Khalisa, Inam A Mansabdar could be paid in cash (a Naqdi Mansabdar) or by a Jagir: a specific piece of land whose land revenue he pocketed directly. This revenue paid his salary and covered the cost of maintaining his army. A Jagir given in lieu of salary = a Tankha Jagir; its holder = a Jagirdar. Iqtadar of the Delhi Sultanate is like the Jagirdar Mansabdar of the Mughals. (Iqta = Jagir in Persian.) Mughal land was divided into these categories: Jagir land: revenue to Mansabdars. Khalisa land: royal land. Revenue goes directly to the King and pays Naqdi Mansabdars plus other State expenses. Inam land: gifted land. Revenue goes to a chosen beneficiary (for example a man of exceptional talent) to sustain himself. Mashrut Jagir: a temporary "top-up" or extra allowance given to an official to cover the extra costs of a specific, difficult assignment. It is revoked automatically when the assignment ends. (Like "base salary" versus "the bonus".)  Mughal land classification: Jagir (Tankha and Watan), Khalisa, Inam, Mashrut Jagir. By the early 18th century there were over 8,000 Mansabdars, and four-fifths of all LR came from Jagirs, only one-fifth from Khalisa land.  Teacher's board: land of the Mughal empire. Khalisa land = 1/5 of total LR; Jagir lands = 4/5, with a small Watan Jagir block (10% to the king, 90% to the Jagirdar). Teacher: Salary in those times. The key source of power was control over land and its resources (today it is money). Mansabdars were about 4,000 to 5,000 at the peak of Mughal power (17th century); about 80 out of every 100 of LR went to them and about 20 to the King. Therefore the richest single person was the King. Teacher: Worked example for LR: ₹100 of wheat is cultivated by the ryot / peasant / Khudkasht. Tax = LR = 1/3 to 2/3 of gross produce. (For the changing LR share by era, see section 7.)  Teacher's board: salary is cash (Naqdi Mansabdar) or allocation of a Tankha Jagir (Jagirdar Mansabdar). LR of a Jagir goes to the Mansabdar. LR = 1/3 to 2/3 of gross produce. Three rules for Tankha Jagirs Transferable. The King could rotate Jagirs among Mansabdars, or convert a Jagirdar into a Naqdi Mansabdar at will. Capped extraction. A Jagirdar could collect only the pre-determined LR, not a rupee more. Royal supervision existed to prevent oppression of peasants and zamindars. Confiscation on death. On the death of a Tankha Jagirdar, both the Jagir and all accumulated wealth were confiscated. The predictable result: Mansabdars spent lavishly in their lifetimes, since saving made little sense.  Tankha Jagir: the King gets his army from it. Of a Jagir's LR, 30 is for personal salary and 70 must be used for maintaining the army as per Sawar. Military corruption after 1707 = the expected army not being maintained. Teacher: From a Tankha Jagir the King gets his army. Teacher's example split: LR = ₹30 pays for personal salary; LR = ₹70 must be used to maintain the army as per Sawar. Military corruption (post-1707) = the expected army is not being maintained. Watan Jagir Watan = hereditary and permanent. Unlike Tankha Jagirs, a Watan Jagir could be passed down and was not subject to rotation or confiscation. Given mainly to Rajput chieftains and autonomous rulers who had submitted to the Emperor, so they could collect revenue in their ancestral domains in exchange for military service and loyalty. The holder paid 10% of LR to the King as Peshkash (tribute), acknowledging the King's ultimate authority and compensating him for giving up his right to reclaim the Jagir. Do not confuse an ordinary Zamindar's Milkiyat (hereditary personal property within his zamindari tract) with a Watan Jagir (a political grant to a chieftain, carrying sovereign-like privileges). Inam vs Watan: Inam is a pure gift and is confiscated after death like Tankha Jagir. Watan is hereditary, given to a Mansabdar doing duty for the King, and passes to heirs.   Axis   Tankha Jagir   Watan Jagir    --- --- ---    Nature   Salary grant   Hereditary, permanent grant     Heritability   Confiscated on the holder's death   Passes to heirs     Transfer   King could rotate it at will   Not rotated     Typical holder   Any Mansabdar   Rajput chiefs / rulers who submitted     Tribute   —   Pays 10% of LR as Peshkash to the King    Tankha vs Watan Jagir.  Teacher's board: power of a Mansabdar. Jagirdar Mansabdars hold Tankha Jagir (all LR to the mansabdar) and sometimes Watan Jagir (90% to the mansabdar, 10% to the king); Naqdi Mansabdars get cash. Teacher: W = Watan / Vatan = hereditary = permanent = 10% of LR to the King as tribute. TJ = temporary = the emperor can take it away = transferable. In the teacher's picture, a Jagirdar with both gets 90% of the LR of the Watan portion, the king taking 10%; on Tankha land the Jagirdar takes 100% of the LR. What held the system together, and its fatal weakness The system ran on a patron-client relationship: the King gave rank and Jagir, and the Mansabdar pledged personal loyalty and maintained the army. This co-opted powerful individuals who might have challenged royal authority. But the loyalty was personal, not institutional. A Mansabdar's loyalty was to the King as a person, not to the State as an institution or to any law. It was transactional and conditional: give and take. If the King could not deliver Mansab and Jagir (land shortage, financial pressure, weak authority), the loyalty dissolved, and dissolved loyalty meant political instability. This differs from a modern State, where bureaucrats and military officers owe their position to merit and service rules: impersonal loyalty to institution and law. Because the whole military strength depended on Mansabdars actually maintaining the Sawar armies, weakened royal supervision meant hollowed-out armies on paper, far fewer men in reality, a silent erosion of State power from within. Patron-client bond; King gives Mansab + Jagir, Mansabdar gives loyalty and maintains the army Loyalty is personal; to the King, not to the State or any law (warn) King cannot deliver the desired Mansab and Jagir (bad) Loyalty dissolves; the bond was transactional and conditional (bad) State erodes; hollow armies on paper, fewer men in reality  The Mansabdari weakness: an institutional / organisational / systemic weakness. Teacher: loyalty should be impersonal (non-human), to religion, land or language. On paper a 2 lakh army, in reality a 1 lakh army.  Teacher's board: Mansab plus Jagir given by the King; loyalty and army given back. A patron-client relationship (senior gives, junior takes). After 1707, mansabdars who did not get the desired mansab and jagir became disloyal. Teacher: Institutional / organisational / systemic weakness. Impersonal loyalty (non-human) means loyalty to the State, law, religion, land or language, not to a person. The teacher's reading of the flow: "King cannot deliver" = cannot deliver the *desired* Mansab and Jagir (the teacher crossed out the handout's "land/revenue runs short" line and replaced it with this). The end state: on paper a 2 lakh army, in reality a 1 lakh army. Teacher: Post-1707: if Mansabdars did not get their desired Mansab and Jagir, they became disloyal. The patron-client picture: the patron is senior and gives; the client is junior and takes.

items.t: 7 · Mughal land revenue (LR) system
items.x: Usually people think all rights in a property are with the owner. That is not correct. Rights in land belong to four stakeholders:   Stakeholder   Rights    --- ---    The owner (in the Mughal system, ultimately the King)   Right to sell, lease out, rent out, and to get money from these; right to fair tax     The tenant / ryot   Right to occupy and cultivate; right to fair rent     The collector of tax   Right to collect tax; right to be paid for the service     The State   Right to assess / fix tax, enforce the demand and receive tax   LR was the financial backbone of the State: it paid the Mansabdars, maintained the army and kept the treasury alive.  Mughal LR system overview: the King owns all land and the State takes a fixed share as LR. Assessors with record-keepers fix the demand per field. Two systems: Zabti and Ijaradari. Teacher: Assessors fix the demand using past data of production and of LR, and so assess the LR demand. The two systems, Zabti and Ijaradari, are ticked. Who collected revenue, and how was it supervised The State did not collect directly. It relied on Zamindars (non-state actors) in zamindari tracts, who also held police duties. Rule of thumb: State actors get salaries. Non-State actors get a commission or profit for service performed for the State. The revenue hierarchy ran through record-keeping, assessment, settlement, collection and oversight:   Step   Level   Officer   Role    --- --- --- ---    A1 Record keeping   Village   Patwari   Maintains ledgers (Bahi / Bahi khata or Khasra) of individual peasant holdings and crops. A non-state accountant paid by the village community. Like the Kulkarni of Maharashtra, but the Patwari had no watan / vatan (hereditary) right; it was a customary right, not a customary vatan right     A2 Record keeping   Pargana   Qanungo   Consolidated Patwari data; a state official and hereditary custodian of historical tax rates (had vatan right)     B1 Assessment   Pargana   Amil   The State's executive revenue officer at the pargana level; assessed the official demand and audited accounts     B2 Assessment   Sarkar (district)   Amalguzar   Supervisor of the Amil at the sarkar level; assessed the demand and audited accounts     C Settlement   Ryot   Patta and Qabuliyat   See below     D Collection   Village   Muqaddam   Village headman who collected from cultivators     E Oversight   Pargana / sarkar   Amil and Amalguzar   Under Akbar 56-05's Zabti system   Patta (the title deed) = the official paper given to the individual peasant by the government. The government used the Patwari's ledger / Khasra to create it. It told the peasant exactly how much land he officially held and how much LR he must pay, and so served as a check against over-extraction. Qabuliyat (the acceptance deed) = the document signed by the peasant and given back to the government, promising to pay the LR written on the Patta.  Khudkasht vs Pahikasht. Teacher: a Patta has information on which field or plot is cultivated by which ryot, and how much LR is to be paid. Zamindar = holds the right to collect LR from a land; Jagirdar = holds the right to consume LR from a land. Teacher: A Patta has two pieces of information: which field / plot is cultivated by which ryot and how much LR is to be paid. It is a "safety tool for the Khudkasht / ryot". Teacher: Zamindar = holds the right to *collect* LR from a land. Jagirdar = holds the right to *consume* LR from a land. Physical collection and the Zabti system Muqaddams collected from cultivators. In zamindari tracts they deposited to Zamindars (who extracted through their own Amlas). Where there were no intermediaries, Muqaddams paid directly to the State. In later periods contractual revenue farmers, the Ijaradars, also collected (covered below). Under Akbar 56-05's Zabti system, the State did not trust Zamindars with autonomous authority. State officials (Amil at pargana level, under the Amalguzar at sarkar level) scientifically measured the land and fixed the exact demand. The land records were archived by the Qanungo at pargana level. LR was calculated as a percentage of gross produce (more LR from more fertile areas). Mughal LR demand was a percentage of Gross Produce, not Net Produce. Subtracting the cost of cultivation before taxing was a British reform, much later, and only after the gross-produce method had caused widespread agrarian ruin.  Mansabdari versus Zamindari / Zabti. Mansabdari = the system of Mughal State structure (king and mansabdars; roles, salaries, hierarchy, ranks). Zamindari / Zabti = the system of collection of LR (assessment by the State, collection by the Zamindar). Teacher: Mansabdari = a system of the Mughal *State structure* (king and mansabdars; roles and responsibilities, salaries, hierarchy and ranks). Zamindari / Zabti = a system of *collection of LR*: assessment (how much LR) by the State, collection by the Zamindar. Don't mix the two. The zamindar's position  Teacher's diagram of the LR chain (Zabti): King gets LR from Khalisa lands; Jagirdar Mansabdars from Jagirs; Intermediary Zamindars (1000-3000 villages) and Primary Zamindars (100-300 villages) each keep 10% commission; ryots at the bottom. The Zamindar was an obedient collection agent under strict supervision, making sure the surplus went to the central treasury, not his pocket. His legally fixed commission, about 10%, was called Nankar or Malikana. His own personal lands were Milkiyat, on which he paid LR like any other landholder. Abwabs = customary tributes, extra demands passed from State to Zamindar to peasant. Intermediary Zamindars = big Zamindars who received LR from Primary Zamindars and collected LR themselves where no Primary Zamindar existed in their assigned land. They passed LR from Khalisa lands to the Imperial Treasury and from Jagir lands to Jagirdars. Sometimes Primary Zamindars sent LR straight to the treasury or the Jagirdar.  The Zamindari system. Teacher: the quantum of LR is decided by the State; the Zamindar's earnings are commission (about 10%), Abwab and his hereditary land; he also has police duties; Abwab is a levy from State to Zamindar and a tribute from ryot. Teacher: The quantum of LR is decided by the State, not the zamindar. In the teacher's circle (the rural economy): ryots pay LR up to the Zamindar; he sends LR to K (king) and J (jagirdar); he keeps 10% as commission, Abwab, and has police duties. Teacher: Zamindar roles. He also had police duties (the teacher compares it with an SHO's work) and was the traditional leader of ryots. Abwab from State to Zamindar = levies; Abwab from ryot to Zamindar = tribute.  Teacher's board: the Patta (name of ryot, LR to be paid, details of fields) is the safety tool for the Khudkasht; the Zamindar is a non-state actor, not a govt employee; salary is only for employees; Zamindar's service to the State is LR collection and police duties, for 10% of LR. Teacher: A Zamindar is a non-state actor: a private person, not a govt employee. Salary is used only for employees. His payment for services to the State (LR collection and police duties) is the 10% of LR. Teacher: A classroom ladder of power (vehicle analogy): King = helicopter; Jagirdar = Ferrari; Intermediary Zamindar = Fortuner; Primary Zamindar = Honda City; Khudkasht = cycle / Luna; Pahikasht = on foot.  The teacher's vehicle analogy for the LR ladder: King (helicopter), Jagirdar (Ferrari), Intermediary Zamindar (Fortuner), Primary Zamindar (Honda City), Khudkasht (cycle/Luna), Pahikasht (on foot).   Level   Collects from   Passes to   Keeps    --- --- --- ---    Ryot (Khudkasht / Pahikasht)   Pays LR   Primary Zamindar (or Muqaddam, or directly to State in non-zamindari areas)   Enough to sustain himself     Primary Zamindar (smaller; 100–300 villages)   Ryots   Intermediary Zamindar   About 10% (Nankar / Malikana)     Intermediary Zamindar (big; 1000–3000 villages)   Primary Zamindars   King (Khalisa) or Jagirdar (Jagir)   About 10% (Nankar / Malikana)     King / Jagirdar   Zamindars   —   King: Khalisa LR. Jagirdar: Jagir LR   Two kinds of ryot   Axis   Khudkasht   Pahikasht    --- --- ---    Land worked   The same land year after year   Different lands each season (often share-croppers)     Occupancy rights   Customary occupancy: cannot be removed   None; no fixed attachment to land     Standing   Small landowner-cultivator; holds a Patta   Landless and rightless (Vagrant / Banjara)   Khudkasht = occupancy rights of cultivation, NOT ownership. The King owned all land. A Khudkasht could not be arbitrarily removed, but could not sell or mortgage the land either.  Khudkasht vs Pahikasht: the Khudkasht holds a Patta; the Pahikasht is a landless, rightless vagrant or Banjara. Teacher: Pahikasht = cultivates different lands (within a village); landless and rightless. Revenue farming: Muqatai, Ijaradari, Farming System The logic: instead of collecting through the Zamindar network under State supervision, the right to collect all revenues from an area (land, traders, shopkeepers) was auctioned to the highest bidder, called an Ijaradar or Revenue Farmer. A farmer, in the economic sense, works with a profit motive; a peasant works for food security. The Ijaradar was not a cultivator but a merchant or moneylender who bid purely for profit. He farmed revenue, not land. The Ijaradar paid the bid amount, fully or partially in advance, to the Jagirdar (on Jagir land) or to the State (on Khalisa land), then collected his investment plus profit from the peasants and traders. Contracts were typically 3 to 5 years. His incentive was to extract as much as possible within that window, with zero interest in irrigation, peasant welfare or long-term growth. If he failed to deliver, the contract was re-auctioned. Ijaradars were urban bankers and merchants with no roots in the countryside: no long-term stake in the land, no relationship with the peasants.  Teacher's board: the Ijaradari system arises when there is need (war, bad harvest, a State short of LR) or greed (for example a Jagirdar who wants to maximise earnings, or a weak Mughal State) for higher LR. Ijaradar = Revenue Farmer. Teacher: Why Ijaradari arises: need or greed, for ↑LR. Need = war, bad harvest, LR collection of the State falling short. Greed = for example a Jagirdar who wants to maximise his earnings, and a weak Mughal State.  Teacher's auction analogy: the right to collect revenue from an area is sold like a painting. All bidders are rich; the seller gets the best price through competitive bidding and gets the money in advance; the buyer's motive is profit. Teacher: The painting analogy. Bidders in the auction are all rich. "HK" (the seller) gets the best price, as a result of competitive bidding, and gets the money in advance. "Bhaskar" (the buyer) then gets the painting. Bhaskar and the other bidders have profit as the motive: he plans to sell it at ₹2 crore, so ₹1 crore is the investment and the return he expects is ₹1 crore. In Ijaradari the right to collect revenue is the painting.  Teacher's board: auctions are held by the Jagirdar (in Jagir areas) or the King/State (on Khalisa lands). Participants are men of money: merchants, moneylenders, bankers (Ijaradars). Motive = profit. Contract 3-4 years. The Zamindar suffers a temporary loss of his Watan right to collect LR. Teacher: Who auctions: the Jagirdar (in a Jagir area) or the King/State (on Khalisa lands). They get money in advance (no wait till harvest) and the best price. Participants are men of money: merchants, moneylenders and bankers = Ijaradars. Motive = profit: collect such LR from ryots as covers the bid/investment plus profits. The teacher writes contract time as 3-4 years (the handout says 3 to 5). The Zamindar suffers a temporary loss of his Watan right to collect LR.  The mechanics: the Jagirdar auctions the right to collect LR over an area; merchants and moneylenders participate; the winner pays the bid amount to the Jagirdar in advance and collects LR from the ryots for profit.  Who is happy and who is not under Ijaradari: King/Jagirdar happy (advance, best price); Ijaradar happy (profits); ryots unhappy (no Patta); Zamindar unhappy (lost Watan right and earnings). A revolt needs a leader and followers. Teacher: Who wins and loses in Ijaradari: King/Jagirdar: happy (advance, best ₹). Ijaradar: happy (profits). Ryots: unhappy (no Patta). Zamindar: unhappy (lost Watan right and earnings). Teacher: A revolt needs a leader (L) and followers (Fo). If both (Zamindar as leader, ryots as followers) are unhappy: strong revolt. If the leader is unhappy but followers are happy: no revolt. If the leader is happy but followers unhappy: weak revolt.  Example: Churaman Jat, a Zamindar-led peasant revolt (about 1695), the grievance being high LR, led to the Jat Kingdom. Teacher: Example: Churaman 95-21 Jat = Zamindar-led peasant revolt (~1695); grievance = high LR; it led to the Jat Kingdom. (Taken up in Chapter 5.) Zamindar vs Ijaradar: why it mattered to the peasant. A Zamindar's right was tied to his bloodline; he and his descendants had to live with the peasants forever, so he rarely squeezed them to starvation. His commission was a state-mandated ~10% (Nankar / Malikana). An Ijaradar promised the State a fixed lump sum (say 1 lakh); if he extracted 3 lakh through torture and extortion, he kept the entire 2 lakh profit. The Zamindar's extraction was capped by law; the Ijaradar's was capped only by the peasant's capacity to endure.  Zamindar versus Ijaradar: basis of right, time horizon, extraction cap, and peasant impact.   Axis   Zamindar   Ijaradar    --- --- ---    Basis of right   Hereditary and traditional leader of rural society   Won an auction; an urban moneylender / merchant     Time horizon   Permanent   Short 3–5 year contract     Extraction cap   Capped (about 10% commission / Nankar / Malikana)   No cap     Peasant impact   Subsistence living possible   Ruined     Parameter   Zabti system   Ijaradari system    --- --- ---    How LR is fixed   Detailed survey   Auction     Settlement with (i.e. LR to be paid agreed with whom)   Ryot (has Patta)   Revenue farmer (Ijaradar), who also has the responsibility to deposit LR to the State     Collection by   Zamindar   Ijaradar     Motive of collector   State-mandated commission   Profit motive     Peasant protection   Patta gives legal right   No protection    Zabti versus Ijaradari. The Ijaradari story across history: rise and decline Auctioning the right to collect tax is ancient, but it was formally institutionalised in the subcontinent during the Delhi Sultanate as the Muqatai system. It lasted until Akbar 56-05 practically abolished it. Ijaradari maps almost perfectly onto the rise and decline of Mughal authority: abolished when the State was strong, revived when it was weak. (Babur 26-30 had no time for revenue reforms in his four-year reign; the decisive break came under Akbar 56-05.) Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526); Muqatai, the first formal institutionalisation of revenue farming (good) Akbar 56-05; practically abolished it, replaced with the Zabti system Jahangir 05-27; re-emerges marginally as control over Jagirdar-Mansabdars loosens Shahjahan 27-58; reintroduced properly, but only for ruined or devastated lands (warn) Aurangzeb 58-07; expanded it significantly; the Deccan campaigns made quick cash irresistible (bad) Jahandar Shah 12-13; institutionalised in Punjab and Bengal, the richest provinces (bad) Farukhsiyar (1713–19); extended into royal Khalisa lands Successor states; Awadh under Sadat Khan 22-39 and Hyderabad under Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 continue it (bad) Warren Hastings 73-85 (1772); formalised as the EIC's Farming System in Bengal  Ijaradari rise and decline, with the teacher's notes: notice the pattern; Shah Jahan for ruined lands (banjar); Jahandar Shah in fertile regions; Farukhsiyar's extension to Khalisa lands hurt the Emperor's social power.  Rising land-revenue extraction: Akbar 1/3rd, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb 1/3rd to 1/2, Later Mughals 1/3rd to 2/3rd. Teacher: wars need money, so the LR demand rises. Teacher: Notice the pattern down the chain. Akbar 56-05: Zamindari system (the teacher writes it beside "Zabti"). Shah Jahan: ruined lands = "banjar". Aurangzeb 58-07: wars. Jahandar Shah 12-13: fertile regions. Farukhsiyar: Khalisa lands, the first time (1st), which hurts the Emperor's social power. Warren Hastings 73-85's Farming System = Ijaradari. Teacher: Wars need money, so the LR demand rises.   Emperor   LR as % of produce (tells the story of decline)    --- ---    Akbar 56-05   1/3rd     Shah Jahan (1627–58), Aurangzeb 58-07   High extraction: 1/3rd to 1/2     Later Mughals (1707+)   Extreme extraction: 1/3rd to 2/3rd   Warren Hastings 73-85 was Governor of Bengal Presidency from 1772 and Governor General of Bengal Presidency from 1773–75 (the Regulating Act of 1773 made him GG, but he formally assumed office as GG in 1774). He formalised revenue farming as the Farming System in 1772. What began as the Muqatai system under the Delhi Sultanate, was abolished by Akbar 56-05 and revived under weaker successors, had become standard practice across large parts of the subcontinent by his time. The ryot at the bottom paid the price at every stage.

items.t: 8 · Akbar 56-05's religious vision: Sulh-i-Kul, Ibadat Khana, Mahzar, Din-i-Ilahi
items.x: Akbar 56-05's approach to religion shaped the political character of Mughal rule for generations. He moved in a clear sequence: Ibadat Khana (1575). A House of Worship at Fatehpur Sikri where scholars from different faiths debated. It exposed him to the diversity of religious thought and to the bitter rivalries among the Ulama. Mahzar, the Infallibility Decree (1579). It gave Akbar 56-05 the authority to adjudicate religious disputes: the Emperor, not the clergy, was the final word on matters of faith. Din-i-Ilahi (1582). A syncretic spiritual order borrowing from Islam, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism and Christianity. It is best understood as a religio-political experiment, not a movement: not many joined, but its real significance lay in the principle it expressed. Sulh-i-Kul: universal peace. The State must treat all religions with equal respect, and no single faith should dominate policy. It became the ideological foundation of Mughal governance under Akbar 56-05 and influenced Mughal politics long after his death.  Akbar's religious vision: Ibadat Khana 1575, Mahzar 1579, Din-i-Ilahi 1582, Sulh-i-Kul. Teacher's goals: mid-path, less conflict; the Emperor is the final word; social peace. Teacher: The goal of each step. Ibadat Khana: a mid-path, to reduce conflict. Mahzar: the Emperor is the *final* word on faith. Din-i-Ilahi: a syncretic religio-political order (a new hybrid religion borrowing from multiple faiths); goal = social peace. Sulh-i-Kul: universal peace via equal respect for all faiths; goal = social peace / order.

items.t: 9 · Who actually introduced Jizya in India?
items.x: Jizya is a tax on non-Muslims. It is often associated with the Delhi Sultanate, but it predates the Sultanate by several centuries. Muhammad bin Qasim first imposed Jizya in Sindh during the 8th-century Arab conquest. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 and his successors institutionalised it as a formal instrument of revenue and policy across the Delhi Sultanate from the early 13th century. The distinction matters: Jizya arrived in India with the Arabs, but became a pan-subcontinental administrative practice only under the Sultanate.  Who introduced Jizya? First imposed by Muhammad bin Qasim in Sindh (8th century); institutionalised by Qutb-ud-din Aibak and successors across the Delhi Sultanate.

items.t: 1 · Framework: how to analyse the decline
items.x: This is where Modern Indian History (MIH) starts. The Mughal State reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb 58-07 and began collapsing right after. Within about four decades it was a small area around Delhi–Agra under Maratha protection.  Chapter title slide with the teacher's timeline: Babur 26-30 to Aurangzeb 58-07, then the Later Mughals (weak) from 1707, Bahadur Shah 07-12 to Zafar 37-57 (the 1800s). "MIH starts." "But foundation of decline laid at Aurangzeb 58-07." Power moves down from the Mughal to the Mansabdars. Teacher: MIH starts here. Later Mughals are weak, from Bahadur Shah (1707-12) in the 1700s to Zafar (1837-57) in the 1800s. Power moves from the Mughal down to the Mansabdars. The foundation of decline was laid at Aurangzeb 58-07. After him, the weak emperors either could not revive the State or contributed to its decline.  Teacher: Aurangzeb 58-07 laid foundations, and then weak emperors could not revive or contributed to decline. The five-part equation State power = Political + Economic + Military + Social + Technological. The Mughal decline is a *simultaneous* weakening across all five.  Framework slide. Teacher: "By 1707 Mughal empire reached its peak" (Aurangzeb's reign), "but" the economic power and social power had not peaked. Travancore never part of the Mughal State; Assam also not. Teacher: By 1707 the Mughal empire reached its peak (territory), but not its economic power peak, and not its social power peak. Travancore was never part of the Mughal State. Assam also not. Two analytical tools (apply to every decline question)   Tool   Meaning   Mughal example    --- --- ---    Vertical power shift = decentralisation   The emperor weakens and power moves downward   After 1707 the emperors were weak personalities, so the Mansabdars under them became the real centre of power     Horizontal power shift = replacement   One entity replaces another at the same level   Delhi Sultanate replaced by the Mughals at Panipat 1526; British super-power replaced by US-USSR at the end of WW2 (1945)   The handout says to apply both lenses to every exam question on decline. The teacher's components board (what each form of power means)  Teacher's board on the framework: political power is proportional to territory; economic power = treasury (the name of the State's bank account); military power = number of soldiers, army size, technology, no military corruption, strong military leadership. Political power = the emperor's word is rule ("vachan hi hai shasan": decision + rule). Teacher: political power is proportional to the territory of the State. Economic power = the treasury, or public exchequer = the name of the bank account of the State. Military power has four parts: number of soldiers / size of the army; technology; no military corruption; strong military leadership. The teacher's World War examples: 1945, USSR had the largest army; 1945, atomic bomb (USA).  Social power: awe and love in people's hearts ("love you emperor"). The common man wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural: religion, language, art). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises; if it rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example 1971, Indira Gandhi, and a film song. Teacher: Social power = awe / love in people's hearts. The common man does not want to be an MP, MLA or minister; he or she wants security (economic, physical, socio-cultural). If social power falls, the chance of revolt rises; if social power rises, the chance of revolt falls. Example: 1971, Indira Gandhi, and the film song of the time. The teacher's list of factors  "Reasons/Factors for decline of Mughals": role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (wars, religious policy); weak emperors post-1707; military weakened (Nadir Shah, rebel states e.g. Marathas); institutional decline (disloyalty of Mansabdars, military corruption); Jagirdari crisis of the 18th century.  Teacher's factors tree, with ticks: Aurangzeb 58-07, institutional line, economic line, military line, weak emperors, lack of reform, all leading to territorial decline. Role of Aurangzeb 58-07: wars, religious policy. Weak emperors post-1707. Military weakened: external (Nadir Shah) and internal (rebel states, e.g. the Marathas). Institutional decline: disloyalty of Mansabdars, military corruption. Jagirdari crisis of the 18th century. Lack of reform (tech and organisation), all ending in territorial decline. Teacher: "We have covered the concepts of decline of the Mughals. Now let's look at factual data and events to support the concepts." Concepts first, then facts. (L4 slide 27 and L5 slide 2 show this two-layer approach: *org = concept + fact.*)  "Concepts of decline of Mughals": facts = organisation of concept plus fact. Concepts: factionalism (R vs R, R vs N, N vs N), weak personality (Rangila 19-48), military weakness plus shrinking of territory (external: Nadir Shah 1738-40; internal: Marathas). Teacher: Concept summary: Factionalism (Royal vs Royal, Royal vs Noble, Noble vs Noble); Weak personality (Rangila, 1719-48 = Muhammad Shah 19-48); Military weakness plus shrinking of territory (external: Nadir Shah 1738-40; internal: Marathas).

items.t: 2 · Why did Aurangzeb 58-07's wars sow the seeds of decline?
items.x: Aurangzeb 58-07 came to power in 1658 after a brutal succession war (he killed his elder brother Dara Shikoh). He governed as an empire-builder on a mission: to conquer all of India, particularly the Deccan. War helps a State only if ROI (return on investment) is positive and a period of peace follows the conquest. If wars never stop and territory won is eventually lost, it becomes an economic disaster.  Teacher's board: war = rapid investment of money (recruit men and horses, produce weapons, logistics of movement, attrition of soldiers, horses and elephants; the domestic economy suffers if war is fought in the homeland). Victory gives a long, slow ROI: gain of territory (more LR, ports, trade) and geopolitical gains (natural frontier; teacher's example: Hitler wanted territory up to the Urals). Teacher: War = rapid investment of money: recruit more men and horses, produce more weapons, logistics (costs of movement of men, food, weapons), attrition of soldiers, horses and elephants. Domestic economy suffers if the war is fought in the homeland. War victory → ROI is long and slow. The gain of territory brings more LR, ports and more trade, and geopolitical gains such as a natural frontier. Example: Hitler wanted territory up to the Urals. What he won, and what it cost Bijapur (annexed 1686; Adil Shahi dynasty 1489–1686) and Golconda (annexed 1687; Qutb Shahi dynasty 1518–1687). Both were successor kingdoms of the Bahmani Sultanate (1347–1527). In Bijapur it was a three-way fight: Mughals, Bijapur, and the Marathas, who never accepted Mughal authority. By 1705 the Marathas were winning; by the 1750s they had reversed most of Aurangzeb 58-07's gains and some of Akbar 56-05's as well. 40 years of warfare drained the treasury (*the government's bank account*), broke the Mansabdars financially (*they had to maintain armies*), and translated directly into later military corruption (*Mansabdars not maintaining the army as per Sawar*).  Aurangzeb's wars: war and ROI; the mission; Bijapur (1686, Adil Shahi 1489-1686); Golconda (1687, Qutb Shahi 1518-1687); the Marathas reversed it.  Teacher's board: Role of Aurangzeb (1658-1707, about 50 years, like Akbar's about 50 years). Left: religious orthodoxy (Jizya 1679, temple policy) and executions (GTB 1675, Sambhaji 1689) make social power sad; contribution to the Jagirdari crisis; continuous wars of about 45 years hurt the economy. Right: Akbar = foundation of rise. Teacher: Role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (about 50 years), versus Akbar 56-05 (about 50 years). Teacher: Aurangzeb 58-07, four lines. (1) Religious orthodoxy: Jizya (1679), temple policy → social power sad. (2) Execution of leaders: GTB (1675), Sambhaji 80-89 (1689) → social power sad. (3) Contribution to the Jagirdari crisis. (4) Continuous wars of about 45 years → economy sad (high LR demand; military corruption → weak military; wars proved useless ultimately; future emperors inherit a weak treasury). Teacher: Akbar 56-05 = foundation of rise. Universal peace, syncretic policies, religious harmony → social power *happy*. LR system fair, no Ijaradari, economic security. Strong state machinery (Mansabdari system) → military *happy*.  Wars table with the teacher's Deccan sketch. Left triangle: Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687, Goa, Vijayanagara 1336-1646. Right triangle: Aurangzeb (external power), Marathas (domestic rebels), Bijapur (existing State). Teacher: The Deccan triangle: Bijapur (1686), Golconda (1687), Goa, and the old Vijayanagara (1336–1646) region below them. The fight triangle = Aurangzeb 58-07 (the external power) + Marathas (domestic rebels) + Bijapur (the existing State).  Gol Gumbaz, Bijapur: mausoleum of Muhammad Adil Shah (r. 1627-56), Adil Shahi dynasty (1489-1686).  Golconda Fort, Hyderabad: seat of the Qutb Shahi dynasty (1518-1687). Gol Gumbaz is the mausoleum (burial building, like the Taj Mahal) of Muhammad Adil Shah (1627–56) of the Adil Shahi dynasty. How 40 years of war drained the State  "40 years of war": endless Deccan campaigns, conquest without a lasting peace ("because Marathas continued rebellion"); treasury drained; Mansabdars suffered economic losses, forced to maintain armies in continuous wars; military corruption post-1707, military weakened, loss of territory for Mughals.  Teacher's sketch: 40-45 years of wars of Aurangzeb, the Mansabdars (rupee sad), post-1707 weak emperors, therefore military corruption, military sad, loss of territory. Endless Deccan campaigns; conquest without lasting peace; Marathas continue rebellion Treasury drained by perpetual warfare (warn) Mansabdars forced to maintain armies in continuous wars; financially crippled (bad) Military corruption post-1707: troops not maintained as per Sawar rank (bad) Military weakened; loss of territory for the Mughals

items.t: 3 · Religious policies and the social foundation
items.x: State power needs social support. Aurangzeb 58-07 followed an orthodox interpretation of Islam in his personal life and his governance, systematically alienating non-Muslim subjects. 3.1 Jizya (1679) and its long history The most damaging measure was the re-introduction of Jizya in 1679 (*abolished in 1564*): an additional tax on non-Muslim adult males. Beyond the money, the manner of collection made people feel religiously discriminated against, and resentment ran deep. Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 first introduced Jizya in an institutionalised manner. He was the first Sultan of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) and founder of the Mamluk dynasty (1206–1290; Mamluk = military slave). Babur 26-30 and Humayun 30-40 continued it. Akbar 56-05 abolished it in 1564 as part of his Sulh-i-Kul (Universal Peace) policy. Aurangzeb 58-07 reintroduced it in 1679. Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13 abolished it again in 1712. The handout says Farukhsiyar (1713–19) re-introduced it in 1717. As the empire weakened, Jizya faded with it.  Jizya in India: 712 CE Muhammad bin Qasim imposes it first in Sindh; 13th c. Aibak institutionalises it (1206-10); 1564 Akbar abolishes it; 1679 Aurangzeb re-introduces it (teacher adds Bahadur Shah 07-12); 1712-17 Zulfiqar Khan abolishes in 1712, Farukhsiyar continues the abolition but later re-imposes; 1719 onwards Jizya fades away.  Handout Diagram 1: Jizya in India, Aibak (1206-10) introduces it, Babur and Humayun continue it, Akbar removes it in 1564, Aurangzeb re-introduces it in 1679, Zulfiqar Khan abolishes it in 1712, Farukhsiyar re-introduces it in 1717, it fades with Mughal decline. Who first introduced Jizya? Muhammad bin Qasim introduced it in 712 CE after conquering Sindh. By paying it, the non-Muslim population was granted the status of Zimmis (Dhimmis), "protected people", allowed to practise their religion and exempted from military service. (Handout aside: *is this a gain or a loss of employment opportunity for the masses?*) Who first institutionalised Jizya? Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10. Discrepancy to check. The handout text says Farukhsiyar *re-introduced* Jizya in 1717. The teacher's slide says Farukhsiyar continued the abolition but later re-imposed Jizya, and that Jizya fades from 1719. Both agree on the direction: abolished 1712, re-imposed by Farukhsiyar, gone by 1719. 3.2 Temple policy: Kashi Vishwanath (1669) Aurangzeb 58-07 refused temple repairs and reduced their land grants. More significantly he demolished important temples. Best-known case: the Kashi Vishwanath temple at Varanasi, demolished 1669, replaced on the same site by the Gyanvapi Mosque. His own court record, the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, documents his order. The temple's troubled history: razed earlier by Qutb-ud-din Aibak 06-10 (1194, then slave-general of Md Ghori, before he became first Sultan in 1206) and Sikandar Lodi (1490). Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore rebuilt it in 1780 near the original site.  Temple policy table: Aurangzeb refused repairs, cut land grants, demolished key temples; Kashi Vishwanath demolished 1669 with Gyanvapi Mosque on the site; court chronicle Maasir-i-Alamgiri documents the order; earlier razed by Aibak (1194) and Sikandar Lodi (1490); rebuilt by Ahilyabai Holkar of Indore in 1780 near the original site. The teacher underlines the Maasir-i-Alamgiri, Aibak (1194), Sikandar Lodi (1490) and Ahilyabai Holkar.  Kashi Vishwanath Temple and Gyanvapi Mosque, Varanasi (old print). 3.3 Executions that backfired 1675: Guru Tegh Bahadur (GTB), the 9th Sikh Guru. 1689: Chhatrapati Sambhaji 80-89, elder son of Shivaji 74-80, after weeks of torture. Both were offered convert-or-die; both refused. The executions did not suppress resistance: they created martyrs, hardening anti-Mughal sentiment among Sikhs and Marathas.  Executions that backfired: Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675), Sambhaji 80-89 (1689), both refused to convert; the backfire: martyrs, hardened Sikh and Maratha anti-Mughal sentiment. Teacher: Both GTB (1675) and Sambhaji 80-89 (1689) are boxed on the board as the "execution of leaders" line, under social power sad.

items.t: 4 · Why did the Mansabdari system turn against the empire?
items.x: The Mansabdari system ran on personal loyalty to the emperor as an individual, not impersonal loyalty to the empire as an institution. It was a give-and-take: the emperor granted Mansabs and Jagirs; nobles gave military service and loyalty. Strong emperors made this work; weak emperors could not. After 1707 the Later Mughals could not control powerful Mansabdars. When the emperor could not grant the desired Mansabs and Jagirs, the Mansabdars became disloyal and acted upon that disloyalty (*earlier, either fear or belief in the fairness of a strong emperor kept them in line*): they engaged in court politics for the best Mansabs and Jagirs, or tried replacing the emperor with their favourite from the royal family. Court politics crippled governance. Those who should have led reforms (economic, administrative and military) were consumed by factional rivalry.  Why the Mansabdari system broke: personal loyalty, a give-and-take, weak Later Mughals, disloyalty, factionalism increased and reforms slowed down. Teacher: "busy in court politics and not on work". Teacher: Busy in court politics and not on work. That is the teacher's one-line reason why reform slowed down.  Teacher's scenario board: a Mansabdar didn't get his desired Mansab and Jagir, so a feeling of disloyalty. Under a strong emperor (good strong = faith in future fairness; bad strong = fear) the Mansabdar takes no action. Under a weak emperor the Mansabdar acts on his feeling of disloyalty. Factionalism = group politics = court politics: lobbying the emperor, backbiting, plot/coup (takhtapalat) to bring the favourite as emperor. Mansabdar does not get the desired Mansab and Jagir Feeling of disloyalty Strong emperor: good strong = faith in future fairness; bad strong = fear; so *no action* by the Mansabdar (bad) Weak emperor: the Mansabdar acts on his feeling of disloyalty (bad) Factionalism = group politics = court politics: lobbying the emperor, backbiting, plot/coup (takhtapalat), bringing the favourite as emperor

items.t: 5 · Why did the Mughal military weaken?
items.x: Three interconnected problems: 5.1 No technological or organisational reform European powers succeeded with smaller numbers because of better command, tighter discipline, and tactical innovations: File firing: rotating lines for continuous fire. Grapeshot artillery: multiple bullets in one shot; lethal at close range. Bayonet (*a knife*) on the Brown Bess musket (*so a rifle became a sword at close range*). Haider Ali 61-82, Mysore) reorganised his military on the European model and stayed formidable. The Mughals, paralysed by factionalism, reformed nothing.  "Why the Mughal military collapsed": no reform while Indian rivals upgraded their military with EU help; weak commanders (court politics, not merit); military corruption. Teacher's sketch of shotgun (grapeshot) fire. Teacher: No reform while Indian rivals upgraded the military with European help. Example in the handout: Haider Ali 61-82 reorganised on the French model (the slide says "on the French model"; the handout says "European model"). 5.2 Weak war commanders Under the Later Mughals (1707–1858), court politics, not merit, decided military appointments. 5.3 Military corruption Under weak supervision Mansabdars maintained far fewer cavalry than their Sawar rank required, pocketing the difference. Aurangzeb 58-07's war drain and the Jagirdari crisis compounded this. By the early 18th century the army was corrupt, under-equipped, poorly led and technologically frozen. Teacher: The Jagirdari crisis increased the chances of military corruption (written at the bottom of the slide).

items.t: 6 · Factionalism: how it operated in the Mughal court
items.x: Factionalism = Royal vs Royal + Royal vs Noble + Noble vs Noble. It is group politics.  The five court factions: Irani (Shia Persian; Zulfiqar Khan, Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13, who ended Jizya); Turani (Sunni Turkish-Uzbek, like the Mughals; Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, Governor/Subadar/Nawab of Hyderabad Suba 1724-48); Hindustani (converted Indian Muslims; the Sayyid Brothers, who brought Farukhsiyar 13-19 to power); Hindu (Rajputs and Jats; Sawai Jai Singh); Deccani (nobles absorbed from Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687).   Faction   Identity   Example    --- --- ---    Irani   Shia Persian   Zulfiqar Khan (Wazir of Jahandar Shah 12-13; ended Jizya)     Turani   Sunni Turkish-Uzbek (like the Mughals)   Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (1724–48), Governor / Subadar / Nawab of Hyderabad Suba     Hindustani   Converted Indian Muslims   Sayyid Brothers (brought Farukhsiyar 13-19 to power)     Hindu   Rajputs and Jats   Sawai Jai Singh 99-43     Deccani   Nobles absorbed from Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687)   none given   After 1707 weak emperors could not control these groups. Mansabdars competed to dominate the sitting emperor or install their preferred candidate: whoever controlled the emperor controlled Mansabs and Jagirs. No clear succession rule: every emperor's death was potentially a new power struggle. Some Mansabdars who could have stabilised the centre chose not to, and instead used the chaos to carve out their own principalities (the successor states).  Factionalism board: Royal vs Royal (succession dispute, coup d'etat), Royal vs Noble (for better Mansabs), Noble vs Noble (for Jagirs). Right: the "Role of Aurangzeb 58-07" tree (economy and social power down, Jagirdari crisis), institutional failure, military down, tech reforms down, J crisis leading to revolt, factionalism. "We have covered concepts of decline of Mughals. Now let's look at factual data/events to support concepts."

items.t: 7 · The Jagirdari crisis: why did it hit so hard?
items.x: The Jagirdari crisis was a structural mismatch: supply of Jagirs and demand for them fell dangerously out of balance.  Teacher's board "Jagirdari crisis": like a water crisis (number of people up, water down). What? Number of Mansabdars up (over-recruitment) plus land down. Land is the same in the kingdom, but land shrunk because of territory loss in wars (post 1705, Marathas winning). Why over-recruitment? Role of Aurangzeb 58-07 (declared most lands of Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687 as Khalisa lands, LR to the King, but the Deccani group came in) and post-1707 factionalism (either to be in or to come to power, over-recruitment). Teacher: Water-crisis analogy: number of people up, water down. Jagirdari crisis: number of Mansabdars up + land down. Teacher: What? (1) Over-recruitment (number of Mansabdars rises). (2) Land is the same in the kingdom; land *shrunk* because of loss of territory in wars (post-1705, the Marathas winning). Teacher: Why over-recruitment? (a) Role of Aurangzeb 58-07: he declared most lands of Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687 as Khalisa lands (LR to the King), but the Deccani group came in as Mansabdars. (b) Post-1707 factionalism: *either to be in power or to come to power*, the emperors over-recruited.  Teacher: the Mughal emperor depended on Mansabdars for the army (Jagir given, from the Jagir the Mansabdar maintains the army as per Sawar).  The Jagirdari crisis table: the crisis (many Mansabdars, less land, demand-supply mismatch); the origin (after taking Bijapur 1686 and Golconda 1687, Aurangzeb declared most of their lands Khalisa to be self-sufficient in funding the war against the Marathas); over-recruitment of Mansabdars (later Mughals kept appointing to buy loyalty while land under Mughal control kept shrinking); gross inequality (5 percent of Mansabdars controlled 61 percent of Jagir revenue); luxury inflation (partly from EIC exports).   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    The crisis   High number of Mansabdars but less land for distribution as Jagirs: demand-supply mismatch     The origin   After taking Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687), Aurangzeb 58-07 declared most of their lands Khalisa to be self-sufficient in funding the war vs the Marathas. Mansabdars rose, the Jagir lands did not     Over-recruitment   Later Mughals kept appointing Mansabdars to buy the loyalty of Mansdar groups while land under Mughal control kept shrinking     Gross inequality   5% of Mansabdars controlled 61% of Jagir revenue     Luxury inflation   Inflation in luxury goods (partly from EIC exports of Indian goods) meant many could not sustain an elite life   The consequences  Teacher: "Impact of J crisis = most imp in decline of Mughals." Factionalism (noble vs noble for Jagirs) leads to political instability (emperor of choice to power). Pressure on the emperor leads to a change in tenure of Jagir given to a Mansabdar (so many Naqdi Mansabdars are waiting), insecurity of tenure (kal ho na ho Jagir), which leads to military corruption and, on the other side, to greater and more frequent application of Ijaradari, over-extraction of LR, peasant revolts under the leadership of Zamindars. Military corruption leads to victories for rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) plus an external power (e.g. Nadir Shah), and to loss of territory (State = organisation = rules + territory). Teacher: Impact of the Jagirdari crisis = most important in the decline of the Mughals. (Written as the slide title and circled.)  The downward spiral: frequent transfers (Jagirs shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars); tenure insecurity (kal ho na ho Jagir); ruthless extraction (maximum in minimum time, no incentive to invest in the land); Ijaradari spreads (revenue-farming strips collection from Zamindars, the rural stabilisers); peasant revolts (Zamindar-led revolts; the Jat Kingdom grew from a 1695 revolt under Churaman Jat). Frequent transfers: Jagirs shuffled to satisfy disgruntled Naqdi Mansabdars (warn) Tenure insecurity: no Jagirdar knew how long he would hold the land (kal ho na ho Jagir) (warn) Ruthless extraction: maximum in minimum time; no incentive to invest in the land (bad) Ijaradari spreads: revenue-farming strips collection from Zamindars, the rural stabilisers (bad) Peasant revolts: over-extraction leads to Zamindar-led revolts (Jat Kingdom from the 1695 revolt under Churaman 95-21 Jat) Effect on the peasantry: over-extraction, stagnation, revolts led by alienated Zamindars. Direct example: the Jat Kingdom emerged from a 1695 peasant revolt under Churaman 95-21 Jat, a Zamindar. Meanwhile Mansabdars did not maintain the army as per Sawar, to maximise their earnings, as no one knew when the emperor would transfer the Jagir (*kal ho na ho Jagir*). The teacher ties the military consequences together: military corruption → victories for rebel states (Sikh, Marathas, Afghans) + an external power (Nadir Shah) → loss of territory.

Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 (Noble vs Noble): Turani + Irani defeat the Sayyids; Wazir 1722-24, quits Delhi for Hyderabad (1724; leaves for good 1740).  Handout Diagram 2: Factionalism and succession turmoil 1707-1724, Aurangzeb dies 1707 (no succession rule), Jahandar Shah, Farukhsiyar, Sayyid Brothers, Muhammad Shah installed as puppet (1719), Nizam-ul-Mulk with the Irani group defeats the Sayyids and exits to Hyderabad in 1740. Farukhsiyar (with the Sayyids) removed and executed Jahandar Shah 12-13.   Jahandar Shah 12-13   Back the right claimant, extract the reward     Royal vs Noble   Farukhsiyar rose with the Sayyid Brothers (Abdullah Khan became Wazir; Hussain Ali Khan became Mir Bakshi).
