items.t: 1 · Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80: who he was and why he rose
items.x: Shivaji 74-80, who he was: born 19 February 1630 to Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai; father a Jagirdar of Poona and a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur (Adil Shahi, 1489-1686); training by Dadaji Kondadev; inspiration from his mother Jijabai; first fort at 16 (1646); worked from the Maval region (Sahyadri), hilly and forested, with local warriors and peasants. Teacher's ink: sketch of the Deccan funnel with Golconda, Bijapur, Goa; the two issues (oppressive land revenue, discriminatory religious policy); guerrilla warfare. 1.1 Who he was Shivaji 74-80 Bhonsle was born on 19 February 1630 to Shahji Bhonsle and Jijabai. His father was a Jagirdar of Poona and served as a General and Mansabdar in Bijapur (1489-1686), ruled by the Adil Shahi dynasty. This dynasty, together with the Qutub Shahi (1518-1687), had replaced the Bahmani Sultanate (1347-1527) in the Deccan. Early training came from his guardian Dadaji Kondadev, who shaped him as a soldier and administrator. The deeper inspiration came from his mother Jijabai and his own fierce ambition. He captured his first fort at the age of 16, in 1646. Working from the Maval region, a hilly, forested terrain in today's Pune district running through the Sahyadri range, he gathered an army of local warriors and peasants. 1.2 Guerrilla warfare: the teacher's boards Teacher: Tactics = guerrilla warfare: hide and seek, attack and withdraw, sabotage. It is not traditional warfare. It uses surprise attacks, speed and geography, and creates shock and awe in the enemy. It is the only way to defeat a much more militarily stronger opponent.  Teacher's board: guerrilla is a tool that can serve positive, neutral or negative goals. Examples written: Naxals in India; Spain (1808-12) against Napoleon; the 1857 Revolt with Kunwar Singh and Tatya Tope; the Ganimi Kava of the Marathas; Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-24, underlined). Teacher: Guerrilla warfare is a tool used for positive, neutral or negative goals. Examples on the board: Naxals in India; Spain (1808-12) against Napoleon; 1857 Revolt (Kunwar Singh and Tatya Tope); Ganimi Kava of the Marathas; Alluri Sitarama Raju (1922-24). 1.3 Why he rose against Bijapur and the Mughals  Shivaji versus Bijapur and the Mughals. Bijapur: from 1657 attacks on the oppressive Adil Shahis; in 1659 killed General Afzal Khan with Bagh Nakh and Bichhwa. Mughals: 1663 defeated Shaista Khan and sacked Surat, enraging Aurangzeb 58-07, who sent Jai Singh; his 1665 siege of Fort Purandhar led to a temporary compromise. Teacher's ink: triangle Aurangzeb, Marathas, Bijapur; Marathas' goal Swarajya (boxed); 1674 coronation of C. Shivaji; 1686 Aurangzeb annexes Bijapur; BG Tilak (1890s). From 1657 onwards, Shivaji 74-80 launched systematic attacks on the Kingdom of Bijapur (1489-1686), which followed economically oppressive and religiously discriminatory policies. This was also the period when Aurangzeb 58-07 became Mughal emperor. In 1659, Ali Adil Shah II, Sultan of Bijapur, sent his General Afzal Khan to kill Shivaji 74-80 under the pretext of negotiations. Instead, Shivaji 74-80 killed the seven-feet-tall Afzal Khan using his concealed Bagh Nakh (Tiger Claws) and a Bichhwa (dagger). When Aurangzeb 58-07 launched his campaign for the conquest of the Deccan, Shivaji 74-80 defeated the Mughal General Shaista Khan 64-88 in 1663 and sacked the wealthy port of Surat, which enraged Aurangzeb 58-07. Aurangzeb 58-07 sent General Jai Singh 99-43, who used an encirclement strategy to cut off supplies to Maratha territories. In 1665 Jai Singh 99-43 laid siege to Fort Purandhar (40-50 km southeast of Pune). Teacher: BG Tilak (1890s) used this cultural history (a Maratha against a Mughal general) to arouse nationalism against the British. Teacher: Triangle on the board: Aurangzeb 58-07, the Marathas and Bijapur. The Marathas' goal is Swarajya (boxed). 1674 = coronation of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80; 1686 = Aurangzeb 58-07 annexes Bijapur.  Fort Purandhar (model photo). Teacher's ink: Gherao means starve the enemy; the 1665 siege by Jai Singh, a powerful Hindu Mansabdar of the Mughal State; result: Treaty of Purandhar 1665. Terms: accepts Mughal as emperor, accepts to be Mansabdar (son Sambhaji sent as Mansabdar), alliance against Bijapur (which lasted till 1686). On the left: the standard-book statement that Shivaji never accepted Mughal sovereignty; teacher: Purandhar 1665 was a temporary tactic.  Handout picture for Fort Purandhar, where Jai Singh's 1665 siege forced Shivaji to terms. Teacher: Gherao = starve the enemy. Jai Singh 99-43 was a powerful Mansabdar of the Hindu group of the Mughal State. The standard books say Shivaji 74-80 never accepted Mughal sovereignty; the teacher's correction: the Treaty of Purandhar 1665 was a temporary tactic. 1.4 Treaty of Purandhar 1665: a tactical pause, not a permanent defeat To prevent the massacre of his soldiers and people, Shivaji 74-80 negotiated the Treaty of Purandhar (1665). Under its terms: He surrendered 23 of his 35 forts to the Mughals. He accepted Aurangzeb 58-07 as Emperor but declined a personal mansab for himself. His son Sambhaji 80-89 was made a Mughal Mansabdar with a rank of 5,000. He agreed to support the Mughals in their war against Bijapur.  Treaty of Purandhar (1665) and Svarajya. Tactical pause: 23 of 35 forts surrendered; Aurangzeb accepted as emperor but no personal mansab; Sambhaji a Mansabdar of 5,000; help against Bijapur. Agra 1666: Shivaji and Sambhaji insulted and imprisoned; legendary escape disguised as Sadhus smeared in ash via Mathura. Svarajya 1674: coronated Chhatrapati at Raigarh, legally independent of the Mughals; kingdom Svarajya (own rule) covered the Marathi region; died naturally 1680. Teacher's ink: treaties are named after the place where signed; the coronation is a legal reversal of Purandhar; Jat kingdom, Svarajya and the Sikh state share the feature of mass participation. In 1666, Shivaji 74-80 and Sambhaji 80-89 visited the Mughal court at Agra. They were insulted and imprisoned. Their escape became legendary: disguised as Sadhus with bodies smeared in ash, they went to Mathura. Shivaji 74-80 left Sambhaji 80-89 there with a Brahmin family and took a long route back to his capital. Aurangzeb 58-07 marched to the Deccan in 1681, when his own son Prince Akbar 56-05 defected to Chhatrapati Sambhaji 80-89. Teacher: Treaties are named after the place where they were signed. The coronation = the legal reversal of the Treaty of Purandhar, giving a fully independent kingdom. Common feature of the Jat kingdom, Svarajya and the Sikh state: the result of people / mass participation (the Jat kingdom = the result of peasant revolts). After the escape, the teacher's ink reads: rebellion resumes. 1.5 The 1674 coronation at Raigarh: Svarajya  Raigarh Fort photo collage, site of the 1674 coronation. Teacher's ink on Vatan rights (Mughal): Vatan means hereditary; Vatan rights include getting the LR of a Jagir (a Vatan Jagir), collecting LR and being paid a commission (Zamindar), holding a job such as Qanungo maintaining land records, and Khudkasht cultivating a plot. In 1674, Shivaji 74-80 was coronated at Raigarh as Chhatrapati, legally declaring himself independent from the Mughals. His kingdom, called Svarajya ("own rule"), covered the Marathi-speaking region. (The handout's heading places the headquarters at Satara; see the capital note in section 8.) The Maratha kingdom had thus been founded in the second half of the 17th century, built through wars against both Bijapur and Aurangzeb 58-07. Shivaji 74-80 died of natural causes in 1680. Teacher: Vatan = hereditary. In Mughal terms, a Vatan right could mean: getting the LR of a Jagir (a Vatan Jagir); collecting LR and being paid a commission (the Zamindar); a job such as Qanungo (maintaining land records); or Khudkasht cultivation of a plot.

items.t: 2 · Military tactics: army, Jagirs, navy and forts
items.x: 2.1 The army: light cavalry and guerrilla warfare  Maratha army and the Saranjami system. Army: 30,000-40,000 cavalry; guerrilla in hills and forests; captured 240 forts; light cavalry for speed against the Mughals' heavy cavalry and elephants. Saranjami: Shivaji paid officers in cash and gave no Jagirs (a centralised polity); Shahu 19-49 later gave Tankha Jagirs to commanders (Saranjams) but never Vatan. Saranjam = Tankha Jagir of military men, temporary, tied to service, NOT heritable; Vatan = hereditary right of civil officials (Patils, Deshmukhs). Teacher's ink: heavy cavalry = elephants plus horses carrying supplies, slow; light cavalry = horses, food and shelter on the way (love or force), speed is the focus of guerrilla warfare; Saranjam will be taken away if not in service. Shivaji 74-80 built a well-organised army of around 30,000 to 40,000 cavalry. He used the mountainous terrain and dense forests to master guerrilla warfare and captured 240 forts, many of them in the Konkan. Their strategy was built on surprise (shock and awe) combined with guerrilla tactics. The major fighting force was a horse-mounted army with light cavalry for faster movement, in sharp contrast to the Mughals, who relied on heavy cavalry (elephants carrying a support system like food). Teacher: Heavy cavalry = elephants plus horses, carrying supplies, slow to move. Light cavalry = horses only; food and shelter on the way (by love or force). Speed = the focus for guerrilla warfare. 2.2 The Saranjami system: military land grants  Teacher's board on Jagirs: transferable = Tankha Jagirs; non-transferable or hereditary = Vatan Jagirs. Shivaji 74-80 never gave a Jagir (all mansabdars were Naqdi, paid in cash). Shahu 19-49 never gave Vatan Jagirs but gave Tankha Jagirs (TJ = Saranjam). Land is the source of power, so whoever controls land and its resources is more powerful; hence greater concentration of power in Shivaji 74-80. Unlike the Mughals, Maratha civil officials did not hold military roles. Shivaji 74-80 never gave Jagirs and paid officials in cash, leading to a centralised polity. Later Chhatrapati Shahu 19-49 gave Tankha Jagirs to military commanders called Saranjams, but never Vatan Jagirs. This prevented military loyalty from getting tied to hereditary land grants and gave the ruler more control. Under this system revenue assignments on Jagirs were given to the Maratha Sardars, the Peshwa (Prime Minister of the Chhatrapati) and various military commanders, each drawing income from designated territories to maintain troops and administration. This led to a fragmented polity as revenue and military power were dispersed rather than centralised.   Land grant   Held by   Nature    --- --- ---    Saranjam (a Tankha Jagir)   Military commanders   Temporary, tied to service, NOT heritable     Vatan / Watan   Civil officials such as Patils (village head) and Deshmukhs (revenue collectors like Zamindars)   A hereditary right, passed within the family   Teacher: Land = the source of power. Whoever controls land and its resources is more powerful, therefore there was greater concentration of power in Shivaji 74-80. A Saranjam will be taken away if not in service. 2.3 The navy: Father of the Modern Indian Navy  Navy: Shivaji as Father of the Modern Indian Navy. Scale: 20 ships (1657), full navy of 200 (1664), overall peak of the Maratha Empire 700 ships. Doctrine: not deep-ocean war but asymmetric coastal defence to protect merchant ships, secure the Konkan and block European powers. Indigenous: local human resources, engineering and strategy; Kolis and Bhandaris; commanders Mayanak Bhandari and Daulat Khan. French link 1668: French factory at Rajapur in return for European cannons, lead and saltpetre. Teacher's ink: Modern boxed; comparable in tech and strength to European navies; goal is protecting the coastline with forts in coastal areas, forts on islands and an intelligence network of fishermen; Desi = indigenous tech, HR, tactics; enemy's enemy is a friend (British = common enemy). Shivaji 74-80 established a naval force of 20 ships in 1657, a full navy of 200 ships by 1664, and the peak Maratha navy reached 700 ships. His doctrine was not about matching the British or Portuguese in deep-ocean warfare. It was a specialised, asymmetric coastal defence strategy designed to: Protect Maratha merchant ships. Secure the Konkan coastline from the Siddis of Janjira. Prevent European powers from dominating Konkan trade routes. He built forts in coastal areas, established naval bases in the Arabian Sea, and focused on intelligence gathering at sea. In 1668 Shivaji 74-80 allowed the French to establish a trading factory at Rajapur. In return he secured high-quality military supplies: European cannons, lead and saltpetre for gunpowder. He is called the Father of the Modern Indian Navy because he relied entirely on indigenous human resources, engineering and strategy, never on European naval architects or shipbuilders. He recruited from local coastal communities, the Kolis and Bhandaris, master seafarers who knew the tides, hidden rocks and shallow creeks of the Konkan. He appointed commanders like Mayanak Bhandari and Daulat Khan. Teacher: Saltpetre = potassium nitrate, used in gunpowder. Desi = indigenous tech, human resources, tactics. "Enemy's enemy = friend": the British were the common enemy. The Maratha navy was comparable in tech and strength to the European navies (the teacher's "modern" box). 2.4 The fleet: tactical ship design  Teacher's board: Konkan coast, Goa and Malabar coast funnel sketch; islands with F (fort) and arrows; patrol = Jaladurg (underlined); a row of forts along the coast.  Teacher's board: land coast and shallow waters serve as hiding places (a small Maratha boat against a British ship); Navy serves Merchant and Military. A key insight was tactical ship design. Copying the massive deep-water (blue water) ships of the Europeans would have been a strategic disaster in the shallow estuaries of the Konkan coast. Instead he built a lighter, faster fleet for coastal defence and hit-and-run:   Vessel   Role    --- ---    Ghurabs   Gunboats carrying heavy artillery     Galbats   Fast, highly manoeuvrable rowboats with light sails that could tow the Ghurabs into position during dead winds or chase fleeing enemy ships     Shibars and Pals   Larger vessels for transport and heavier engagements   To ensure self-reliance, Shivaji 74-80 set up shipbuilding yards, sourcing timber from the teak forests of the Sahyadri. 2.5 The forts: the Jaladurg doctrine  Fleet, sea-forts and the coast. Tactical ship design (Ghurabs, Galbats, Shibars and Pals; shipyards used Sahyadri teak). Jaladurg doctrine: sea-forts on rocky islands or peninsulas guarded docked ships (ink: parked); coastal cannons kept enemies at bay, for example Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Suvarnadurg. On the coast: fear of the Marathas forced the EIC to shift its western HQ from Surat to Bombay (Bombay Presidency, 1687); Marathas took ports from the Portuguese (1736) and held Salsette and Bassein by 1739. Teacher's ink: 1668 EIC in Bombay; Presidency = HQ; 1687 Bombay Presidency; Bombay = a group of 7 islands; British navy strong; goods better protected; Surat = fear of cavalry. A Ghurab sketch with Galbats towing. His greatest strategic innovation was the Jaladurg doctrine: sea forts on rocky islands or peninsulas along the coast. They provided security to docked vessels, and cannons in these forts and along the coast kept enemy ships at a distance. Key examples: Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg and Suvarnadurg. In Gujarat the EIC so feared the Marathas that they made Bombay their main base for trade, leading to the Bombay Presidency in 1687. The Marathas actively captured ports from the Portuguese: in 1736 they removed the Portuguese and Ethiopian Muslims from the Konkan coast, and by 1739 effectively controlled Salsette and Bassein. Teacher: 1668: EIC already in Bombay. 1687: Bombay becomes the Presidency (HQ). Bombay = a group of seven islands. Reasons to shift from Surat: British navy strong, goods better protected at Bombay; at Surat there was fear of (Maratha) cavalry.  Teacher's board: Britain became the No. 1 naval power. China: chaos, kingdom wars and plunder, so goods go through Hong Kong (British) ringed by navy; India: goods go through Bombay (British).  Map: Maratha Military Landscapes of India, 12 UNESCO Heritage Forts: Lohagad, Khanderi Fort, Raigad, Suvarnadurg, Vijaydurg, Sindhudurg, Salher Fort, Shivneri Fort, Rajgad, Pratapgad, Panhala Fort and Gingee Fort (UNESCO World Heritage Site #1739).  Handout map of the 12 UNESCO Heritage Forts of the Maratha military landscapes.  Sindhudurg Fort, the island sea-fort on the Konkan coast built by Shivaji under the Jaladurg doctrine. 2.6 After Shivaji 74-80: Admiral Kanhoji Angre  After Shivaji, Admiral Kanhoji Angre (at Shahu 19-49): the Shivaji of the Seas dominated the Arabian Sea for about 30 years in the early 1700s until his death in 1729; fought British, Portuguese, Dutch, Sawants and Siddis. Against the EIC, 1714-24 raids on Bombay: small fast Maratha ships beat heavy British vessels in shallow waters, a stalemate. The British defeated the Maratha navy by 1756, one year before Plassey (1757). Teacher's ink: Sawants = small Indian kingdom; Siddis = Africans; a wave sketch with Shivaji's peak and Kanhoji's peak in naval power; monsoon sketch. After Shivaji 74-80 the dominant naval figure was Admiral Kanhoji Angre, called the "Shivaji 74-80 of the Seas", who dominated the Arabian Sea for 30 years in the early 1700s until his death in 1729. Kanhoji fought the British, Portuguese, Dutch, the Sawants (a small kingdom since 1627) and the Siddis or Habshis (people of African ancestry, now found in Gujarat, Karnataka, Andhra and parts of Sindh and Baluchistan in Pakistan). From 1714 to 1724 he frequently attacked the EIC in Bombay with guerrilla warfare at sea. The bigger, heavier British ships could not pursue the small, fast Maratha vessels in shallow waters. The result was a stalemate, and Kanhoji eventually offered peace to the British. The British defeated the Maratha Navy in 1756, one year before the EIC defeated the Bengal Suba at Plassey (1757).

items.t: 3 · Sambhaji 80-89 and Rajaram 89-00: the troubled succession
items.x: Chhatrapati means Emperor. Shivaji 74-80 was the first Chhatrapati, ruling from 1674 until his death from natural causes in 1680. After him, his elder son Sambhaji 80-89 took charge. He was captured by Aurangzeb 58-07 and, after weeks of torture, was assassinated in 1689. The younger son Rajaram 89-00 then took over but died of tuberculosis in 1700 at just 30 years of age. With no adult male heir ready, Rajaram 89-00's widow Tarabai stepped in. She ruled as regent in the name of their infant son Shivaji II. This held until 1707, when the Mughals released Shahu 19-49, the elder son of Sambhaji 80-89, who had been in Mughal imprisonment. Shahu 19-49's release triggered a civil war between Shahu 19-49 and Tarabai that lasted until 1719 (section 6).  The Chhatrapati succession chain: Shivaji 74-80, first Chhatrapati, died naturally 1680); Sambhaji 1680-89 (captured and assassinated by Aurangzeb after torture); Rajaram 1689-1700 (Shivaji's younger son, died of TB); Tarabai, regent for the infant Shivaji II, 1700-07, then a succession dispute leading to civil war 1707-19; Shahu 1719-49 (released by the Mughals in 1707, won by 1719, the last strong Chhatrapati).  Handout Diagram 1: the Chhatrapati succession chain. Shivaji (1674-80), Sambhaji (elder son, killed by Aurangzeb 1689), Rajaram (younger son, died of TB 1700), Tarabai regent for the infant Shivaji II until 1707, Shahu (released 1707, civil war 1707-19), Treaty of Warna 1731 splitting into Satara and Kolhapur lines, Ramraja/Rajaram II (1749-77, ceremonial head after Sangola 1750), Shahaji (last Satara Chhatrapati, 1848 EIC annexes Satara).  Teacher's board: the family tree. Shivaji 74-80 leads to Sambhaji 80-89 and Rajaram 89-00. Sambhaji's son Shahu 19-49 was released from prison by the Mughals in 1707, which caused the civil war (1707-19) of Shahu versus Tarabai; Shahu's adopted son Ramraja (1749+). Rajaram's son Shivaji II (infant) with his regent widow Tarabai, and Sambhaji II, the son from his second wife. Ink: Regent = rules in the name of the king because the king cannot rule (age, health); war is internal (civil war) or external. Teacher: Regent = rules in the name of the king, because the king cannot rule (age, health). A war is either internal (civil war) or external.

items.t: 4 · The Ashtapradhan and Maratha administration
items.x: 4.1 The Chhatrapati was not an absolute ruler The Chhatrapati governed with a council of eight ministers, the Ashtapradhan. This was similar in concept to the British Monarch and his Privy Council, or the Mughal Emperor and his Darbar. Separation of powers (a separate legislature, executive, judiciary) is a modern concept. The Ashtapradhan was simply a council of ministers serving the Chhatrapati. 4.2 The eight ministers  Ashtapradhan table: Peshwa = Prime Minister (right hand of the Chhatrapati); Amatya = Finance; Sachiv = Correspondence; Sumanta = Foreign Affairs; Senapati = Military Commander; Panditrao = Religious Affairs; Nyayadhish = Justice; Waqenavis = Intelligence. Teacher's ink: like a British monarch with a Privy Council (had ministers), while the Mughal had a Darbar of Mansabdars (Irani, Turani, Hindu, Deccani and so on); today: PM plus Council of Ministers.   Post   Portfolio    --- ---    Peshwa   Prime Minister (the right hand of the Chhatrapati)     Amatya   Finance     Sachiv   Correspondence     Sumanta   Foreign Affairs     Senapati   Military Commander     Panditrao   Religious Affairs     Nyayadhish   Justice     Waqenavis   Intelligence   Teacher: The Chhatrapati was like a British monarch with a Privy Council (he had ministers), while the Mughal emperor had a Darbar of Mansabdars (Irani, Turani, Hindu, Deccani and others). Today = Prime Minister plus Council of Ministers. 4.3 The Peshwa's own council: Darakhdars and the Barbhai Mandal  Teacher's board: Chhatrapati, then the Ashtapradhan of 8 ministers (one is the Peshwa, the PM), then the ministers of the Peshwa = Darakhdars. After Shahu 19-49 a weak Chhatrapati meant power shifted downwards to the Peshwa. Parallel: British Monarch, then Privy Council (one was the PM), then Council of Ministers: power shifted from the monarch to the PM and his Council; democracy weakened the monarchy.  Maratha administration table. Chhatrapati with Ashtapradhan. Peshwa's council: Darakhdars; in 1774 twelve formed the Barbhai Mandal under Nana Fadnavis; Hazur Daftar secretariat at Poona with about 200 staff. Provinces (Sarkars): each under a Governor, the office auctioned; dual reporting lets the Peshwa cross-check. Villages: self-contained under a Patil; Kulkarnis kept accounts; Deshmukhs collected LR and kept a 10% commission; all with Vatan rights. Ink: Mughal terminology, Sarkar = District; the Governor got a share of LR during his term, recovering the auction cost plus profit. Just as the British PM had his own Council of Ministers beneath the monarch, the Peshwa had his own council of senior civil servants, the Darakhdars. In 1774, twelve of these powerful men came together under Nana Fadnavis to form the Council of Twelve Ministers, the Barbhai Mandal. The Peshwa's secretariat at Poona was the Hazur Daftar. Around 200 people worked there; all records important for governance, including financial records, were kept there. Teacher: Barbhai = "12 Bros" ("Bar" underlined on the board). Power drifted downwards: as the Chhatrapati weakened after Shahu 19-49, it moved to the Peshwa, exactly like the British monarch's power moving to the PM and Council of Ministers as democracy grew. 4.4 Provincial and village administration Within Svarajya the territory was divided into Sarkars (provinces), each under a Governor. Notably, the office of Governor was auctioned. There were checks: many hereditary officers had dual reporting lines, to the Governor and directly to the Peshwa. The Governor's accounts submitted to the Peshwa were tallied against those submitted independently by the Deshmukhi directly to the Peshwa. This cross-checking prevented Governors from manipulating revenue figures. At the lowest level villages functioned as self-contained units. Each was under a Patil, who held all powers (financial, executive, judicial) including revenue collection, and reported directly to the Peshwa. Village accounts were kept by Kulkarnis. Both Patils and Deshmukhi (revenue collectors) held heritable Vatan rights. Teacher: Note the Mughal terminology: a Sarkar = a District. The Governor got a share of LR during his term, so he recovers what he paid in the auction and makes some profit. Deshmukhs collected LR and kept a 10% commission. 4.5 The judicial system  Justice and revenue. Panch at the village up to the Peshwa in Svarajya and the Maratha Sardar in Samrajya; law = Dharma Shastras (Hindu law); a real rule of law, even top authorities were jailed for violations. Revenue: LR primary; proper field surveys for assessment (like MQK 17-27 in Bengal); plus customs and octroi, judicial Nazrana and Jurmana, permit and licence fees. Ink: octroi = taxes on local or domestic trade, customs = international trade. Pro-peasant: dams, canals, low-interest loans; Deshmukhs and Patils kept in check. Sketch: river, canal, agricultural fields. In Svarajya the final judicial decision rested with the Peshwa; in Samrajya, with the respective Maratha Sardar. There was a hierarchy of courts from the Panch at the village level up to the Peshwa. The Peshwa, as far as possible, respected the decisions of the Panchs. The law used was from the Dharma Shastras. The policing was as efficient as the London Police of that era, with a very good information network. Crucially there was a rule of law: even the highest authorities could be and were imprisoned for violations. 4.6 Sources of revenue Land revenue was the primary source, fixed on the basis of the quality of soil, irrigation facilities and the crop sown. Beyond this: (1) customs duty and octroi on trade; (2) judicial proceeds: Nazrana paid by the winning party and Jurmana paid by the losing party; (3) fees from permits and licences for cutting wood, manufacturing drugs and private minting of coins. To support peasants, dams and canals were built and loans given at low interest. The Deshmukhi and Patils were kept under check so they would not oppress the peasantry.  Teacher's board: Canals serve transport (for example the Suez Canal) and irrigation. Teacher: Octroi = taxes on local / domestic trade; customs = international trade. The Maratha LR assessment used proper field surveys, like MQK's in Bengal (1717-27) (see Chapter 3). Canals serve two purposes: transport (e.g. the Suez Canal) and irrigation.

items.t: 5 · Shahu 19-49's release (1707): was the Mughal "pacifist policy" really pacifist?
items.x: Was the Mughal pacifist policy really pacifist? Claim: after Aurangzeb the Mughals turned pacifist to Sikhs and Marathas (Shahu released 1707). Reality: pragmatic real-politik, reconciliation plus opportunism plus divide-and-rule; nominal pacifism with deniability for hostile acts by Mughal Governors. Sikh example: 1707 Bahadur Shah 07-12 gave Guru Gobind Singh (1676-08) a high mansab and promised Anandpur, yet Wazir Khan (Faujdar of Sirhind) had him assassinated in 1708 at Nanded (Maharashtra); no action; Anandpur never handed over. Maratha example: Shahu was released but attacks did not stop; the Mughals exploited the Shahu-Tarabai civil war. Ink: better relations with rivals, the Maratha civil war of 1707-19, the enemy weakened from within. After the death of Aurangzeb 58-07 it is often said the Mughals adopted a pacifist policy towards adversaries, including the Sikhs and Marathas, the policy under which Shahu 19-49 was released in 1707. This is a flawed interpretation. What emerged was pragmatic real-politik: reconciliation plus opportunism plus divide-and-rule. The Mughals were weakened and relied more on diplomacy, but the diplomacy included conspiracies and manipulation. It was nominal pacifism with plausible deniability for hostile acts by Mughal Governors. The Sikh case (1707-08): in 1707 Bahadur Shah (1707-12) granted Guru Gobind Singh 76-08 a high Mansab and promised him Anandpur. Very soon after, the Faujdar of Sirhind, Wazir Khan, had the Guru assassinated in 1708 at Nanded, Maharashtra, where the Guru had accompanied Bahadur Shah. No action was taken against Wazir Khan and Anandpur was never handed over. Note from the handout: Sirhind was a Sarkar (a district) within the Lahore Suba, and a Faujdar held military, judicial and land-revenue functions over a district. He was not a Governor, as some books incorrectly describe him, though Wazir Khan had much greater influence than a typical Faujdar. The Maratha case (1707 onwards): Shahu 19-49's release was a gesture of reconciliation, yet the Mughals did not stop attacking the Marathas, and his release triggered a civil war with Tarabai. The Mughals encouraged divided loyalties among Maratha Sardars and Deshmukhs, who kept switching sides between Shahu 19-49, Tarabai and the Mughals. This was shrewd diplomacy, not pacifism. Teacher: Why release Shahu 19-49? To keep better relations with a rival, and because a Maratha civil war (1707-19) would weaken the enemy from within.

items.t: 6 · Tarabai and the Maratha civil war (1707-1719)
items.x: Tarabai and the civil war. Tarabai regent for the infant Shivaji II since 1700; the 1707 release of Shahu under the Mughal pacifist policy triggered a civil war to 1719 (Sardars and Deshmukhs switched sides, Mughals continued to attack); Shahu won by 1719. Treaty of Warna 1731: Shahu gave Kolhapur to Sambhaji II, making two Chhatrapati lines (Shahu's at Satara, Sambhaji II's at Kolhapur). After Shahu: Ramraja (Rajaram II, 1749-77); the Chhatrapatis became ceremonial; the Satara line ended 1848 (EIC annexation); Kolhapur survived as a Princely State until 1947. Ink: Sambhaji II = son of Rajaram 89-00 from his second wife.  Teacher's tree: Shivaji leads to Sambhaji 80-89, whose son Shahu 19-49 was released in 1707 and fought the civil war of 1707-19 against Tarabai; Rajaram 89-00 leads to Shivaji II with the regent Tarabai (1700-19). 6.1 Why the civil war broke out After Rajaram 89-00's death from TB in 1700, Tarabai stepped in as regent for infant Shivaji II. This arrangement held the Maratha state together for seven years. In 1707 the Mughals released Shahu 19-49, the elder son of Sambhaji 80-89. This triggered a civil war between Shahu 19-49 and Tarabai that lasted till 1719. Sardars and Deshmukhs kept switching sides between Shahu 19-49, Tarabai and the Mughals, which the Mughals deliberately encouraged. Teacher: By 1705 the Marathas had begun winning against the Mughals, and the credit goes to Tarabai (1700+). 6.2 Treaty of Warna 1731: the family settlement The dispute was finally settled by the Treaty of Warna (1731). Shahu 19-49 gave Kolhapur to Sambhaji II, the son of Rajaram 89-00 from his second wife Rajasbai, who had taken control from Shivaji II around 1714. From this point there were two Chhatrapati dynasties: Shahu 19-49's line at Satara and Sambhaji II's line at Kolhapur. 6.3 After Shahu 19-49: the Chhatrapati becomes ceremonial After Shahu 19-49 his adopted son Ramraja (Rajaram II) ruled 1749-77. From here the Chhatrapatis became largely ceremonial, like a powerless President. Real power had moved to the Peshwa (section 8). The last Chhatrapati of the Satara line was Shahaji (1839-48), when the EIC annexed Satara. Kolhapur survived much longer, as a Princely State from 1858 until its merger into India in 1947.

items.t: 7 · Why Shahu 19-49 won, and who the Maratha Sardars were
items.x: Teacher's board: reasons for victory in any war: technology, leadership, tactics, geography, money, number of soldiers or size of army (alliance), military infrastructure (forts). Teacher: Reasons for victory in any war: technology, leadership, tactics, geography, money, number of soldiers / size of army (alliances), military infrastructure (forts). Use this checklist on any war question.  Why Shahu won and the four Sardars: the 6th Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath (1713-20) won him the Brahmin banking families and the new Sardars, and turned Admiral Kanhoji Angre from Tarabai to Shahu in 1714. Four kingmaker Sardars: Gaikwad to Baroda, Holkar to Indore, Scindia (Shinde) to Gwalior, Bhonsle to Nagpur. Shape: five provinces (Peshwa plus four Sardars) with the Chhatrapati as head of state; by 1750 a Confederation (weak centre, strong provinces). 7.1 Why Shahu 19-49 prevailed A critical reason was the sixth Peshwa, Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, a highly able leader who won for Shahu 19-49: The support of powerful Brahmin banking families. The support of the new independent Maratha Sardars (who emerged precisely in this period). Telling example: during the civil war Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 convinced Admiral Kanhoji Angre to switch from Tarabai to Shahu 19-49 in 1714. Without Kanhoji's coastal and naval power, Shahu 19-49's victory would have been far harder. 7.2 Who were the Maratha Sardars?  Teacher's board: Local chief = Shivalik hill chiefs = Misl chiefs = Bundela chiefs = Rajput chiefs = Maratha Sardars = Poligars. A local chief is a mini king with his own private army, dominating the polity and wealth of a small region, with his own fort. Today the negative examples are Bahubali and Kaleen Bhaiya of Mirzapur. Right: it is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality. Every first king began as a local chief, e.g. Maharaja Ranjit Singh 01-39 was chief of the Sukerchakia misl. Many strong Maratha Sardars emerged as kings: Holkar, Bhonsle, Scindia, Gaikwad. The Maratha Sardars were local chiefs, essentially mini-kings, who held their own armies and forts and dominated smaller territories. Post-1719 some expanded dramatically to a king-like status. Each is a "mini mini king" with a private army, dominating the politics and wealth of a small area, with his own fort. (Today's negative version: Bahubali; Kaleen Bhaiya of Mirzapur.) It is in the nature of power to centralise in a strong personality. Every first king began as a local chief, e.g. Maharaja Ranjit Singh 01-39, chief of the Sukerchakia misl. Many strong Maratha Sardars emerged as kings: Holkar, Bhonsle, Scindia, Gaikwad. The Maratha Empire can be visualised as five provinces (Peshwa plus four Sardars as rulers) with the Chhatrapati as head of state. Treaty of Sangola 1750 between Peshwa and Chhatrapati: all powers of the Chhatrapati given to the Peshwa, so the Chhatrapati is symbolic.

items.t: 8 · Svarajya and Samrajya, Chauth and Sardeshmukhi, the Peshwa as the real authority
items.x: 8.1 Svarajya versus Samrajya  Svarajya vs Samrajya table. Territory: the original kingdom inside Maharashtra versus lands outside Maharashtra (from 1719). Ruled by: the Chhatrapati or Peshwa directly versus the Maratha Sardars in their own right. Capital or HQ: Raigarh to Jinji to Satara, Peshwa at Poona, versus varies by Sardar. Character: culturally homogeneous and governed versus real administration only in parts (Gujarat, Khandesh, Malwa), elsewhere mainly Chauth and Sardeshmukhi collection.   Axis   Svarajya   Samrajya    --- --- ---    Territory   The original kingdom inside Maharashtra   Lands outside Maharashtra (from 1719)     Ruled by   The Chhatrapati / Peshwa, directly   The Maratha Sardars, in their own right     Capital / HQ   Raigarh, then Jinji, then Satara; Peshwa at Poona   Varies by Sardar     Character   Culturally homogeneous and governed   Real administration only in parts (Gujarat, Khandesh, Malwa); elsewhere mainly Chauth / Sardeshmukhi collection    The same table repeated in Lecture 7, with the teacher's ink: Shivaji 74-80 with an arrow to Raigarh; Rajaram 89-00 to Jinji; Shahu 19-49 to Satara; next to Varies by Sardar: Baroda, Nagpur, Gwalior, Indore. Chauth underlined with the note: until annexed, but not thereafter. On the right: the Maratha Sardars conquered this (Samrajya) majorly with their own resources and efforts, autonomous from the beginning but within the Maratha empire. Jinji/Ginjee (Carnatic) is an important fort; after Sambhaji 80-89 the Marathas under Rajaram 89-00 set up their capital here. Svarajya: the original Maratha kingdom established by Shivaji 74-80, capital Raigarh (1647-1689); then conquered by Aurangzeb 58-07, so capital = Jinji (1689-1698); capital = Satara under Rajaram 89-00 (as the handout prints it), with the Peshwa's headquarters at Poona. It was the territory within Maharashtra, under direct rule, and culturally homogeneous. Samrajya: the territory outside Maharashtra, ruled by the Confederate chiefs (the Maratha Sardars); administration varied from one Sardar to another. Effective administration existed only in parts of Samrajya, notably Gujarat, Khandesh and Malwa. Elsewhere the primary concern was not governance but collection of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. From 1719 onwards the territories added beyond the original Svarajya were called Samrajya, governed not by the Chhatrapati but by the Sardars who held power in their own right. Flag on the capital: the handout's section 1.4 says Svarajya's headquarters was Satara, while section 8.1 (and the teacher's boards) trace it as Raigarh, then Jinji (1689-98), then Satara. The handout adds "Capital = Satara by Rajaram 89-00" while the teacher's ink on the slide ties Jinji to Rajaram 89-00 and Satara to Shahu 19-49. Use the teacher's chain Raigarh, Jinji, Satara for answers. Teacher: Jinji / Ginjee (in the Carnatic) = an important fort. After Sambhaji 80-89 the Marathas under Rajaram 89-00 set up their capital there. The Sardars conquered Samrajya largely with their own resources and efforts: autonomous from the beginning, but within the Maratha empire. 8.2 Chauth: one-fourth, externally collected  Chauth and Sardeshmukhi table. Rate: one-fourth (25%) of revenue versus an extra 10% of land revenue. Who and why: paid by a protected state for military protection versus Deshmukhs collect it from ryots and deposit it to the Chhatrapati. Scope: external only versus internal and external. Meaning: a tool of empire-building (weaken a state, then annex it) versus a symbol of recognising the Chhatrapati's authority (Shivaji 74-80 was Sardeshmukh). Division: Chhatrapati- or Peshwa-collected goes wholly to Svarajya; Sardar-collected (external) is two-thirds kept, one-third sent to Svarajya. Both Chauth and Sardeshmukhi were tribute systems that existed even before the Marathas. Chauth = one-fourth (25%) of the revenue paid by a protected state to the Marathas in exchange for military protection. It was also a deliberate tool of foreign policy: the annual payment weakened the protected state economically and militarily over time. When it could no longer pay, the Marathas annexed it. Chauth thus functioned as a tool of empire-building.  Chauth and Sardeshmukhi table again (Lecture 7), with the teacher's ink: a sad face marked "not ideal" and "ideal: Deshmukh bears the burden". 8.3 Sardeshmukhi: an additional 10%, internal and external Sardeshmukhi was an additional levy of 10% of land revenue, collected over and above the regular land revenue. Deshmukhs collected Sardeshmukhi from the ryots and deposited it to the Chhatrapati. Shivaji 74-80 declared himself Sardeshmukh, the head of all Deshmukhs, so payment by the Deshmukhs was a symbol of their recognition of the Chhatrapati's authority. When extracted from states outside the Maratha Empire, Sardeshmukhi served as a symbol of Maratha authority being recognised by that state. Important distinction: Chauth was collected only externally, while Sardeshmukhi could be collected both internally and externally. 8.4 The teacher's boards: how Chauth and Sardeshmukhi work  Teacher's board for Prelims: Tributes split into Chauth and Sardeshmukhi (1/10). Chauth: on states outside the Maratha Empire, 1/4 of the annual revenue of the external state; if paid, the Marathas will not attack (protection). Steps: the Marathas defeat the external state; in the peace treaty the external state agrees to pay Chauth. Sardeshmukhi = 1/10: internally (on Deshmukhs): a Deshmukh collects Rs 100 as land revenue from ryots, commission Rs 10 (boxed), Rs 90 goes to the state; now Sardeshmukhi = 10 percent of the Deshmukh's Rs 10 = Rs 1 to the Chhatrapati, so Rs 90 plus Rs 1 = Rs 91 to the state or Chhatrapati. Externally: on states outside the Maratha Empire: after defeat the peace treaty obliges them to pay Chauth plus Sardeshmukhi, 25% plus 10% = 35% of the external state's annual revenue. Teacher: Prelims. Tributes are of two kinds: Chauth and Sardeshmukhi (1/10). Other names for tribute we have seen earlier: Nazrana, Abwab, Peshkash.  Chauth: on states outside the Maratha Empire, 1/4 of the external state's annual revenue. "If paid, Marathas will not attack" (protection from Maratha attack). Steps: (1) the Marathas defeat the external state; (2) in the peace treaty the external state agrees to pay Chauth. Sardeshmukhi internally (the teacher's example): a Deshmukh collects Rs 100 as land revenue from ryots. His commission = Rs 10; Rs 90 goes to the state. Sardeshmukhi = 10% of the Deshmukh's Rs 10 = Rs 1 to the Chhatrapati. So the state or Chhatrapati gets Rs 90 + Rs 1 = Rs 91.  Sardeshmukhi externally: after defeating an external state, the peace treaty makes it pay Chauth + Sardeshmukhi = 25% + 10% = 35% of its annual revenue. Reading the two descriptions together. The handout and slide table describe Sardeshmukhi as an extra 10% of land revenue. The teacher's worked example applies the 10% to the Deshmukh's Rs 10 commission when it is collected internally (the Deshmukh is paying respect to the Chhatrapati). Both are in the class material, so learn the table wording and the Rs 100 / Rs 10 / Rs 1 / Rs 91 example for the internal case.  Teacher's board: when applied internally. Sardeshmukhi = 10% of the income of a Deshmukh (in the example Rs 10). Why? When Person A pays Rs to Person B, it establishes that B is respected. The Chhatrapati = Sardar of the Deshmukhs (Head), and Shivaji (1674-80) declared himself so (Sardeshmukh), hence Sardeshmukhi internally. Teacher: Why pay Sardeshmukhi internally? When Person A pays money to Person B, it establishes that B is respected. The Chhatrapati = the Sardar (head) of the Deshmukhs; Shivaji 74-80 declared himself so (Sardeshmukh), hence Sardeshmukhi internally. 8.5 How Chauth was divided Revenue from Chauth and Sardeshmukhi collected outside the Maratha Empire helped reduce the tax burden on the people within the empire. When Chauth was extracted by the Chhatrapati / Peshwa, all of it was retained by Svarajya. When Maratha Sardars extracted it from a state outside the empire, they retained two-thirds and sent one-third to Svarajya:   Division   %   Purpose / beneficiary    --- --- ---    Mokasa   66% (about 2/3)   Kept by the Maratha Sardars to maintain troops and cavalry contingents     Babti   25% (1/4)   Sent directly to the Chhatrapati for personal use and the royal treasury     Sahotra   6%   Allocated to the Pant Sachiv, head of the royal secretariat and a member of the Ashtapradhan     Nadgaunda   3%   At the Chhatrapati's discretion: charitable grants, royal gifts or minor officials    Teacher's board: example of the Chauth division. A Maratha Sardar defeats an external state, a peace treaty is made and annual Chauth is extracted. What does the Chhatrapati get? Boxed: 1/3 of Chauth. Sketch: Samrajya as an arc wrapping around Hyderabad with Svarajya at the lower left. Teacher: A Maratha Sardar defeats an external state, a peace treaty follows, annual Chauth is extracted. What does the Chhatrapati get? 1/3 of the Chauth (boxed). 8.6 Chauth as a tool of empire-building: the teacher's boards  Teacher's board: War, then the peace treaty: how good, how harsh? Depends on the power differential between winner and loser; the more the gap, the harsher the treaty. A harshness scale with a rising differential: (1) Chauth; (2) Chauth plus Sardeshmukhi; (3) Chauth times 2 plus Sardeshmukhi (note: 1727 Gujarat was made to pay 60 percent of its revenue annually); (4) annexation of territory.   Harshness (rising power differential)   Treaty term    --- ---    1   Chauth     2   Chauth + Sardeshmukhi     3   Chauth x 2 + Sardeshmukhi (note: 1727, Gujarat made to pay 60% of its revenue annually)     4   Annexation of territory   Teacher: After a war comes a peace treaty. How good or harsh it is (for the losing party) depends on the power differential between winner and loser: the more the gap, the harsher the treaty.  Teacher's handwritten board: an example of a peace treaty today (Russia and Ukraine). 1 War reparation; 2 no import duty on Russian exports to Ukraine, or preferential treatment to Russian goods and services; 3 non-aggression pact by Ukraine, it will never join NATO; 4 imposed military alliance, Ukraine becomes a protectorate of Russia; 5 some territory of Ukraine; 6 significant territory; 7 full annexation. Teacher: Peace treaty today (the Russia-Ukraine example), from mild to severe: 1 war reparation; 2 no import duty on Russian exports to Ukraine, or preferential treatment to Russian goods and services; 3 non-aggression pact, Ukraine never joins NATO; 4 imposed military alliance, Ukraine a protectorate of Russia; 5 some territory; 6 significant territory; 7 full annexation.  Teacher's board: Chauth and the external state's budget. Revenue Rs 100 (external state), budget (income Rs 100, expenditure): Rs 25 to the Marathas, Rs 75 available for army, agriculture, irrigation, technical reforms and so on. The loop: pay 25% to the Marathas, less investment back into the economy and less spent on the army, GDP decreases, state revenue decreases (for example Rs 90 instead of Rs 100), pay 25% again; over the years: DRAIN. Unable to pay Chauth, militarily weak, the Marathas attack and annex.  Teacher's handwritten board: how Chauth is a tool of empire building. Scenario 1: the Marathas go for annexation of an external state: a long war, expensive, high loss of men (for the Marathas). Scenario 2: the Marathas fight a SHORT war, defeat the external state and offer peace; in the treaty they extract Chauth; after 10 years of Chauth the external state has a weak economy and weak army, is unable to pay, so a short war and easy total victory leads to annexation. Short war: the Marathas defeat the external state quickly and offer peace Peace treaty: the external state agrees to pay Chauth (25% of annual revenue) (warn) The drain: Rs 25 of every Rs 100 leaves, so less investment, less spent on the army, GDP and revenue fall (Rs 90 instead of Rs 100), yet 25% is still due (bad) Over the years: a weak economy and weak army, the state is unable to pay Chauth (good) Short war, easy total victory: the Marathas annex, avoiding the long, costly, high-casualty war of direct annexation Teacher: Scenario 1: go for annexation straight away = long war, expensive, high loss of men. Scenario 2: fight a short war, offer peace, extract Chauth; after ten years of Chauth the external state has a weak economy and weak army, cannot pay, and a short war means easy total victory and annexation. The 25% drain means less invested back into the economy and less on the army. 8.7 How the Peshwa office became hereditary; the power shift and Sangola 1750 The Peshwa's office was originally not hereditary. Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, the sixth Peshwa, changed this in practice. His son Baji Rao 20-40 became the next Peshwa, then his son Balaji Bajirao 20-40 / Nana Saheb (1740-61) followed. Once this custom held across three generations, the office became hereditary in effect. Shahu 19-49 was an effective ruler but progressively delegated more and more power to the Peshwa. After his death a crisis emerged when Tarabai claimed that Shahu 19-49's adopted son Ramraja was not her grandson, as had been stated at the time of adoption. To prevent the state being left without a Chhatrapati, Peshwa Nana Saheb (1740-61) backed Ramraja, but made him sign the Treaty of Sangola in February 1750, which transferred all real power from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa.  Teacher's board: power shift downwards from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa. Shahu 19-49 was a powerful personality and an effective Chhatrapati, but he over-delegated to the Peshwa because of trust (the Peshwa also never backstabbed Shahu). Ramraja (1749-77) was adopted with controversy over his identity at adoption, a weak personality, so the legitimacy of being Chhatrapati went down, leading to Sangola 1750: the Chhatrapati purely symbolic and all power given to the Peshwa.  Teacher's board: Sangola 1750, real power shifts from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa. Left: the Chhatrapati with Peshwa (B1), Gaikwad (B2), Scindia (B3), Bhonsle (B4), Holkar (B5) as brothers. The family-table analogy: before, the father sits at the head of the dining table with B1, B3, B5 on one side and B2, B4 on the other; after 1750, B1 moves to the head of the table. Bottom: whenever real power shifts down to a lower authority, (1) chances of factionalism increase (for example Bhonsle did not fight in the Third Battle of Panipat, 1761), (2) more dependence on the personality of the lower authority to prevent factionalism. Teacher: Shahu 19-49 = a powerful personality and effective Chhatrapati, BUT he over-delegated to the Peshwa because of trust (and the Peshwa also never backstabbed Shahu 19-49). Ramraja (1749-77) was adopted, with controversy over his identity at the time of adoption, and a weak personality, so his legitimacy as Chhatrapati fell, leading to Sangola 1750: the Chhatrapati purely symbolic, all power with the Peshwa.  Whenever real power shifts downward to a lower authority: (1) factionalism increases (Peshwa versus Sardars, Sardars versus Sardars; e.g. Bhonsle did not fight at the Third Battle of Panipat, 1761), and (2) there is more dependence on the personality of the lower authority to prevent factionalism. Teacher's family analogy: after 1750 the eldest brother (Peshwa) takes the father's seat at the head of the table while the other four brothers sit around. 8.8 The series of Peshwas Baji Rao 20-40 had a brother, Chimaji Appa, whose son Sadasiv Rao Bhau commanded the Maratha army at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and died fighting. Nana Saheb (1740-61) did not fight but died within weeks of the defeat. His elder son Vishwas Rao also died fighting at Panipat.  Teacher's board: the Peshwa family tree. (1) Balaji Vishwanath 13-20, 6th Peshwa; his son (2) Baji Rao 20-40, whose sons are (5) Balaji Bajirao / Nana Saheb 40-61 (died within two weeks of the 3rd Battle of Panipat) and (6) Raghunath Rao (73-74); (3) Chimaji Appa, whose son is (4) Sadasiv Rao Bhau (commanded the Maratha army in the 3rd BoP 1761 and died fighting). Sons of Nana Saheb: (7) Vishwas Rao (died in the 3rd BoP, the eldest), (8) young Madhav Rao 61-72, (9) Narayan Rao 72-73 (murdered by his uncle RR 73-74). (10) Madhav Rao II 74-95 (son of Narayan Rao, regent Nana Fadnis, infant; died by suicide because of over-controlling Nana Fadnavis). (11) Baji Rao II 96-18, last Peshwa, linked by a dashed line from Raghunath Rao. Right box: Svarajya (minus Satara and Kolhapur) annexed by the EIC after the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19). Reason: to give a signal to people that their Chhatrapati are respected. Left ink: regent = rules in the name of the king; war: internal = civil war, external = war.
