usurped the office     7   Madhav Rao II 74-95   Infant Peshwa, son of the murdered Narayan Rao 72-73; Nana Fadnavis regent; his overbearing control drove him to suicide in 1795     8   Baji Rao II 96-18   Last Peshwa, son of Raghunath Rao 73-74 (his claim rested on bloodline); ended by the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817-19)    The Peshwas (1713-1818) table as shown in Lecture 6: Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 (6th Peshwa; backed Shahu, made the office hereditary; 1750 Treaty of Sangola moved real power to the Peshwa); Baji Rao 20-40 (plundered Delhi 1737, Treaty of Bhopal 1738); Balaji Bajirao / Nana Saheb 40-61 (the Panipat era, died within weeks of the 1761 defeat); Madhav Rao 61-72 (young but able, temporary revival, died naturally 1772); Narayan Rao 72-73 (murdered; uncle Raghunath Rao 73-74 usurped the office and the Barbhai Mandal of Nana Fadnavis plus 12 removed him); Madhav Rao II 74-95, then Baji Rao II 96-18, the last Peshwa, the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War and EIC annexation 1818.  The Peshwas table (Lecture 7 version), with the teacher's extra notes: Baji Rao signed the Treaty of Bhopal (1738) after defeating a large Mughal army led by the Nizam, getting the Suba of Malwa and all territory between the rivers Chambal and Narmada. Nana Saheb signed the Treaty of Sangola (1750) with Ramraja; it legally made the Chhatrapati a symbolic head and shifted all real power to the Peshwa; reason: loss of legitimacy due to the dispute over Ramraja's real identity during his adoption by Shahu. Barbhai Mandal (12 Darakhdars or ministers of the Peshwa led by Nana Fadnis) removed Raghunath Rao to avenge the death of Narayan Rao (ink: 12 Bros). The Barbhai Mandal replaced Raghunath Rao with the infant Madhav Rao II (regent Nana Fadnavis); Baji Rao II = last Peshwa. Nana Fadnavis: the man who led the Barbhai conspiracy removing Raghunath Rao 73-74 as revenge for Narayan Rao 72-73's murder. He had fought at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) and is regarded as a "modern Chanakya." Crucially, he was the first to recognise that the EIC had territorial ambitions in India and was not merely a commercial enterprise. 8.9 The three broad phases of Maratha polity after Shivaji 74-80   Phase   Years   Character    --- --- ---    1   1680-1719   Turmoil: continuous Mughal warfare after Shivaji 74-80's death; civil war 1707-19     2   1719-1761   Growth and expansion     3   1761 onwards   Decline, with a temporary revival in the 1770s, notably the First Anglo-Maratha War of 1775-82

items.t: 9 · Wars, treaties and territories up to the Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
items.x: 9.1 The 1719 turning point: alliance with the Sayyid Brothers  1719, the turning point. The deal: Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 allied with the Sayyid Brothers (the Mughal kingmakers); they removed Farukhsiyar 13-19 and installed Md Shah 19-48 as a puppet. Maratha gains: recognition of autonomy in Maharashtra; the Chauth of Malwa and Gujarat; Chauth plus Sardeshmukhi of six Deccan provinces (Khandesh, Hyderabad, Aurangabad, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur). The reversal: 1720, Nizam 24-48 and others defeated the Sayyids; once he was Subahdar of Hyderabad (1724) he refused to pay the Marathas. 1719 was a turning point. Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath 13-20 allied with the Sayyid Brothers, the kingmakers of the Mughal court. Together they removed Farrukhsiyar 13-19 and placed Muhammad Shah 19-48 on the throne as a puppet. In return the Marathas secured three concessions: The Mughals formally recognised Maratha autonomous status in Maharashtra. The Marathas received the Chauth of Malwa and Gujarat. They gained the right to collect Chauth and Sardeshmukhi from six Mughal provinces of the Deccan: Khandesh, Hyderabad, Aurangabad, Berar, Bidar and Bijapur. Since Bijapur was later merged into Golconda, some sources name Golconda as the sixth instead. The Nizam's Hyderabad State was later constituted from precisely these six erstwhile Mughal provinces. This did not last. In 1720 the Nizam (1724-48), Governor of Hyderabad Suba, defeated the Sayyid Brothers. Muhammad Shah 19-48 became a joint puppet of the Irani and Turani factions of Mansabdars. When the Nizam established Hyderabad Suba as an independent successor state in 1724, he refused to pay Chauth and Sardeshmukhi to the Marathas.  The 1719 table again (Lecture 7) with ink: the Maratha gains boxed for Prelims; of Mughal empire; the six provinces underlined. A sketch shows Malwa (oval) between the Chambal (above) and the Narmada (below).  Map (with the teacher's ink) of India around 1700 with the Mogul boundary: Malwa boxed (blue); Khandesh, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur underlined or circled as the Deccan provinces; Oudh circled; Rajputana underlined; coastal European settlements marked: Diu, Daman, Surat, Bassein, Bombay (1661, 1668), Chandarnagar, Calcutta, Masulipatnam.  Handout map (with the teacher's marks) used for the six Deccan provinces, Malwa and the European coastal settlements.  The coloured historical map again (Lecture 7) with ink: Rajputana underlined; Oudh circled; MALWA boxed in blue; red circles on Berar, Khandesh, Aurangabad, Bidar (circled), Bijapur and Hyderabad = the six Deccan provinces; Diu, Surat, Daman, Bombay, Masulipatnam, Calcutta and Chandar Nagar (French) marked. 9.2 The Maratha decade of expansion (1727-39)  The Decade of Expansion (1727-39) timeline: 1728 Gujarat and the Deccan; 1729 Malwa; 1737 Delhi plundered; 1738 Treaty of Bhopal; 1739 Bassein.  The decade timeline in Lecture 7 with ink: 1728 tribute of Gujarat and the Deccan; 1729 control of Malwa, but the Mughals did not accept it and conflict continued; 1737 Delhi plundered (Md Shah 19-48 a prisoner briefly; Baji Rao 1720-1740); 1738 Treaty of Bhopal (large Mughal army led by the Nizam 24-48), with a sketch of the Chambal above, Malwa oval and the Narmada below; 1739 Salsette and Bassein (near Bombay) trade. The Marathas responded to the Nizam's refusal with a decade of relentless military expansion: 1727-28: defeated the Mughals in Gujarat and extracted 60% of revenue as annual tribute. 1728: defeated Hyderabad and regained the Chauth and Sardeshmukhi of the Deccan. 1729: captured Malwa and pushed their reach into Rajasthan. 1731: defeated a joint attack by the Nizam and local Gujarat chiefs. 1736: defeated the Portuguese and Ethiopian Muslims on the Konkan coast. 1737: Peshwa Baji Rao 20-40 plundered Delhi itself and held Muhammad Shah 19-48 prisoner temporarily. 1738: defeated a large Mughal army commanded by the Nizam and signed the Treaty of Bhopal (1738), under which the Marathas received the Suba of Malwa (formalising what they had controlled de facto since 1729) and sovereignty over all lands between the rivers Chambal and Narmada. 1739: Treaty of Bassein with the Portuguese led to the annexation of Bassein (Vasai). 9.3 Expansion continues on many fronts (1745-54)  Expansion on Many Fronts (1745-54): 1745-51 Raghuji Bhonsle forced Alivardi Khan 40-56 to cede Odisha and pay the Chauth of Bengal and Bihar (until Plassey, 1757); 1748-67 Ahmad Shah Abdali launched at least 7 invasions, the first checked at the Battle of Manupur (1748); 1751 Treaty of Bhalke, Salabat Jung 51-62 ceded Khandesh; 1752 took Ahmedabad, Gujarat complete (Damaji Gaikwad, HQ Baroda), and the weakened Mughal Empire came under Maratha protection; 1754 installed Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet on the Delhi throne, the top power in India by the mid-18th century.  Same table in Lecture 7. Teacher's ink: marked not imp; Homework: plot on the last map annexation, control (and a sum sign for the total). 1748-67: Sikh smiley. 1751 Bhalke: sad face, loss of access to the Arabian Sea for Hyderabad. 1752: annexation; because of fear of Afghan invasion the Maratha army was in Delhi; Ahmad Shah Bahadur 48-54. 1745-51: Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur regularly attacked Bengal Suba and forced Alivardi Khan 40-56 to give up Odisha and pay the Chauth of Bengal and Bihar, paid until Plassey (1757). 1751: Peshwa Nana Saheb attacked Hyderabad and forced Salabat Jung 51-62 to cede Khandesh via the Treaty of Bhalke. 1752: the Marathas took Ahmedabad, completing the annexation of Gujarat. The Peshwa appointed Damaji Gaikwad as Chief and Governor of Gujarat, HQ Baroda. From 1751 the Marathas regularly attacked the Rajputs, extracting annual tributes and interfering in succession disputes, but never fully conquered Rajputana. They also failed to dominate the Sikhs. 1752: the weakened Mughal Empire came under Maratha protection, driven by fear of Afghan invasions. Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 launched at least seven invasions between 1748 and 1767. The first, 1748, was checked at the Battle of Manupur, where the Mughal army fought the pitched battle while the Sikh misls harassed his supply lines. 1754: the Marathas interfered in the Mughal succession and installed Alamgir II 54-59 as their puppet. By the mid-18th century the Maratha State had emerged as the top power in India.  Teacher's hand-drawn schematic regional map of India in the 1750s (yellow boundary lines). Labels: Punjab, Rohilkhand, Sindh, Delhi, Rajasthan, Farrukhabad, Awadh, Bihar, Bengal, Chambal, Malwa (oval), Narmada, Gujarat, Orissa, Khandesh, Konkan Coast, Goa, Malabar Coast, Marathas, Hyderabad, Northern Sarkars, Mysore, Carnatic, Travancore.  Handout map: India 1756-1825, British acquisitions, states under subsidiary alliance and the Maratha Confederacy.  Handout map: the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, with the Gaikwad, Holkar, Scindia and Bhonsle domains and the Nizam's dominions.  Teacher's board: two ways to capture power. (a) Replace the rival (annexation): costly but fast. (b) Capture the enemy from within: less costly but slow. By 1752 the Marathas are in the power position once held by Zulfiqar Khan, the Sayyid Brothers, and the Nizam 24-48 (Wazir 1722-24). Teacher: Two ways to capture power: (a) replace the rival (annexation) = costly but fast; (b) capture the enemy from within = less costly but slow. By 1752 the Marathas stood in the power position once held by Zulfiqar Khan, the Sayyid Brothers and the Nizam (Wazir 1722-24). Homework on the last map: plot Annexation, Control (and the total).

items.t: 10 · The Third Battle of Panipat (1761)
items.x: 10.1 Sides and background  The Third Battle of Panipat (1761), the sides. The Marathas (about 50,000) were commanded by Sadasiv Rao Bhau; in 1758 Raghunath Rao had even removed Abdali's son Timur Shah from Lahore, the peak of Maratha power. The Afghan alliance (about 60,000): Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 (founded the Afghan state in 1747), plus the Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 of Rohilkhand, plus the Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan 50-82 of Farrukhabad, plus Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 of Awadh.  The same table in Lecture 7 (more detail): 1756, Abdali invaded, captured Lahore and Kashmir and installed his son Timur as Governor. In 1758 Raghunath Rao was sent by Balaji Bajirao to remove Timur Shah from Lahore; hence 1758 = the peak of Maratha power. Abdali = loyal commander of Nadir Shah and Governor of Afghanistan who founded the Afghan state in 1747 after Nadir Shah's death by seceding from the Persian empire. Right ink: if Awadh is part of the Mughal empire and Awadh is part of Abdali's alliance, what is this proof of? Factionalism (Mughal versus Mughal), weak centre or emperor, Awadh being a successor state (underlined). Teacher: If Awadh was part of the Mughal empire and yet joined Abdali's alliance, what is that proof of? (1) Factionalism (Mughal against Mughal); (2) a weak centre / emperor; (3) Awadh being a successor state (underlined). Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72, also known as Durrani, founded the modern borders of the Afghan State in 1747, declaring himself independent King after the death of Nadir Shah, Emperor of Iran and Afghanistan. Before 1747 he had been a trusted commander of Nadir Shah and Governor of Afghanistan, and took part in Nadir Shah's invasion of India in 1738-40. His invasion of 1756 culminated in the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. The two sides: the Marathas (about 50,000) and an alliance of Abdali (about 60,000) comprising Abdali himself; the Rohillas under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 of Rohilkhand; the Bangash Pathans under Ahmad Khan (1750-82) of Farrukhabad; and Awadh under Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75. By 1752 the weakened Mughal Emperor was under Maratha military protection and the Marathas effectively controlled Delhi. From 1756 Abdali's forces frequently raided north India. Abdali had installed his eleven-year-old son Timur Shah as Governor of Punjab and Kashmir. In 1758 Nana Saheb sent his brother Raghunath Rao 73-74, who removed Timur from Lahore. This was the peak of Maratha power, the maximum territory ever under Maratha domination. Nana Saheb even contemplated making his son Vishwas Rao the Emperor of Hindustan. Then the Third Battle of Panipat changed everything.  Why Abdali came, the immediate trigger: to avenge the Marathas' expulsion of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. March 1758: Raghunath Rao crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah (Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir). The Marathas then made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year; on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge. Sabaji Scindia held the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border and defended them fiercely. The Maratha conquest of Punjab from the Afghans was the direct challenge Abdali could not ignore. Prelims 2010: What was the immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 to invade India and fight the Third Battle of Panipat? Answer (a): to avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore. In March 1758 the Marathas drove Timur Shah out of Lahore. The fast expansion of the Maratha Empire was general background, not the immediate trigger; there was no Mughal tribute dispute; and there was no "Sultan of Punjab" refusing safe passage.  Prelims 2010 question slide: What was the immediate reason for Ahmad Shah Abdali to invade India and fight the 3rd Battle of Panipat? (a) To avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore; (b) The fast expansion of the Maratha Empire across the subcontinent; (c) Refusal of the Mughal Emperor to pay annual tribute; (d) Refusal of the Sultan of Punjab to grant safe passage. 10.2 Why Abdali won: six factors  The Third Battle of Panipat, 1761: a drawing of a man firing a swivel gun mounted on a kneeling camel.  Handout picture of the camel-mounted swivel gun in action.  Why Abdali 47-72 won, factors. Alliance: Awadh felt encircled and joined the Islamic alliance; Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali; the Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats stayed neutral after years of Maratha plunder; 60k versus 50k. Logistics: Abdali cut the Panipat-Delhi supply route, famine for men and horses. Terrain: open plains nullified Maratha guerrilla tactics (which needed hills and passes). Firepower: horse-mounted swivel guns pierced Maratha armour. Leadership and factionalism: Abdali and Najib coordinated well; Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur refused to fight.  Why Abdali 47-72 won, Lecture 7 version with the teacher's ink. Alliance: Awadh felt encircled and joined the Islamic alliance; Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali in hope of greater political influence under an Afghan emperor (ethnicity = soft power); the Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats stayed neutral because of the Maratha plunders of the past; the Jats offered help to the Marathas, but the alliance failed over tactics (Surajmal wanted guerrilla war, Sadashiv Rao Bhau did not; the Jats still sent supplies); greater military: 60k versus 50k. Logistics (ink: TACTICS), Terrain (ink: TACTICS). Ink: plunders = attack, then loot (boxed) = Chauth, Sardeshmukhi; a sketch of Panipat and Delhi with the supply line cut.   #   Factor   Detail    --- --- ---    1   Strength of his alliance   Awadh felt strategically encircled by the Marathas (Chauth from Bihar and Bengal since 1751 in the east, control of Delhi in the west since 1752, Samrajya to the south) and, when the Marathas sought an alliance with Shuja, he chose the Islamic alliance. The Indian Afghan kingdoms of Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad backed Abdali hoping for greater influence under an Afghan emperor. Sikhs, Rajputs and Jats stayed neutral, a direct consequence of years of Maratha plundering and tribute extraction. 60,000 versus 50,000.     2   Logistics   Abdali cut the supply routes between the Maratha camp at Panipat and Delhi. Famine-like conditions: no food for men, no fodder for horses.     3   Terrain   Panipat's vast open plains gave no advantage to Maratha guerrilla tactics, which depended on hills, forests and narrow passes.     4   Firepower   Abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce Maratha armour.     5   Military leadership   Abdali and Najib-ud-Daula 57-70 provided strong, coordinated command.     6   Maratha factionalism   Raghuji Bhonsle of Nagpur refused to fight, being opposed to Nana Saheb as Peshwa. In 1765 the Peshwa even plundered Nagpur in retaliation. Bhonsle also did not take part in the First Anglo-Maratha War (1775-82).    Horse-mounted swivel gun, Abdali's firepower: an engraving of a gun on an ornate saddle.  Abdali's horse-mounted swivel guns could pierce Maratha armour (a man in a fur cap beside a kneeling camel with a swivel gun mounted on its saddle). Teacher's ink: better stability of the gun; better aiming because it is attached to the seat. Teacher: Why the mounted swivel gun was better: better stability of the gun and better aiming, because it is attached to the seat. Teacher: The alliance factor on the board: Jats offered help to the Marathas, but the alliance failed over tactics. Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla war; Sadashiv Rao Bhau did not; the Jats still sent supplies. Rohilkhand and Farrukhabad hoped for greater political influence under an Afghan emperor (ethnicity = soft power). On the Maratha plunder, the teacher's chain: plunder = attack, then loot = Chauth and Sardeshmukhi. Logistics and terrain both fall under TACTICS. 10.3 Impact of the defeat  Panipat 1761, the impact. Maratha losses: Sadasiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao died fighting; Nana Saheb 40-61 died within weeks; about 50,000 lost in all. Deeper crisis: factionalism deepened, a run of young or weak Peshwas (Madhav Rao 61-72, Narayan Rao 72-73, infant Madhav Rao II 74-95). Abdali too: heavy losses and a revolt at home; he took his loot but could not consolidate any presence in India. The real result: a power vacuum at the centre; NEITHER the Marathas nor Abdali would rule India; the EIC eventually filled it.  Panipat 1761, the impact, Lecture 7 version. Ink: weak military; arrow under Factionalism. Abdali also suffered: heavy losses plus a revolt at home (a coup attempt) by military commanders, in Afghanistan. The real result: a power vacuum at the centre; it decided that neither the Marathas nor Abdali would rule India; the EIC eventually filled the vacuum. Military losses: Sadasiv Rao Bhau and Vishwas Rao died fighting. Nana Saheb had not fought (someone was needed to guard other frontiers in the south); he arrived with reinforcements when the battle was already lost and died within weeks. The Marathas lost 50,000 men in total, combatants and non-combatants. Factionalism deepened: young, inexperienced Peshwas followed one another: the young but brilliant Madhav Rao 61-72, then the incompetent Narayan Rao 72-73, then the infant Madhav Rao II 74-95. Abdali too paid a heavy price: serious losses and an anti-Abdali revolt among his own generals back in Afghanistan. He went home with his loot but could not consolidate any lasting presence in India. The deeper consequence: a power vacuum at the centre. Panipat did not decide who would rule India; it decided that neither the Marathas nor Abdali would. The vacuum was eventually filled by the British EIC, which defeated the regional Indian states one by one.

items.t: 11 · After Panipat: decline with moments of strength (1761-1819, about 60 years)
items.x: After Panipat, decline with moments of strength: 1765 Marathas defeated Mysore and extracted tribute; 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad, Northern Sarkars ceded to the EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year plus protection against both Marathas and Mysore; 1771 Mahadji Scindia recaptured Delhi from the Rohillas; 1775-82 First Anglo-Maratha War, the Marathas defeated the EIC (its only loss of that period); 1782 Treaty of Salbai, a Maratha-EIC alliance; 1784 Mahadji Shinde hired Benoit de Boigne to raise the Fauj-i-Hind (the Campoo system); 1798 to 1803 Hyderabad signed the first Subsidiary Alliance (1798) and the EIC took Delhi in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803); 1817-19 Third Anglo-Maratha War, Svarajya annexed by the EIC.  The same table in Lecture 7 with extra notes: 1761-1819 = about 60 years. 1765 (Haider Ali 61-82 strong). 1771: since 1761 Delhi was under the Rohillas; ink: 1752-1803 (minus 1761-71) Delhi with the Marathas. 1782 Treaty of Salbai: a Maratha-EIC alliance that held until the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 (signed by Mahadji Scindhia; Salbai is near Gwalior). 1784: each Campoo was an integrated force having its own infantry, cavalry and artillery, thus self-sufficient units. 1803: EIC took Delhi from Scindhia in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 (sad face). 1817-19: 3rd Anglo-Maratha War, Svarajya annexed (sad face). 1765: the Marathas defeated Mysore and extracted tribute. 1766 Treaty of Hyderabad: Hyderabad gave the Northern Sarkars to the EIC for an annual payment of seven lakh rupees and protection against both the Marathas and Mysore. The Northern Sarkars (Northern Circars) were initially four districts: Chicacole (Srikakulam), Rajmandri (Rajahmundry), Ellore (Eluru) and MustafaNagar (Kondapalli), with MurtuzaNagar (Guntur) added later as a fifth. Guntur was not transferred to the EIC in 1766. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans, who had taken it in 1761. 1775-82 First Anglo-Maratha War: the Marathas defeated the EIC, the only war in this period the EIC lost. 1782 Treaty of Salbai: a Maratha-EIC military alliance. 1784: Mahadji Shinde (Scindia) hired the French military adventurer Benoit de Boigne, who raised and trained the Fauj-i-Hind, also called the Campoo system (each Campoo was an integrated force with its own infantry, own cavalry, own artillery, thus self-sufficient units). It transformed the army from a traditional light-cavalry force into a modern, disciplined European-style infantry-cavalry-artillery machine (similar to Haider Ali 61-82's army (1761-82), also modernised with French help). Other Sardars followed: Holkar hired the Frenchman Dudrenec. 1795 Battle of Kharda: a Maratha victory over Hyderabad. The EIC stayed neutral as the Marathas were still its ally under Salbai 1782. The last battle between Hyderabad and the Marathas. 1798: Hyderabad became the first Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance (also called a subordinate alliance) with the EIC, securing guaranteed protection and ending its vulnerability to Maratha pressure. 1803: the EIC captured Delhi in the Second Anglo-Maratha War. 1817-19 Third Anglo-Maratha War: Svarajya was annexed by the EIC, ending the last Peshwa Baji Rao II 96-18's rule. Flag on the length of the Salbai alliance. The handout says the Treaty of Salbai (1782) alliance held until 1795; the teacher's note on the Lecture 7 slide says it held until the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05). Both appear in the class material: the handout's 1795 is tied to the Battle of Kharda (the EIC staying neutral), the teacher's version marks the breakdown at the next Anglo-Maratha war.  Teacher's board: the Campoo system. Left: the Chhatrapati, the Peshwa with M1, M2, M3, M4 and Nana Fadnavis under the Peshwa. Later link: Risala system of Hyder Ali 61-82. King (Scindhia): multiple regiments and every regiment is like a mini army, self-sufficient, with its own transport, own infantry, own cavalry, own supplies, own weapons; all converge on Regiments. Speed (smiley); political stability: chances of a coup by a commander are down (yes). Note: today we are doing this again. Teacher: Campoo = "multiple regiments, and every regiment is like a mini army": self-sufficient, with its own transport, infantry, cavalry, supplies and weapons. Benefits: speed; political stability because the chances of a coup by a commander go down. Later link: the Risala system of Haider Ali 61-82. The teacher adds: "Today, we are doing this again" (the modern parallel to integrated, self-sufficient military units).

items.t: 12 · Why couldn't the Marathas establish all-India rule?
items.x: Why no all-India Maratha rule? Tribute not annexation; weak centre, strong Sardars; Treaty of Sangola 1750; even Svarajya not centralised (local assemblies of Vatan-holders pressured the Peshwa); much of Samrajya had no government machinery on the ground.  Why no all-India Maratha rule? (Mains). Ink: Admin on the ground, making and implementing of laws by the King (circled) = Centre (circled). Reasons: focused on tribute, not annexation; weak centre, strong Sardars (power never fully centralised in the Maratha Emperor); Treaty of Sangola 1750 (factionalism increased even more after 1761 as now weak Peshwas); even in Svarajya power was not 100% centralised (ink on local assemblies: Democratic spirit, smiley; Strong Centre, sad face); no effective Rule in the whole of Samrajya (much had no government machinery on the ground). Ink bottom right: Control tick, Rule X, not 100%. The Marathas came closer than any other power in the 18th century to an all-India empire, but the reasons they never crossed that threshold are structural: Tribute, not annexation. Often after a victory they limited themselves to Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rather than annexing and establishing direct rule. Extracting tribute is not ruling. Ruling means making and implementing policies through your own administration on the ground; for one central authority to rule effectively, power must be centralised: one country, one ruler, one law, rule of law. Weak centre, strong Sardars. The centre was never strong enough and factionalism weakened it further; the Sardars had always been autonomous. Shivaji 74-80 never gave Jagirs to his officers and Shahu 19-49 never gave Vatan Jagirs to military commanders, so ambitious Sardars seeking their own principalities ventured out on their own to build Samrajya. In territories brought under Maratha control through the Sardars' own efforts, the Chhatrapati's authority would naturally be weak. The Treaty of Sangola 1750. As power shifted down to the Peshwa, the Sardars felt even less constrained and factionalism grew; after 1761 a succession of weak Peshwas accelerated this. Power was not properly centralised even in Svarajya: local assemblies of Vatan right-holders (Deshmukhs and Patils) asserted themselves and pressured the Peshwa. In Samrajya, effective centralised rule did not exist at all in many areas: certain areas were under a Maratha Sardar militarily, but no effective government machinery was present on the ground. Teacher: "Rule" = administration on the ground: making and implementing laws by the King (= the Centre). Control, tick; Rule, cross: not 100%. Even in Svarajya the local assemblies of Vatan-holders show a "democratic spirit" (smiley) but not a "strong centre" (sad face). Mains 2014: why so many battles at Panipat?  Why so many battles at Panipat? (Mains 2014). The real reason: not the city but the GATEWAY to Delhi; any power from Central Asia or Afghanistan via the Khyber staged here before the final push, so Delhi rulers chose to stop the enemy at these gates. Practical factors: vast open fields for large armies; weather suited to long campaigns; many warrior communities eased recruitment; farm productivity and proximity to Delhi eased supply. The record: Thanesar (1014 and 1191); Panipat I (1526) and II (1556); Karnal (1739); Panipat III (1761).  The same table in Lecture 7 with ink: the gateway to Delhi (HQ or Capital) for armies marching from the north-west via the Khyber Pass; Delhi's rulers chose to fight the enemy here to keep the capital secure. Geographic factors: vast open fields, weather, many warrior communities, farm productivity and proximity to Delhi easing the supply of food, weapons and transport. Mains 2014: why have so many empire-shaking battles been fought near Panipat? The battles were not fought for the city of Panipat itself. The region is the gateway to Delhi. Any power advancing from Central Asia or Afghanistan had to come through the Khyber Pass, and the natural staging ground before the final push runs through the region of Panipat, Karnal, Kurukshetra and Thanesar. For a ruler in Delhi the sound move was to stop the enemy at these gates. Supporting factors: (1) vast open fields for set-piece battles; (2) weather supporting prolonged campaigns; (3) many warrior communities easing recruitment; (4) agricultural productivity plus proximity to Delhi easing supply. items.t: 1 · The middle path between king and rebel
items.x: Teacher's board: in case of rebels establishing their rule in an area. Option 1: continue fighting and end the rebellion. Option 2: lose territory (T, circled) and the rebel establishes an independent kingdom. Mid path: the rebel accepts to be a Mansabdar of the emperor, accepts the Mughal as emperor, sends tribute (Z) to Delhi, agrees to maintain an army and help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts: dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, non-interference in the rebel's rule. Teacher: When rebels establish their rule in an area, the emperor has two options: (1) continue fighting and end the rebellion; (2) lose the territory (T) and let the rebel establish an independent kingdom. The middle path: the rebel accepts to be a Mansabdar of the emperor, accepts the Mughal as emperor, sends tribute to Delhi, agrees to maintain an army / help the emperor militarily. The emperor accepts: dynastic governorship, the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir, and non-interference in the rebel's rule.  Teacher's board: both sides' core interest is met. Emperor: the empire's territory shall not shrink, and revenue and military come from that territory. Rebel: king of that territory and wants dynastic rule in it.  The middle path, king and rebel. King: the rebel provides an army; the empire does not shrink. Rebel: opportunity as a Mansabdar at the centre (recall: successor states); dynastic governor status; the king accepts the territory as the rebel's Watan Jagir. Footer: except for the Sikhs, who never accepted Mughal symbolic sovereignty (except once in 1707), this pattern appears among the Jats, Marathas, Rohilkhand, Farrukhabad, Mysore and Rajputs. items.t: 2 · Framework: three more Rebel States
items.x: Framework, three more Rebel States. Apart from the Marathas the 18th century saw three more: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur (East Rajasthan, south of Delhi); Farrukhabad (est. 1714), the Bangash Pathans of central Uttar Pradesh; Rohilkhand (process began 1721, completed 1737-40), the Rohilla Afghans around Bareilly. All three turned local military power into territorial rule as the Mughal Empire weakened, yet none could build a large, sustainable empire. Ink: establishment years with an arrow to 1737-40. Apart from the Marathas, there were three more Rebel States in the 18th century: the Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur in East Rajasthan, and the two Afghan kingdoms, Farrukhabad (est. 1714) and Rohilkhand (crystallised 1737-40). All three used the opportunity created by the weakening Mughal Empire to convert local military power into territorial rule, but none could establish a large, sustainable empire.

items.t: 3 · The Jat Kingdom (1695-1763)
items.x: The Jat Kingdom (1695-1763): the Jats an agrarian community hostile to the Mughals since Jahangir 1605-27; harsh land revenue and the Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed them into organised resistance under the Zamindars. Chain: Gokla (1669-70), Rajaram (1670-88), Churaman (1695-1721) Bharatpur, Badan Singh (1722-55) consolidates, Surajmal (1756-63) peak, 1763 onwards collapse. Teacher's ink: LR over land revenue; ending over local autonomy; imp with lines to Churaman and Surajmal (both underlined); under Churaman: est of Jat kingdom; under Surajmal: most powerful. 3.1 Who were the Jats and why did they resist? The Jats were primarily an agrarian community of North India, with cultivation as their traditional occupation. Their hostility to the Mughal State stretched back to the reign of Jahangir 05-27, when harsh land revenue policies and the Mughal drive to subordinate local autonomy pushed the Zamindars, the traditional leaders of rural society, toward organised resistance. 3.2 How the resistance developed The first organised Jat revolt came in 1669 (teacher's slide: 1669-70), led by the Zamindar Gokla. The torch passed through Rajaram 89-00 to Churaman 95-21, then Badan Singh (1722-55, consolidation), then Surajmal 56-63, each pushing resistance further. Their preferred method was guerrilla warfare: fast, decentralised and hard for a large Mughal army to counter. The Jat Kingdom of Bharatpur, in East Rajasthan, south of Delhi, bordering the Mathura and Agra districts, was formally established by Churaman 95-21 Jat (1695-1721). Like many rebel-state founders (Marathas, Sikhs), Churaman 95-21 turned peasant discontent over high land revenue into political and military power. Teacher: Note the two names marked imp: Churaman 95-21 = establishment of the Jat kingdom; Surajmal 56-63 = the most powerful. The hostility is about LR (high land revenue) and ending local autonomy.  Lohagarh Fort, Bharatpur: the Iron Fort, never conquered, even by the British, built by Maharaja Surajmal (1756-63). Aerial photograph of the moated fort with round bastions and a bridge. 3.3 Surajmal 56-63: the peak  Surajmal's reign (1756-63), the peak. Status: built a strong, centralised State; forced the Mughal emperor to recognise him as an autonomous ruler. Reform 1: recruited European soldiers to modernise the military. Reform 2: introduced a Mughal-style revenue system. Reform 3: removed relatives from court posts to cut factionalism. Extent: from Delhi to Agra, from the Chambal to the Ganga (today's Delhi, Haryana, UP and Rajasthan). Panipat 1761: offered help to the Marathas but the alliance failed over tactics. Teacher's ink: Alamgir II 54-59 = puppet of the Marathas; status: the same thing was accepted during Churaman Jat; Reform 1: Mahadji Scindhia's Campoo = Fauj-i-Hind; Reform 3: R vs R (royal family infighting). Under Maharaja Surajmal 56-63 the Jat State reached its peak. He built a strong, centralised State and forced the Mughal emperor to formally recognise him as an autonomous ruler (within the Mughal Empire). His reforms: He recruited European soldiers to modernise his military. He introduced a Mughal-style revenue system for administrative efficiency. He removed relatives from court positions to reduce factionalism. At its peak the Jat State stretched from Delhi to Agra and from the Chambal River to the Ganga, across present-day Delhi, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan. After Surajmal 56-63's death in 1763 the Jat State collapsed. Panipat 1761: Surajmal 56-63 offered help to the Marathas before the Third Battle of Panipat, but the alliance could not be established because of differences on war strategy and tactics. Surajmal 56-63 wanted guerrilla warfare, but the Maratha commander Sadasiv Rao Bhau disagreed. The Jats still sent essential supplies to the Marathas during the war. Teacher: On the status row: "the same thing was accepted during Churaman 95-21 Jat" (recognition of an autonomous ruler within the Mughal Empire). On the Panipat row, the Maratha link: Alamgir II 54-59 was a puppet of the Marathas. On Reform 1: Mahadji Scindia 68-94's Campoo = Fauj-i-Hind is the same kind of modernisation (see Chapter 4). On Reform 3: the Mughal family's infighting (R vs R) is the contrast.  Map: the Jat State at its peak (orange, Delhi in green). Labels include Hariana, Meerut, Delhi, Rewari, Nuh, Ballabhgarh, Narnaul, Alwar, Aligarh, Mathura, Bharatpur, Mahwa, Hindaun, Agra, Gohad, Jalaun, Kalpi, Mastura, Pichhore, Uchad, Datia, Samthar, Narwar, Mahoba. From Delhi to Agra, from the Chambal to the Ganga.  Handout Diagram 1: the Jat Kingdom. Gokla 1669-70 (first organised Jat revolt), Rajaram (1670-88, guerrilla continuation), Churaman (1695-1721, founds Bharatpur Kingdom), Badan Singh (1722-55, consolidation), Maharaja Surajmal 1756-63 (peak; reforms: European troops, Mughal-style revenue, kin removed from court), peak territory Delhi, Agra, Chambal, Ganga, then 1763 Surajmal dies and the State collapses: not a peasant utopia, the same extractive structure it rose against. 3.4 Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant?  Was the Jat Kingdom a better deal for the peasant? No peasant utopia. Land revenue stayed high; real power rested with the Zamindars, not the ryots. Though born of peasant revolt, the Jat State replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against. After Surajmal's death in 1763 the Jat State collapsed. Teacher's ink: Dreamland (arrow from No peasant utopia); underlines on land revenue, peasant revolt, same extractive structure. Though the kingdom was the result of peasant revolts, it was no peasant utopia. Land revenue remained high, and real power rested with Zamindars, not with the ryots. The Jat State replicated the same extractive structure it had risen against.

items.t: 4 · The Afghans: migration and the rise of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45
items.x: The Afghans and the rise of Sher Shah Suri. Afghans had migrated into North India since the 15th century (poor economy and instability at home), working its military labour markets as wandering warlords. Steps: the Sur clan migrates from the Sur region of Afghanistan in the Lodi period (late 15th c); a jagir at Sasaram granted to his grandfather under the Lodi Sultans (Bihar); Farid Khan rises, serves many masters including the Mughals after 1526 and studies their administration; 1540 Battle of Kanauj, defeats Humayun and seizes the throne of Delhi. Teacher's ink: a top timeline with 1540-55 SURIS; 1737-40 ROHILKHAND; 1748-61 ABDALI; FARUKHABAD 1714; family = Mansabdars in the Delhi Sultanate; (Bihar); SHER SHAH SURI with an arrow to Farid Khan; 30-40 under 1540 (Humayun 1530-40). 4.1 Who were the Afghans and what brought them to North India? Afghans had been migrating into North India since the 15th century, driven by poor economic conditions and political instability back home. In the military labour markets of North India they functioned largely as wandering warlords, skilled fighters available to whoever could pay. 4.2 Was there ever a moment when Afghans actually ruled Delhi? The story of Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 is the story of all these Afghan migrants compressed into one life. His family, the Suris, a clan of the Pashtun tribe, had migrated from the Sur region of Afghanistan to India during the Lodi Sultanate in the late 15th century. His grandfather had received a small jagir in Sasaram (present-day Bihar) in service of the Lodi Sultans. Sher Shah 40-45, born Farid Khan around 1486 in Sasaram, grew up not in Afghanistan but in Bihar, as a second-generation Indian Afghan, a product of the North Indian military labour market. He served under various masters, rising through ability rather than birth. He served as an administrator under the Afghan governor of Bihar, then briefly under the Mughals after Babur 26-30 defeated the Lodis in 1526. During this Mughal service he closely studied Mughal administrative methods, knowledge he later turned against them. He built his power base in Bihar and Bengal and by 1540 had defeated Humayun 30-40, first reign) at the Battle of Kanauj, driving him into exile in Persia and seizing the throne of Delhi. Handout comparison: compare Suri with the Bangash Pathans of Farrukhabad (same Afghan migrant background, same military-labour-market entry), but a very different ceiling on what they could achieve, partly because the political window available to them was much narrower. Teacher: The Suri family were Mansabdars in the Delhi Sultanate (Bihar). The Afghan markers on the board timeline: Suris 1540-55; Farrukhabad 1714; Rohilkhand 1737-40; Abdali 1748-61. 4.3 What Sher Shah 40-45 Suri 40-45 achieved in five years  Sher Shah Suri (1540-45), five years that mattered. Administrative hierarchy: Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Sub-district (Pargana), a structure Akbar (56-05) later adopted almost wholesale. Grand Trunk Road: upgraded Uttarapath connecting Bengal to the North-West Frontier (ink: ECO and TRADE smileys). Dak Chowki: a reliable postal-relay system (ink: like a relay race, with a sketch of dots in a line). The Rupiya: a standardised silver coin, the basis of Indian currency for centuries (ink: imp, degree of TRUST between buyer and seller, standardisation needs a CENTRAL AUTHORITY). Revenue: land surveys and a fair demand fixed directly with the peasant (ink: in PATTA and QUBULIAT, HEAD and TAIL, one document in 2 copies; Patta with the RYOT, Qubuliat with the GOVT). After 1545: he dies, the Suri Interregnum (1540-55), Humayun retakes Delhi at the Battle of Sirhind (1555).   Reform   What he did   Teacher's note    --- --- ---    Administrative hierarchy   Centre, Province (Suba), District (Sarkar), Sub-district (Pargana)   Akbar 56-05 later adopted it almost wholesale     Grand Trunk Road   Upgraded the Uttarapath connecting Bengal to the North-West Frontier   Boosts economy and trade     Dak Chowki   A reliable postal-relay system   "Like a relay race"     The Rupiya   A standardised (by weight and value) silver coin, the basis of Indian currency for centuries   Important: the degree of trust between buyer and seller; standardisation needs a central authority     Revenue   Land surveys and a fair land revenue demand fixed directly with the peasant, cutting out the middleman Zamindar   Recorded in a Patta (with the ryot) and a Qubuliat (with the government): "head and tail," one document in two copies   Handout: Suri was in a sense the first ruler to seriously attempt "administrative reform": streamlining the State machinery to make it efficient and fair. Unfortunately he had only five years. His successors could not hold together what he built. After his death in 1545 the Afghans fragmented again into competing warlord groups. The period 1540 to 1555, the Suri Interregnum, was a brief Afghan interruption of Mughal rule, ending when Humayun 30-40 recaptured Delhi in 1555 after the Battle of Sirhind and briefly restored Mughal authority before his death in 1556. Sher Shah Suri's tomb, Sasaram (Bihar): the red-sandstone mausoleum of the five-year Afghan ruler of Delhi, a domed mausoleum in the middle of a lake. items.t: 5 · The 18th century: a new surge of Afghan migration
items.x: The 18th century brought a new surge of Afghan migration as political instability in their homeland intensified. The progressive weakening of the Mughal State created exactly the opportunity these groups had been waiting for. Two Afghan kingdoms emerged: Farrukhabad (today a district in Uttar Pradesh; Bangash Pathans) and Rohilkhand (also called Rampur, with capital Bareilly; Rohilla Afghans).  Map: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand. North India: Gadhwal, Kumaon, Mughals (green, Delhi area), Rampur (purple), Bangash (red), Oudh (large, peach), Bharatpur / Hindu Jats (yellow), Gohad, Karauli. The two Afghan kingdoms, Rohilkhand (Rampur) and the Farrukhabad belt, lie between Awadh and the Marathas. Teacher's ink: Delhi with a line to the green Mughal area; = Rohilkhand [1737-40] to Rampur (Rohilla Afghans); Farukhabad (1714) to Bangash (Bangash Pathans).  Teacher's board: Afghan kingdoms (within the Mughal Empire), with the ink ART 370 plus. Farrukhabad (Bangash Pathans): 1714-1743 Md Khan Bangash (underlined); weak Mughal power = opportunity; factionalism, R vs R: Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother; Farrukhsiyar 13-19 killed Jahandar Shah. Third Battle of Panipat (1761): both supported Abdali. Awadh annexed both. Rohilkhand (Rohillas): 1721-1748 Ali Md Khan (underlined). Boxed 1737-1740: Marathas and Nadir Shah weaken the Mughal. Mughal interests: territory does not shrink, military and money. Rebels' interest: dynastic rule over some territory. Teacher: Afghan kingdoms within the Mughal Empire (Article 370-type status): Farrukhabad (Bangash Pathans), 1714-43, Md Khan Bangash. Both kingdoms supported Abdali at Panipat (1761); Awadh annexed both.

items.t: 6 · Farrukhabad (est. 1714)
items.x: 6.1 How did a Bangash Pathan warlord found a kingdom near Agra? The founding of Farrukhabad shows how factional Mughal court politics created vacuums that outsiders could exploit. It was structurally weak from the start, sitting between powerful neighbours, principally Awadh, which preyed on it whenever it could. Its history is best understood as a sequence across three rulers.  Farrukhabad (est. 1714), three rulers. Md Khan Bangash (1714-43): a Pathan warlord who backed Farukhsiyar with 12,000 troops; rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue near the Ganga; founded Farrukhabad (1714), naming it after the emperor. Qaim Khan (1743-49): in 1749 Safdar Jung, Nawab of Awadh and Wazir of Ahmed Shah Bahadur, engineered Qaim Khan's death; Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered. Ahmad Khan Bangash (1750-1802): retook it (1750); fought beside Abdali at Panipat (1761) to recover it; the EIC finally annexed it in 1802; the Bangash Pathans later joined the 1857 Revolt. Teacher's ink: mansabdar over rank of Nawab; JAGIR linked to revenue near the Ganga; Mughal followed mid path; Safdar Jung 39-54; Ahmed Shah Bahadur 48-54; after this other mansabdars accused Safdar of misusing his position, so he was forced to resign, leading to the virtual break of Awadh from the Mughal empire.   Ruler   What happened    --- ---    Md Khan Bangash (1714-43)   A Pathan warlord who backed Farrukhsiyar 13-19 with 12,000 troops; rewarded with the rank of Nawab and revenue assignments near the Ganga; founded Farrukhabad (1714), naming it after the emperor. Died 1743, succeeded by his son Qaim Khan.     Qaim Khan (1743-49)   In 1749 Safdar Jung 39-54 (Nawab of Awadh and Wazir of the emperor) engineered his death in battle; Farrukhabad was annexed to Awadh and plundered.     Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71   Retook it in 1750; driven out in 1751-52 by Marathas and Jats; fought beside Abdali at Panipat (1761) to recover it; the EIC annexed it in 1802. The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated.   Jahandar Shah 12-13 and Farrukhsiyar 13-19: the handout (section 4.2) says that in 1712-13 Jahandar Shah 12-13 seized power by killing the father of Farrukhsiyar 13-19, and Farrukhsiyar 13-19 avenged this by removing Jahandar Shah 12-13; the teacher's board says Jahandar Shah 12-13 came to power by killing his brother. Both are in the class material; the point for answers is Mughal succession violence (R vs R). Md Khan Bangash's gesture (handout): he first founded a town called Mohammadabad after himself, which annoyed Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Farrukhabad ("the city of Farrukh") was the diplomatic correction: the classic pattern of a rebel State acknowledging Mughal sovereignty in name while building real autonomy on the ground. Teacher: Reading the rows: Nawab = a mansabdar rank; the revenue near the Ganga = a Jagir; the Mughal followed the "mid path." After Safdar Jung 39-54's misuse of the Wazir's post, other Mansabdars accused him of misusing his position and he was forced to resign, which was the virtual break of Awadh from the Mughal empire (see Chapter 3). Qaim Khan (handout): the textbook example of the Wazir's loyalty being to his own State, not the Emperor he nominally served; the highest Mughal Mansab had become a tool for personal and regional ambition. 6.2 Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750 onwards Ahmad Khan fought back and retook Farrukhabad in 1750. In 1751-52 the Marathas, specifically Malhar Rao Holkar and Jayappaji Rao Scindia sent by Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao 40-61, along with Jats under Surajmal 56-63, drove him out. (Note: Awadh had requested the Marathas and Jats in 1751.) As Abdali's invasion progressed, the Marathas signed a treaty in 1752 that allowed him to return and resume rule, at the price of handing half of Farrukhabad to Holkar and Scindia. In 1761 he fought alongside Ahmad Shah Abdali 47-72 at the Third Battle of Panipat. With the Marathas defeated, he recovered his full dominions, including the half ceded in 1752. Once Abdali left India in 1761, Farrukhabad weakened. In 1802 the EIC annexed Farrukhabad. (The "Ceded Provinces" refers to territories Awadh was forced to hand over under the Subsidiary Alliance of 1801; Farrukhabad was merged into the Ceded Provinces after annexation.) The Bangash Pathans joined the 1857 Revolt but were defeated. Flag on Ahmad Khan's dates: the handout's heading reads "Ahmad Khan Bangash 50-71, 1750-1802", and in the Panipat line-up (Chapter 4) it writes Ahmad Khan 50-82. The slide table reads 1750-1802. The class material is not consistent about the short form (50-71 or 50-82), so remember the anchor dates: retook Farrukhabad 1750; EIC annexed it 1802.

items.t: 7 · Rohilkhand (est. 1737-40)
items.x: Rohilkhand (est. 1737-40), the story. Zamindars of Katehr (Bareilly, Moradabad) hire Afghan mercenaries, the Rohillas, who grow dominant under Daud Khan (ink: UP circled over Katehr). 1721: Ali Md Khan takes over on Daud Khan's death and spends two decades consolidating. 1739: the trigger, Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi; Ali Md Khan stops paying taxes and rules Katehr independently. 1740: co-opted, Emperor Md Shah (19-48) grants him the Subadar title (a Mansabdar); Katehr is renamed Rohilkhand (ink: via mid path). 1761-71: Najib-ud-Daula backs Abdali at Panipat; Delhi falls under Rohilla influence. 1771-74: the end, Mahadji Scindia retakes Delhi (1771); most of Rohilkhand annexed by Awadh with EIC help in 1774 (military alliance since the Treaty of Allahabad 1765); the small remainder became the autonomous State of Rampur with capital Bareilly, under Awadh legally and from 1801 under the EIC when Awadh gave half of Awadh in the Subsidiary Alliance. 7.1 How Afghan mercenaries became rulers The region that became Rohilkhand was originally called Katehr: western Uttar Pradesh, around Bareilly and Moradabad. In the 17th and early 18th century, as Mughal authority weakened, local Zamindars and regional governors in Katehr hired Afghan mercenaries to settle disputes and enforce authority. These Afghan fighters, called Rohillas, became a dominant armed presence. Note: Rohilkhand was formed by settled Afghan mercenaries consolidating power from within the region, already entrenched in Katehr long before Abdali entered India. The word "Rohilla" comes from "Roh," the Afghan homeland, so Rohilkhand means the land of the Rohillas. 7.2 1721: the starting point When Daud Khan, the Afghan commander who had consolidated the mercenary groups, died in 1721, his adopted son and protege Ali Md Khan (1721-48) took over leadership. This is the starting point, not yet an independent State, but the moment one man gained control of a significant armed force. After 1721 he moved methodically: for two decades he consolidated, slowly absorbing lands from the very Zamindars his men had been hired to protect and uniting the scattered Afghan groups under his sole command. 7.3 What finally pushed Ali Md Khan to declare independence? Nadir Shah's devastating invasion of Delhi in 1739. With the Mughal State paralysed, Ali Md Khan stopped paying taxes to Delhi and began ruling Katehr as an independent power, capturing key districts including Bareilly and Moradabad. Handout comparison with Farrukhabad: both Afghan kingdoms used the same window (Mughal paralysis) to convert military presence into territorial control. Md Khan Bangash did it earlier and more formally through Mughal court politics; Ali Md Khan did it through slow ground-level consolidation followed by outright defiance during the 1739 crisis. 7.4 How the Mughals responded Too weak to crush him, the Mughal State fell back on its standard strategy: co-opt what you cannot defeat. In 1740 Emperor Md Shah (1719-48) formally granted Ali Md Khan the title of Subadar. From 1740 Katehr was officially renamed Rohilkhand and functioned as an autonomous State under nominal Mughal sovereignty. (Ali Md Khan took control in 1721 but was officially recognised as Nawab of Rohilkhand by the Mughals in 1740.) The title gave the rebel legitimacy; it gave the Mughals the illusion of control. Both sides understood the fiction. 7.5 How Rohilkhand ended The arc is the same as Farrukhabad: rise on Afghan military power, peak during the Abdali alliance, collapse once that external prop was removed. 1761: under Najib-ud-Daula 57-70, Rohilkhand actively supported Abdali at the Third Battle of Panipat. 1761-71: Delhi was effectively under Rohilla influence (the Mughal emperor was in Awadh). 1770: Najib dies; with no Abdali to support since 1761, Rohilkhand weakens. 1771: Mahadji Scindia 68-94 recaptured Delhi and allowed Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06 to return home (the Red Fort). 1774: Most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help, because of the Treaty of Allahabad (1765), which led to a military alliance. The rest, a small part, became the autonomous State of Rampur with capital Bareilly, legally under Awadh, and from 1801 under the EIC when Awadh gave half of Awadh in the Subsidiary Alliance.  Handout Diagram 3: Farrukhabad and Rohilkhand combined. 1714 Md Khan Bangash founds Farrukhabad (Farukhsiyar's backing, Nawab and jagir); Rohilkhand: Afghan mercenaries in Katehr, 1721 Ali Md Khan consolidates; 1739 Nadir Shah paralyses Delhi, Ali Md Khan declares independence, 1740 Md Shah grants the Nawab title; 1749 Safdar Jung (Awadh Nawab and Wazir) kills Qaim Khan, annexes Farrukhabad; 1752 Marathas (Holkar and Scindia plus Jats) restore Ahmad Khan for half of Farrukhabad; 1761 Panipat, both back Abdali (Ahmad Khan Bangash, Rohilla Najib-ud-Daula); 1761-71 Delhi under Rohilla influence; 1771 Mahadji Scindia retakes Delhi; 1774 Awadh plus EIC (Treaty of Allahabad 1765) annex Rohilkhand, leaving Rampur; 1802 EIC annexes Farrukhabad.

items.t: 8 · Why Abdali came: the immediate trigger
items.x: Why Abdali came, the immediate trigger: to avenge the Marathas' expulsion of his son Timur Shah from Lahore. March 1758: Raghunath Rao crossed into Punjab and drove away Timur Shah (Abdali's son and Governor of Punjab and Kashmir). The Marathas then made Adina Beg Khan Governor of Punjab for Rs 75 lakh a year; on his death Sabaji Scindia took charge. Sabaji Scindia held the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar on the Afghan border and defended them fiercely. The Maratha conquest of Punjab from the Afghans was a direct challenge Abdali could not ignore. Sabaji Scindia commanded the Maratha garrisons at Attock and Peshawar (on the Afghan border) and fiercely defended them against Abdali. The Maratha conquest of Punjab from the Afghans was a direct challenge Abdali could not ignore: that was the immediate trigger. (a) To avenge the expulsion by the Marathas of his viceroy Timur Shah from Lahore; (b) The fast expansion of the Maratha Empire across the subcontinent; (c) Refusal of the Mughal Emperor to pay annual tribute; (d) Refusal of the Sultan of Punjab to grant safe passage. items.t: 9 · Synthesis: three Rebel States, one pattern
items.x: Synthesis, three Rebel States, one pattern. The Jats: from an agrarian base upward, Zamindar-led revolt, territory, a reforming ruler (Surajmal). Farrukhabad: from Mughal court politics downward, 12,000 troops for Farukhsiyar, a Nawab title, a city, a dynasty. Rohilkhand: from the ground up over two decades, hired mercenaries, consolidation, independence in the 1739 Delhi paralysis. The common rule: each needed external support to peak (Abdali for the Afghans, Maratha tactical backing for Surajmal) and each collapsed once that support was removed. items.t: 1 · How did Sikhism begin, and what were its core beliefs?
items.x: How did Sikhism begin and what were its core beliefs? Founder: Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539), a contemporary of Babur 26-30. Rise: Sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on 4 core principles: one supreme and formless God; direct access to God without rituals or priests; rejection of the caste system; emphasis on honest living and selfless service. Udasis: 4 major spiritual journeys over 30 years, about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. Kartarpur: he finally settled there (present-day Pakistan). Langar: there he established the institution of Langar, a free communal kitchen designed to promote equality. Guru Nanak Dev (1469-1539) was a contemporary of Babur 26-30. Sikhism rose from 1500 onwards, built on four core principles: One supreme and formless God. Direct access to God without rituals or priests. Rejection of the caste system. Emphasis on honest living and selfless service. Guru Nanak undertook four major spiritual journeys (Udasis) over 30 years, covering about 30,000 km across India, South Asia, Tibet and Arabia. He finally settled in Kartarpur (present-day Pakistan), where he established the Langar, the free communal kitchen designed to promote equality.

items.t: 2 · When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State?
items.x: When did conflict begin between the Sikhs and the Mughal State? No conflict at first, but as the Sikh population grew and Sikhs began demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla and south of Chamba, an area under Shivalik Hill Chiefs who were Mughal allies), religious and political tensions began. 1606, first flashpoint: the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, executed by Jahangir 05-27; a turning point, a peaceful spiritual movement began transforming into a martial community. 1675, second flashpoint: the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07. Initially there was no conflict. But as the Sikh population grew and Sikhs began demanding a Sikh State in and around Anandpur (west of Shimla and south of Chamba), an area under the Shivalik Hill Chiefs who were Mughal allies, religious and political tensions built up. First flashpoint, 1606: the 5th Guru, Arjan Dev, was executed by Jahangir 05-27. A turning point: a peaceful spiritual movement began its transformation into a martial community. Second flashpoint, 1675: the 9th Guru, Teg Bahadur, was executed in Delhi by Aurangzeb 58-07.

items.t: 4 · December 1704 to October 1708: the Sahibzadas and the Guru's death
items.x: December 1704 to October 1708: Sahibzadas and the Guru's death. Dec 1704, Battle of Chamkaur: the Guru's 2 elder sons, Sahibzada Ajit Singh (aged 18) and Sahibzada Jujhar Singh (aged 14), died in battle. The same month his 2 younger sons, Sahibzada Zorawar Singh (aged 9) and Sahibzada Fateh Singh (aged 6), were buried alive in a wall on Wazir Khan's orders. 1707: the new emperor Bahadur Shah 07-12, following a pacifist policy (diplomacy more than war), granted the Guru a high Mansab and promised a Sikh State in and around Anandpur, but the promise was never fulfilled. Oct 7, 1708: Wazir Khan sent assassins to attack the Guru at Abchal Nagar Sahib Gurdwara, Nanded, Maharashtra, where he had accompanied Bahadur Shah. items.t: 5 · Why the Guru declared the Guru Granth Sahib the final Guru
items.x: Why did Guru Gobind Singh declare the Guru Granth Sahib Ji the final Guru? Declaration: a few days before his death, at Abchal Nagar Sahib, he would be the last living Guru and all spiritual authority would henceforth be vested in the Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the holy book he had compiled. Why, deliberate: to prevent tensions between the Jat community, which dominated the Khalsa, and the Khatri community of traders, to which all 10 Gurus belonged; vesting authority in the holy book rather than a human successor permanently closed the question of community dominance. Installed at: the Akal Takht, in the Golden Temple complex, Amritsar. Akal Takht: from here the Gurus issued Hukumnamas (formal orders) and Sikh warriors took blessings before battle against the Mughals. Later exception: the 19th-century sects of Nirankaris and Namdharis believe in a living Guru, which historically led to serious conflicts within the community. items.t: 6 · Banda Bahadur 08-15: the first Sikh State, and why it collapsed
items.x: How did Banda Bahadur 08-15 establish the first Sikh State? From 1708 the rebellion was carried forward by Banda Bahadur. May 10, 1710, the Battle of Chappar Chiri: he defeated and killed Wazir Khan, which also led to the conquest of Sirhind. The 1st Sikh State was established between the Ravi and the Jamuna, with its own coins, officials and seal (ink: full independence). Mughal response: Farukhsiyar 13-19 appointed Abdus Samad Khan Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress the Sikh State. 1715: defeated as the economic and military support base eroded; Banda Bahadur was captured and executed in Delhi in 1716 by Farukhsiyar. From 1708 the rebellion was carried forward by Banda Bahadur 08-15. He defeated and killed Wazir Khan at the Battle of Chappar Chiri on 10 May 1710, which also led to the conquest of Sirhind. He established a Sikh State over territories between the River Ravi and the River Jamuna, with its own coins, its own officials and its own seal for administrative orders (the teacher's ink: full independence). Farrukhsiyar 13-19 appointed Abdus Samad Khan as Governor of Lahore specifically to suppress this Sikh State. By 1715 Banda Bahadur 08-15 was defeated; captured and executed in Delhi in 1716 by Farrukhsiyar 13-19. Flag on the territory: the handout places Banda's State between the Ravi and the Jamuna; the teacher's ink on the board says "a small state in and around Patiala." Both appear in the class material; the handout's wording is the answer-writing one.  Why did Banda Bahadur 08-15's Sikh State collapse by 1715? (1) Khatri traders turned against him: constant warfare hurt trade, and the commercial class needs decisive victors and political stability. (2) Divide and Rule: Jahandar Shah 12-13 introduced Ijaradari (revenue farming) in Punjab specifically to co-opt Khatri traders with business opportunities; both Jahandar Shah and Farukhsiyar offered Mansabs to Khatri traders, who switched sides (this further increased the number of Mansabdars, adding to the Jagirdari Crisis discussed earlier). (3) Jat zamindars: Hindu Jat zamindars switched sides; Churaman Jat (1695-1721), for instance, went over to the Mughals after they recognised his Jat Kingdom, conditional dynastic autonomy in exchange for loyalty. (Note: this further increased the number of Mansabdars, adding to the Jagirdari Crisis; see Chapter 2.) Hindu Jat zamindars switched sides. items.t: 7 · What kept the Sikh State alive: the Misl confederacy
items.x: What kept the Sikh State alive after Banda Bahadur 08-15's defeat? After defeat: the defeat did not end the Sikh State; the Mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab and power was decentralised among Misl Chiefs. Misls: kinship-based clans, united during wars (particularly against Afghan invasions), otherwise independent. Land shares: whenever a Misl conquered territory, lands were distributed among members in proportion to military and monetary contribution; even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share. By 1770: 12 major Misls in Punjab, with the Dal Khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the Misl chiefs, a confederacy structure (weak centre, strong constituent units). Takeaway: this mirrors the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, a nominal centre holding largely autonomous regional chiefs; decentralisation was both a source of resilience and ultimately a vulnerability. The defeat of Banda Bahadur 08-15 did not end the Sikh State. The Mughals were too weak to fully reassert control over Punjab, and power became decentralised among Misl Chiefs. Misls are kinship-based clans. They united during wars, particularly against Afghan invasions, but otherwise operated independently. Whenever a Misl conquered territory, the lands were distributed among its members in proportion to their military and monetary contribution. Even the lowest-ranking soldier received a share of land. By 1770 there were 12 major Misls in Punjab, with the Dal Khalsa at the centre under a leader chosen by the Misl chiefs: a confederacy structure with a weak centre and strong constituent units. Takeaway (handout): compare it to the Maratha Confederacy under the Peshwas, where a nominal centre held together largely autonomous regional chiefs. Decentralisation was both a source of resilience and, ultimately, a vulnerability.  Teacher's board: misl confederacy. Death of Banda Bahadur 08-15 = no strong centre, so power decentralised to misl chiefs. Polity structure: a Confederacy (of misls); fragmented. Picture: a big circle Punjab containing about 12 smaller circles (misls), roughly 40-60 misls. Plus the Dal Khalsa = assembly of misl chiefs: e.g. on Abdali's 1748 invasion the Dal Khalsa will meet and a joint defence will be prepared; e.g. Manupur 1748 (written Bomanpur): Abdali defeated by the Sikhs. items.t: 9 · The Treaty of Amritsar (1809)
items.x: The 1809 Treaty of Amritsar with the EIC. Outcome 1: the EIC recognised Ranjit Singh as the sovereign ruler of Punjab. Outcome 2: it led to a military alliance (later link to the EIC's Policy of Ring Fence). Outcome 3: the Sutlej River was fixed as the border between the Sikh State and the Company State. Outcome 4: Ranjit Singh was free to expand his State on his side of the Sutlej without British interference. items.t: 11 · What kind of State did Ranjit Singh 01-39 build?
items.x: What kind of State did Ranjit Singh 01-39 build? Power built by a skilful combination of coercion, diplomacy and careful balance between Misl chiefs, the Khalsa army, Khatri traders and non-Sikh nobles like the Dogras (similar to the successor states discussed earlier). Character: militarily strong and economically prosperous. Revenue policy: fair for the masses; trade flourished as a strong State delivered the law-and-order stability commerce requires. Land and King: only 40% of land under the Jagirdari system; from the remaining land revenue went directly to the King, giving considerable monetary power.  What kind of State did Ranjit Singh build (contd.)? Kardar: land revenue, the main income source, collected by Kardars, the chief administrative officer at the Taluqa (district) level, who acted as revenue collector, local magistrate (judge), police chief and customs officer. Ijaradari: Ranjit Singh heavily relied on the Ijaradari system; instead of a fixed cash salary a Kardar often acted as an Ijaradar, but it was ensured the ryot was not oppressed by very high LR. Village autonomy: State authority stopped at the village level; the power of local chiefs and clans was respected (this will connect directly to the Mahalwari Settlement in Punjab, where even the British respected this tradition of village-level autonomy).  What made the Sikh State hold together? Secular administration: key positions held by men from different religious backgrounds, Fakir Azizuddin (a Muslim) as Foreign Minister and Dewan Dina Nath (a Hindu) handling the finances as Finance Minister. Culturally broad: Ranjit Singh was magnanimous; Sikh identity expanded to include non-Khalsa Sikhs, the Sahajdhari Sikhs, who do not maintain the 5 Ks of Khalsa identity (Kesh, Kangha, Kada, Kirpan, Kachhera). The State he built: politically inclusive, respecting village and local autonomy, and culturally broad. The story of the Sikh State after Ranjit Singh (the Anglo-Sikh Wars and eventual annexation by the EIC) continues in a later chapter. items.t: 1 · Akbar 56-05 and the Rajputs
items.x: Akbar 56-05 and the Rajputs. 16th-c Rajputana: no single central power, roughly 20 major Rajput clans, each controlling its own territory (modern IR: multi-polar world, many power centres, no single dominant one). Akbar's approach: defeating all would be expensive and uncertain, so he co-opted more powerful Rajput chiefs as Mansabdars (ranked nobles with military and administrative responsibilities); home territories recognised as Vatan Jagirs (land remained theirs but within the Mughal framework); obligations: accepted the Mughal Emperor as sovereign, paid tributes, contributed troops; they formed a Hindu bloc within the Mansabdari system (about 15% of all Mansabdars); in return Akbar helped them subdue smaller Rajput Chiefs; result: partial consolidation of power. Teacher's ink: (Centralization) under Result; a row of circled numbers 1 2 3 ... 20 (the clans) with an arrow to a block labelled Mewar with a tick for Marwar (a few strong clans swallowing smaller ones); whole Rajputana not under 1 king; a triangle crossed out (no single king or pyramid). items.t: 2 · Rajputs against Aurangzeb 58-07, and the Marathas
items.x: 1680 Rajput revolt, trigger and collapse. Mewar expands: the arrangement held through most of the 17th c, trouble came under Aurangzeb 58-07, with Mewar under Raj Singh expanding aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states. Aurangzeb was uneasy: he did not want one Rajput power to dominate all Rajputana and become a rival to the Mughal State. 1680, the trigger: a child came to the throne in Marwar, a kingdom astride the trade route connecting Delhi and Agra to Ahmedabad; Aurangzeb interfered in the succession. Marwar and Mewar revolted, and collapsed: the other Rajput chiefs refused to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them if the revolt succeeded; each stood aside, so the rebellion collapsed. Mewar expands: under Raj Singh, aggressively against neighbouring Rajput states Aurangzeb 58-07 is uneasy: he did not want one Rajput power to dominate all Rajputana and rival the Mughals (warn) 1680, the trigger: a child comes to the throne in Marwar (astride the Delhi/Agra to Ahmedabad trade route); Aurangzeb 58-07 interferes in the succession Marwar and Mewar revolt (bad) The rebellion collapses: the other Rajput chiefs refuse to join, fearing Mewar would dominate them  Handout Diagram 1 (Rajputs): 16th century Rajputana with about 20 major clans and no single centre (multi-polar world); Akbar co-opts powerful Rajput chiefs, who help subdue the smaller; Rajputs = Hindu bloc of Mansabdars (about 15%), accept the Mughal emperor, pay tribute, contribute troops; Aurangzeb uneasy as Mewar under Raj Singh expands; 1680 Marwar and Mewar both revolt, other chiefs refuse to join, rebellion collapses; post-1707 Sawai Jai Singh (1699-1743) of Amber rules Jaipur and remains a Mansabdar in Delhi but on his own terms; 1751 onwards Marathas raid Rajputana (tribute, succession meddling), never conquer the region; post-2nd Anglo-Maratha War 1803-05 the EIC signs Subordinate / Subsidiary Alliances with Rajput states. Post-1707: the Rajputs increasingly acted on their own terms, the most prominent being Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber, who ruled Jaipur and remained a powerful Mansabdar in Delhi but on his own conditions. 1751 onwards: the Marathas begin regular raids into Rajputana, extracting tribute and interfering in succession disputes, never fully conquering the region. After the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05): the EIC replaced the Marathas as the regional power and signed Subordinate Alliances (also called Subsidiary Alliances) with Rajput states. Subordinate Alliance terms: like World History's term Protectorate, the Indian ruler kept his throne but surrendered control of foreign policy and defence to the EIC, which stationed its own troops, paid for by the Indian ruler; in Suzerainty = loss of external sovereign functions plus loss of symbolic sovereignty. items.t: 3 · Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber (1699-1743)
items.x: Sawai Jai Singh 99-43 of Amber (1699-1743). Sawai: a title (1.25 more able than any contemporary ruler) conferred by Aurangzeb 58-07. 4 roles at once: Mughal Mansabdar, regional state-builder, astronomer and town planner (ink: arrows to Prelims). Subedar: held the Subedari of Malwa (1729-37) and Agra (ink: [Governor]). Hurda conference, 1734: a conference of Rajput rulers to forge a united front against the Marathas, which collapsed due to internal Rajput rivalries. Treaty of Bhopal: 1738, Malwa annexed by the Marathas (ink: Sawai Jai Singh = Mughal Governor of Malwa). Jaipur founded, 1727: designed by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya on Vastu Shastra principles, a grid-pattern layout; Jaipur = the 1st planned city of modern India; Sawai Ram Singh painted it pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales. Social reform: attempted to curb dowry and excessive marriage expenditure among Rajputs, with limited success. Last Yajnas: the last Indian ruler to perform Ashvamedha and Vajapeya Yajnas, a conscious assertion of Hindu Chakravartin status as Mughal authority collapsed. items.t: 4 · Travancore: Marthanda Varma 29-58
items.x: Travancore under Marthanda Varma 29-58. Mughal relation: never part of the Mughal Empire, the Mughal State simply never expanded far enough south to include it. Centralised State: by the 1740s built a strong, centralised State by subjugating local chiefs across the region. European-style military: modern weapons, trained soldiers. Takeaway, trade to State capacity: a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast; revenues reinvested into the military, irrigation works and transport infrastructure, a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity. Travancore was never part of the Mughal Empire. The Mughal State simply never expanded far enough south to include it. By the 1740s, Marthanda Varma 29-58 had built a strong, centralised State by subjugating local chiefs across the region, and a European-style military: modern weapons, trained soldiers. Takeaway: Travancore established a State monopoly over the trade of the Malabar coast. The revenues were reinvested into the military, irrigation works and transport infrastructure: a classic example of a small State using trade income to build State capacity. 4.1 Colachel 1741 and the fall of the Dutch  Colachel 1741 and the Dutch fall in India. Since 1663: the Dutch East India Company's Malabar headquarters at Cochin (central Kerala), captured from the Portuguese. 1741, Battle of Colachel: a landmark in the history of Kerala; Marthanda Varma's army crushed the Dutch East India Company. Effect, terminal: it permanently ended Dutch political and military ambitions in Kerala, relegating them to mere merchants in Cochin. 1759, Battle of Bedara (also called the Battle of Chinsura): the British EIC defeated the Dutch in Bengal, crushing their remaining ambitions in India. 1795: final expulsion from South Asia by the British, Ceylon / Sri Lanka. items.t: 5 · Travancore against Mysore and the EIC
items.x: Travancore under Rama Varma 58-98. Character shift: became a centre of art and scholarship but military strength declined; consequences were quick. 1766: Haider Ali 61-82 of Mysore annexed Malabar and Calicut. Why Malabar mattered: the heart of the spice trade (pepper, cardamom, ginger); whoever controlled Malabar's ports controlled a significant share of Indian Ocean commerce, which is why both Mysore and the British were so interested. After 1798: Travancore came steadily under British influence. Under Rama Varma 58-98 Travancore became a centre of art and scholarship, but military strength declined. The consequences were quick: in 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 of Mysore annexed Malabar and Calicut. (Malabar was the heart of the spice trade: pepper, cardamom, ginger. Whoever controlled Malabar's ports controlled a significant share of Indian Ocean commerce, which is why both Mysore and the British were so interested.) After 1798 Travancore came steadily under British influence.  Subsidiary Alliance 1805 to the Velu Thampi revolt 1809. 1805, Nair mutiny: a mutiny among Nair troops over non-payment of salaries (note: Shashi Tharoor is from the Nair community). Travancore sought British help and in return was made to sign a Subsidiary Alliance (1805), effectively ending its independence. Anger at the 1805 terms (heavy financial burden and interference in internal affairs); resistance led by Velu Thampi Dalawa, the Prime Minister (Dalawa) of Travancore. 1809: revolt against the British Resident; he rallied the Nair troops and issued a public proclamation, the Kundara Proclamation (1809), calling on the people to rise against British control. Suppressed: the British moved swiftly and Velu Thampi, seeing no escape, took his own life (one of the earliest organised resistance movements by an Indian ruler against the Subsidiary Alliance system, directly tested in UPSC). Dalawa = Prime Minister and Chief of Armed Forces; Dewan (for a State subordinated by the British) = Head of ALL administration (revenue, civil, police and criminal justice), the military being with the British. 1805 Nair mutiny: troops unpaid Travancore seeks British help (warn) In return it signs the Subsidiary Alliance (1805): independence effectively ends Anger: heavy financial burden and interference in internal affairs; Velu Thampi Dalawa leads resistance 1809 revolt: against the British Resident, Kundara Proclamation calls the people to rise (bad) Suppressed: Velu Thampi, seeing no escape, takes his own life Teacher: A light note: Shashi Tharoor is from the Nair community.
