items.t: 6 · Mysore: from Vijayanagar to Haider Ali 61-82
items.x: Mysore, Vijayanagar to Haider Ali 61-82. The Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646): Mysore was part of it. 1565, Battle of Talikota: a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated Vijayanagar forces; the dynasty lingered until 1646, but 1565 was the operational end as a major power. Wodeyar dynasty: after Vijayanagar's decline Mysore gradually became autonomous; under Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar 72-04 it was militarily powerful and centrally governed. By 1761 the Wodeyars were reduced to puppets by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj. 1761: Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj: began as a junior military officer (the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts); capable, ambitious and strategic, he seized effective power, keeping the Wodeyar as the nominal head of State. Pattern alert at the 18th c: the King becomes a puppet as personality weakens (recall Peshwa and Chhatrapati). Mysore was part of the Vijayanagar Empire (1336-1646). The Empire's effective power was shattered at the Battle of Talikota (also called Rakkasa-Tangadi) in 1565, when a coalition of Deccan Sultanates decisively defeated Vijayanagar. The dynasty lingered until 1646, but 1565 marks the operational end of Vijayanagar as a major power. After Vijayanagar's decline Mysore gradually became autonomous under the Wodeyar dynasty. Under Chikka Devaraja 72-04 Wodeyar (1672-1704) it was militarily powerful and centrally governed. By 1761 the Wodeyars had been reduced to figureheads by a powerful and corrupt Prime Minister, NanjRaj. Haider Ali 61-82 ended that. He began as a junior military officer, his early career made possible partly because the Wodeyars had helped pay off his family's debts. Capable, ambitious and strategic, in 1761 he overthrew NanjRaj and seized effective power, keeping the Wodeyar as a nominal head of State. Pattern alert at the 18th century: the king becomes a puppet as personality weakens. Recall the Peshwa and Chhatrapati relationship (Chapter 4). 6.1 Haider Ali 61-82's military machine  Haider Ali 61-82's military machine. French assistance: military training, technology transfer and organisational reform. Risalas: the army structured on a European model, organised into Risalas (regiments). Each Risala: a commander directly appointed by the King (personal loyalty to the King); a clear chain of command; self-sufficient, with its own weapons, transport and supplies (recall the Campoo system of Scindhia). Result: a fast, efficient military, regiments capable of independent action. Poligars subjugated: local chiefs and landlords who controlled land, the wealth of temples and their own armed men, the real rulers of the rural areas since the Vijayanagar era (1336-1646); a civil war of roughly 20 years spent subjugating them. Deshmukhs subjugated: next slide. Outcome: the power of Non-State Actors was systematically ended. Haider Ali 61-82 took French assistance for military training, technology transfer and organisational reform. The army was now on a European model, organised into Risalas (regiments): Each Risala's commander was directly appointed by the King, ensuring personal loyalty upward. Each unit had a clear chain of command. Each was self-sufficient: its own weapons, transport and supplies (recall the Campoo system of Scindia, Chapter 4). Result: a fast, efficient military with regiments capable of independent action. He then spent roughly twenty years subjugating the Poligars (local chiefs and landlords who controlled land, the wealth of temples and had their own armed men, the real rulers of the countryside since the Vijayanagar era) and the Deshmukhs (revenue collectors who functioned like primary zamindars). Non-State power was systematically dismantled. 6.2 How Mysore funded this machine: Military Fiscalism  Military fiscalism of Tipu 82-99 (and Haider Ali 61-82): Mysore's revenue reforms. Khalisa lands expanded: more revenue went to the State treasury. Jagirdari minimised: maximised State income while reducing the independent economic power of nobles. Direct collection: Deshmukhs were removed as intermediaries; State officials collected taxes directly and received salaries, far smaller than the commissions intermediaries take.  Military fiscalism (contd.). Detailed field surveys: assessed land revenue scientifically (soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access and past production trends), preventing over-assessment so ryots were not oppressed. Investing in agriculture: 1. old irrigation canals repaired and new ones built; 2. cash crops promoted; 3. sericulture (cultivation of silk via silkworms) introduced. Boosted tax collection: more income for peasants meant more tax revenue for the State; even Tipu's enemies acknowledged that Mysore's population was among the most prosperous. All of this and the last slide = Military Fiscalism: huge generation of State wealth for a stronger military for empire building.   Policy   Effect    --- ---    Khalisa land expanded   More revenue went directly to the State treasury     Jagirdari minimised   Maximised State income, reducing the nobles' independent economic power     Direct collection   Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries; State officials collected taxes and got salaries (far smaller than commissions)     Detailed field surveys   Assessed LR by soil fertility, crop type, irrigation access and past production trends; prevented over-assessment     Investing in agriculture   Canals repaired and built; cash crops promoted; sericulture introduced     Boosted tax collection   More peasant income meant a larger tax base; even enemies admitted Mysore's population was among the most prosperous   These policies are called Military Fiscalism: the systematic generation of State wealth as a foundation for military power. (The handout's analogy: replacing a commission-based agent with a salaried employee; the State kept far more of the revenue.) Khalisa land = land whose revenue went directly to the State treasury. Jagirdari land = land whose revenue was assigned to nobles or commanders.

items.t: 7 · Tipu 82-99 Sultan (1782-99): innovations and why he still lost
items.x: Tipu 82-99's innovations. Modern navy and trading company: a government-owned trading company like the EIC for oceanic trade in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk and cardamom; 30 trading centres inside and outside India, including Muscat, Oman. Factory then: before the age of machines a factory meant a warehouse and so on (details in Ch 8). Iron-cased rocket artillery: Haider Ali and Tipu, 100% indigenous; range 2 km; iron casings did not burst and took high pressure (versus the centuries-old cardboard-casing rockets and fireworks of India and China); studied closely by the British, William Congreve's rockets (deployed in the early 19th c) were inspired by Tipu's designs. 1785, independence and sanad: formally declared independence from both the Wodeyars and the Mughal Emperor; requested a sanad (official order) from the Khalifa (religious head of the Muslim world) recognising him as a ruler independent of Mughal authority. Modern embassies: in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar (Prelims 2001). Modern navy and trading company: a government-owned trading company modelled on the EIC, trading in sandalwood, sulphur, rice, pepper, silk and cardamom, with 30 trading centres inside and outside India, including Muscat, Oman. (Before the age of machines a "factory" meant a warehouse or trading depot, not a production facility; a trading settlement meant warehouses, homes, offices and sometimes a fort. Details in Chapter 8.) Iron-cased rocket artillery: developed by Haider Ali 61-82 and Tipu 82-99, 100% indigenous, range 2 km; the iron cylinder casings did not burst and could take high pressure compared with cardboard-cased rockets (fireworks), which existed for centuries in India and China. The British studied them closely: William Congreve's rockets, deployed in the early 19th century, drew directly from Tipu 82-99's designs. 1785: Tipu 82-99 formally declared independence from both the Wodeyars and the Mughal Emperor, and requested a sanad from the Khalifa recognising him as independent of Mughal authority. Modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. 7.1 Tipu 82-99 and Revolutionary France  Tipu 82-99 and Revolutionary France. 1790s: sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British. The 23-year Wars (1792-1815): the French Revolution of 1789 pitted France against the rest of the European monarchies. 1798: Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East, partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea. Alliance with France (did not materialise into military support): exchanged communications with Napoleon; planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore (a symbol of the French Revolution, planted across France and later across Europe); joined the Jacobin Club, the radical political organisation at the heart of the French Revolution. The British were alarmed and this also became a reason for the 4th Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. In the 1790s Tipu 82-99 sent an ambassador to France seeking military technology and a formal alliance against the British. Since 1789 the French Revolution had set France on a collision course with the monarchies of Europe, including Britain (the 23-year wars, 1792-1815). In 1798 Napoleon attacked Egypt and the Middle East, partly to disrupt British trade in the Arabian Sea. Tipu 82-99 exchanged communications with Napoleon and planted a Tree of Liberty in Mysore (a symbol of the French Revolution), and joined the Jacobin Club. The alliance did not materialise into military support. The British were alarmed, and it became a reason for the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War of 1799. Prelims 2001: who established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? Answer (d): Tipu 82-99 Sultan. He set up modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt, alongside new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar. The Jacobin membership and Tree of Liberty marked him in British eyes as an ideological adversary, not merely a military one. 7.2 Why Mysore lost  Why Mysore lost. Over-ambitious: wanted to dominate all of South India and control its international trade = Vijayanagar 2.0. Drain due to war: constant warfare against neighbouring Indian powers and the EIC drained the State's resources faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish them. 1766, trigger: Haider Ali invaded and annexed Malabar and Calicut [could not successfully invade Travancore], leading to the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), as the EIC feared losing coastal trade access through Malabar. 4 Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. 1799, end: the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War ended with the death of Tipu at Seringapatam, Mysore's power broken. Mysore's long-term ambition was to dominate all of South India and control its international trade (Vijayanagar 2.0). But constant warfare against neighbouring Indian powers and the EIC drained the State's resources faster than Military Fiscalism could replenish them. The ambition was real; the capacity, ultimately, was not enough. 1766: Haider Ali 61-82 annexed Malabar and Calicut, triggering the First Anglo-Mysore War (1767-69), as the EIC feared losing coastal trade access through Malabar. Four Anglo-Mysore Wars: 1767-69, 1780-84, 1790-92, 1799. The Fourth (1799) ended with Tipu 82-99's death at Seringapatam; Mysore's power was broken. Flag on Travancore: the handout's section 7 says that in 1766 Haider Ali 61-82 "had invaded Travancore and annexed Malabar and Calicut", while the same chapter (section 4) says he annexed Malabar and Calicut, and the teacher's bracket on the slide adds "could not successfully invade Travancore." Use the slide's wording: Malabar and Calicut were annexed; Travancore was not successfully invaded.  Handout Diagram 3: Mysore's rise and the ambition-versus-capacity collapse. Vijayanagar Empire 1336-1646, 1565 Talikota (Rakkasa-Tangadi) breaks it; Wodeyar dynasty rises in Mysore, Chikka Devaraja Wodeyar (1672-1704) militarily powerful and centrally governed; by 1761 the Wodeyars are figureheads under corrupt PM NanjRaj; 1761 Haider Ali (junior officer whose debts Wodeyars paid) overthrows NanjRaj, Wodeyar kept nominal (pattern: Peshwa-Chhatrapati mirror); French military reform: Risala regiments (personal loyalty to the King, self-sufficient, 20 years subjugating Poligars and Deshmukhs); Military Fiscalism: Khalisa land expanded, Jagirdari shrunk, Deshmukhs removed as intermediaries, field surveys, sericulture, cash crops, irrigation; Tipu 82-99: modern navy, government trading company (30 centres including Muscat), iron-cased rockets (Congreve copies), independence from Wodeyars and Mughals (Khalifa sanad); 1790s embassy to France (Prelims 2001 trap: Tipu = modern embassies), Tree of Liberty, Jacobin Club; 1799 Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu dies at Seringapatam.  Prelims 2001 question slide: Who among the following Indian rulers established embassies in foreign countries on modern lines? (a) Haider Ali (b) Mir Qasim (c) Shah Alam II (d) Tipu Sultan.  Prelims 2001, answer key. Answer: (d) Tipu Sultan. Why (d) is correct: Tipu set up modern embassies in France, Turkey and Egypt alongside other administrative innovations such as a new coinage and the Mauludi Lunisolar Calendar; the chapter also covers his iron-cased rocket artillery (later studied by William Congreve), his government-owned trading company (30 trading centres including Muscat, Oman), his sanad request to the Khalifa and his French alliance (Tree of Liberty and Jacobin Club membership). Why the others are wrong: (a) Haider Ali built the Mysore army on a French model (with Risalas) and fought the EIC in the early Anglo-Mysore Wars but did not set up modern embassies; (b) Mir Qasim was a Nawab of Bengal who fought the EIC at Buxar (1764) and did not establish foreign embassies; (c) Shah Alam II 60-06 was a Mughal Emperor whose authority was reduced after Buxar; foreign embassies were not part of his programme. 1761 Haider Ali 61-82 overthrows NanjRaj; the Wodeyar stays nominal French-assisted Risalas: self-sufficient regiments under commanders loyal to the King Military Fiscalism: Khalisa expanded, Deshmukhs removed, surveys, canals, sericulture: wealth for war Tipu 82-99: navy, government trading company, iron-cased rockets, 1785 independence, modern embassies, French link (warn) Overreach: ambition to dominate all South India (Vijayanagar 2.0); constant war drains the State faster than fiscalism refills it (bad) 1799: Fourth Anglo-Mysore War, Tipu 82-99 dies at Seringapatam; Mysore's power broken   Feature   Rajputs   Travancore   Mysore    --- --- --- ---    Relation to the Mughals   Co-opted by Akbar 56-05: Mansabdars with Vatan Jagirs; Hindu bloc (15%)   Never part of the Mughal Empire   Part of Vijayanagar, then autonomous under the Wodeyars     Key figure   Sawai Jai Singh 99-43   Marthanda Varma 29-58   Haider Ali 61-82, Tipu 82-99     Strength   Astronomy, Jaipur, politics on own terms   Trade monopoly, centralised State, Colachel 1741   Risalas, Military Fiscalism, rockets, trade company     End   Subordinate Alliances after 1803-05   Subsidiary Alliance 1805; revolt 1809   Four wars; Tipu 82-99 dies 1799

items.t: 1 · Asia, the economic power of the world
items.x: Sec 1 Asia: Economic Power of the World. Three main attractions: Indonesia (Java and Sumatra) for spices, India for textiles (plus Malabar for spices), China for silk and tea. Routes: China by land (the Silk Route); India and Indonesia a mix of land and sea through the Middle East and the Arabian Sea. Arab traders dominated the Arabian Sea leg; Italian merchants of Genoa and Venice carried goods across the Mediterranean into Europe; both earned enormous profits at each handoff. Teacher's sketch: EU at the top, Mediterranean Sea and Arabian Sea as funnels meeting at a point, a new-route arrow from EU round to the Cape of Good Hope, and a note: the empire of Arabs and Ottoman. items.t: 2 · The Ottoman blockade (1453) and the Age of Discovery
items.x: Sec 2 Ottoman Blockade and Age of Discovery. 1453 interruption: the Ottoman Empire captured Constantinople (today's Istanbul) and blockaded the traditional land trade routes connecting Europe to Asia; European traders needed a new way east. Age of Discovery (16th c): this necessity became the engine of one of history's great turning points; European powers, led initially by Portugal and Spain, sent ships into the Atlantic searching for a direct sea route to the East. The era gave: 1 better use of the astrolabe for location and the magnetic compass for direction; 2 the system of latitudes and longitudes and the modern world map; 3 geography as a formal discipline; 4 the invention of the Caravel, a ship able to sail at an angle against the wind. Teacher's ink: effectively blockaded; not literally (they demanded a share of profits on trade, making trade unviable for Europeans); a sketch of a ship sailing at an angle to the wind. items.t: 4 · The Portuguese in India
items.x: 4.0 · Da Gama at Calicut (1498)  Sec 4 Portuguese Arrive in India. Da Gama at Calicut (1498): armed with the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) and backed by the Portuguese Crown, Vasco Da Gama reached Calicut (today's Kozhikode, Kerala) in 1498, having sailed around the Cape of Good Hope, the southernmost point of Africa. He traded and left: he received permission to trade from the Zamorin of Calicut but faced heavy opposition from Arab traders; no factory or permanent settlement on this voyage. Teacher's ink: NOT COCHIN (beside Calicut); King of Calicut kingdom (over Zamorin). Right-hand board: Primary purpose of Europeans = Trade, not Empire building. But empire building took place in the Americas (weak states) while India had strong states (land powers, i.e. strong armies). Bottom board: resources from mining e.g. gold and silver; if empire building is possible then greater trade profits, and they can get land revenue (LR) and other taxes; with political control, as Government in any territory you can export goods to the home country at low price. No factory or permanent settlement on this voyage   The handout adds: the Cape was named "Cape of Good Hope" by Portugal's King John II, as it represented hope of finally finding a sea route to India. The teacher wrote "NOT COCHIN" beside Calicut: Da Gama landed at Calicut (1498), and the first permanent factory was at Cochin (1500), not his landing place. Why South India was vulnerable (handout): when the Portuguese arrived, the Mughal Empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist in India. South India was divided between the Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, without a unified central naval power. This fragmentation let the Portuguese dominate trade and some territory in the 16th century. Character of the Portuguese approach: part commerce, part conquest, part coercion. Teacher: Learn the west coast from north to south: Diu, Surat, Daman, Bombay, Goa, Mahe, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore. Calicut = a small kingdom; Cochin = a small kingdom on the northern border of Travancore. The dates printed on this map differ from some dates in the handout text (for example Goa 1610 on the map against 1510 in the text; Bombay 1638 on the map against 1668 in the handout). Use the handout text and tables (T1) for exam dates; the map is for locating places and showing who came where. 4.1 · Structure of trade: a State enterprise  4.1 Portuguese Trade Was a State Enterprise. Not a private company: unlike the private companies the British and Dutch would later set up, Portuguese trade was operated as a State enterprise. Estado da India (boxed): directly controlled by the Portuguese Crown through its official administration, so the Portuguese government itself was the trader. Teacher's ink: English EIC, Dutch VOC/EIC (arrows to British and Dutch); like PSU / Govt; right side: French EIC initially a private company, later taken over by the French Govt. Unlike the private joint-stock companies the British and Dutch later set up, Portuguese trade was a State enterprise called the Estado da India, directly controlled by the Portuguese Crown through its official administration. The Portuguese government was the trader. Teacher: [Like a PSU / Govt]. The English EIC and the Dutch VOC were private companies. The teacher's side note: the French EIC was initially a private company; later taken over by the French Govt. Depot, Factory, Settlement In this period a "factory" did not mean a manufacturing unit. It was a trading post: warehouses for storing goods, offices for trade, homes for company employees, and often a fort for protection. The word comes from "factor," a merchant agent; the factory was where factors worked.  4.1 Depot vs Factory vs Settlement (table). Primary function: Trading Depot (Warehouse) purely storage for goods awaiting ship arrival; Factory (Commercial Hub) administrative and commercial HQ for merchant agents; Settlement (Colonial Enclave) small territorial colony with civil and town administration. Components: basic godowns; offices, warehouses and homes for factors (also called Trading post); factory complex plus surrounding towns and annexed lands. Permanent staff: No; Yes (factors); Yes (factors, soldiers, administrative personnel). Legal status: minimal, simple permission to store goods; factory via formal Imperial or local farmans; Zamindari (revenue) and other sovereign territorial rights. Territorial jurisdiction: No; No; Yes over a defined zone or town. Tax or customs authority: No; No; Yes (taxes can be applied only by a State-like organization). Teacher's ink: think bus depot; Trading post; Don't confuse with LEJ here; for going out of India; Office; multiple factories, warehouses; collect LR and consume LR; L E J (Legislative, Executive, Judicial); Taxes can be charged only by Ruler/Govt.  4.1 Depot vs Factory vs Settlement (State enterprise), continued. Security level: Depot unfortified, low-level guards; Factory often fortified (e.g. Fort Manuel); Settlement heavily fortified military zones with troops. Example: Portuguese warehouses before the Calicut factory (1500); English Factory at Surat (1613); Goa for the Portuguese post-1510, Pondicherry for the French post-1674, Calcutta for the British post-1690. A factory is also called a trading post; its function is the "Office." A settlement has multiple factories and warehouses and "collects LR (land revenue) and consumes LR." Don't confuse "LEJ" here: a depot has no (L)egislative, (E)xecutive, (J)udicial jurisdiction; a settlement has sovereign territorial rights: L E J. [Taxes can be charged only by the Ruler / Govt.] Farman, Parwana, Nishan  Teacher's board: Farman (Govt order or notification) branches into three: Imperial or Royal = issued by the King or Emperor; Local or Parwana = by the Governor of a Province; Nishan = by a Prince (son of the King). Left: King, then Governors of Provinces (three branches). Order   Issued by Farman (Imperial or Royal)   King or Emperor Parwana (Local or Provincial)   Governor of a Province Nishan   Prince (son of the King, of the royal blood) The handout defines these when discussing the Danes: Farman (Imperial Decree by the Mughal Emperor), Nishan (Princely Decree by a Prince of the Royal Blood), Parwana (Provincial Decree or Order by a Provincial Governor).  Teacher's board: UPSC Prelims asks (1) where and who set up a factory or fort, (2) a rough idea of the time of setting up of the factory or fort, (3) chronology (1st ORDER, underlined). Teacher: UPSC Prelims: where / who set up a factory or fort; a rough idea of the time; chronology (1st order). 4.2 · Early factories, the first fort and the aggression (1498-1503)  4.2 Early Factories, 1st Fort Manuel (1503) and Aggression (1498-1503). i) Cabral's factories (1500): 1st Portuguese factory in India at Calicut in 1500 by Pedro Cabral, on permission from Samoothiri (Zamorin); short-lived, destroyed by Arab merchants (about 50 Portuguese killed). Zamorin did not evict Arab traders, so Cabral bombarded Calicut, then sailed south to Cochin where the 1st PERMANENT Portuguese factory was set up (1500) under the Raja of Cochin's protection. ii) Da Gama's 2nd voyage (1502): goal to avenge Cabral's men, force the Zamorin into submission and violently expel Arab competitors; when the Zamorin refused, he bombarded Calicut and massacred innocent fishermen; it disrupted Arab and Venetian domination of the Indian Ocean and Arabian Sea trade. iii) Fort Manuel (1503, Cochin) by Albuquerque: naval commander Afonso de Albuquerque (1509-15) arrived in 1503, defended the Raja of Cochin against the Zamorin and built Fort Manuel before sailing back in 1504; 1st European fort in India. Cochin was the 1st capital of Portuguese India until the HQ shifted to Goa in 1530. Teacher's ink: sketch of a slanted line Zamorin, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore; (1st - 1498) beside Da Gama's 2nd voyage; Notice nature of Portuguese; 1504-15 under Albuquerque; Goa annexed in 1510 (arrow to 1530). 1498: Da Gama at Calicut; trade permission from the Zamorin; no factory 1500, Cabral: first Portuguese factory, Calicut (permission of the Samoothiri/Zamorin); destroyed by Arab merchants (about 50 Portuguese killed) (bad) Cabral bombards Calicut (the Zamorin would not evict the Arabs) and sails south (good) 1500: first PERMANENT factory, Cochin (protection of the Raja of Cochin) (bad) 1502, Da Gama's 2nd voyage: bombards Calicut, massacres innocent fishermen; aims: avenge Cabral, subdue the Zamorin, expel Arab rivals 1503: Fort Manuel, Cochin (Albuquerque 09-15, then a naval commander): first European fort in India Cochin = first capital of Portuguese India until the HQ shifted to Goa in 1530 Teacher: The teacher sketched Zamorin, Calicut, Cochin, Travancore along a slanted line, and marked (1st - 1498) next to Da Gama's second voyage. "Notice the nature of the Portuguese" (the violence). Under Albuquerque 09-15: 1504-15. [Goa annexed in 1510] with an arrow to 1530 (HQ shift). The 2nd voyage disrupted the Arab-Venetian domination of the trade; Europe could now trade directly with India (Portugal a player in the Indian Ocean trade). In the handout, the second voyage marked the forcible integration of Indian Ocean trade into the European mercantilist framework. Albuquerque 09-15's years are written as 09-15 beside his name in the handout, to tell him apart from Almeida 05-09 (05-09); in 1503 he was not yet Governor. 4.3 · Blue Water Policy and the Cartaz System (Almeida 05-09, 1505-09)  4.3 Blue Water Policy and Cartaz System (Almeida 1505-09). Teacher's title note: the decision of the Portuguese to focus on blue waters (oceans or seas); expected also because the primary goal in the 16th c Age of Discovery = Trade; Goa 1510 = exception to this BW policy. 1st Governor: Almeida (1505-09) was the 1st Governor (Viceroy in common usage; legal title Governador, not Viceroy) of the Portuguese Estado da India (ink: CEO of company in India; 1510+ Governor = CEO + CM of Goa). Blue Water Policy: emphasis on NAVAL supremacy rather than territorial conquest; since India had powerful land-based States, the Portuguese chose to dominate oceans and maritime trade routes. Why South India vulnerable: the Mughal Empire (1526-1858) did not yet exist; South India divided between Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and Deccan Sultanates, with no unified central naval power. Their approach: focused on commerce, used coercion in trade and engaged in some (boxed) conquest (Goa 1510). Left board: WHY: had a better navy; GOAL = oceanic trade; Indian armies strong; weak since Talikota 1565. Since India had powerful land-based States, the Portuguese chose to dominate oceans and maritime trade routes. The objective: a monopolistic trading regime without extensive territorial expansion     Why South India was vulnerable   No Mughal Empire yet (1526-1858); South India divided between Vijayanagara (1336-1646) and the Deccan Sultanates, with no unified central naval power     Their approach   Commerce, coercion in trade, and some (boxed) conquest: Goa 1510   Teacher: Blue Water = oceans and seas. The decision to focus on the blue waters was expected, since the primary goal of the Age of Discovery (16th c) was trade. Goa 1510 = the exception to this Blue Water policy. Almeida 05-09 was the "CEO of the company in India"; from 1510+ the Governor = CEO + CM of Goa. WHY: they had a better navy, the goal was oceanic trade, and Indian armies were strong (so land conquest was hard); the south was also weak since Talikota 1565 (the note is partly unclear on the slide).  Teacher's board: Military, Navy versus Territorial Army. A territorial army was strong for Indian kingdoms (plus some had a Navy). Therefore in the 16th c Age of Discovery the Navy of the Europeans was greater than the Navy of Indian powers, usually (why: where Indian navy was good, e.g. Marathas and Travancore, books talk about it). Right: Portugal, Dutch, French, British, Spain: a state with coastal borders versus a state with only land borders. Land-only: focus on the territorial army. Coastal: focus on territorial army plus Navy, in the budget and technology. Teacher: Territorial army was strong for Indian kingdoms. Europe's navy was usually greater than the Indian powers' navy (Marathas and Travancore had good navies, and books talk about it). Land-locked states focus on the territorial army; states with a coast focus on the territorial army plus a Navy, in budget and technology. (Examples on the board: Portugal, Dutch, French, British, Spain.)  Teacher's board: CARTAZ (circled) analogy. Land: a highway, with a car passing through a TOLL booth. Oceans: a waterway or trade route, with a ship passing through a CARTAZ fees booth. Teacher: Cartaz = a toll booth on the sea. On land a car on a highway pays at a TOLL booth; in the oceans a ship on a trade route pays Cartaz fees.  4.3 (contd). Cartaz System (a naval licensing system, part of the Blue Water Policy): all non-Portuguese ships were forced to buy a pass (a Cartaz) and pay a licence fee to sail safely in the Indian Ocean; pay and get a pass, refuse and face attack. Target Arabs: the Portuguese regularly raided and brutally attacked Arab merchants who controlled the Arabian Sea for generations, and forced local rulers and later Mughal ships to pay for the Cartaz. Battle of Diu (1509): Almeida decisively defeated a massive joint Muslim naval coalition of the Sultanate of Gujarat, the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and the Zamorin of Calicut, backed by the Ottoman Empire (troops and galleys) and the Republic of Venice; the victory consolidated Portuguese naval supremacy for the next century over the Arabian Sea. Teacher's ink: Indian (beside local rulers); only under Akbar (1556-1605) coastal area added to the Mughal state; Not for Diu itself but for domination of the Arabian Sea; Arabs (over Egypt); all stakeholders of old routes; military ships (beside Ottoman); 1502: defeated Arabs and Zamorin in India; 1509: top player of the Arabian Sea. The coalition was "all stakeholders of the old routes": Arabs (Egypt), Indian (Gujarat, Zamorin), military ships from the Ottoman. 1502: Arabs and the Zamorin defeated in India; 1509: top player of the Arabian Sea. The teacher also notes that only under Akbar 56-05 was the coastal area added to the Mughal state. The handout: the coalition's scale shows how seriously the established trading powers of the Old World viewed the Portuguese threat; Venice's trade was being destroyed by Portuguese dominance of the Indian Ocean. 4.4 · Afonso de Albuquerque 09-15 (2nd Governor, 1509-15)  4.4 Afonso de Albuquerque (2nd Governor, 1509-15). Teacher's title note: set up the 1st fort (Manuel) 1503 in Cochin. Imprisonment and release: Albuquerque brought the King's orders of his appointment as next Governor but was imprisoned as Almeida did not trust him; after the Battle of Diu (1509) a new fleet confirmed the King's orders, so he was released and became 2nd Governor (Governador / Viceroy). Territorial transformation: turned the Portuguese presence from a purely trading enterprise into a territorial colonial State, annexing Goa (1510) from the Sultan of Bijapur for better control of the Arabian Sea (Goa 1510 a notable exception to the Blue Water Policy, a rare land conquest). Teacher's ink: Babur (1526-30) not in India; a sketch of the coast with Goa between north and south. Luso-Indian policy: encouraged intermarriage between Portuguese settlers and Indian women (a substantial share were war widows or captured women, often forced into these marriages without consent); greater political stability via increased numbers; more mansabdars (co-opted). Administrative and religious: integrated local elites into the administration, attempted to regulate practices such as Sati, and promoted Christianity as a tool of political control. The Portuguese dominated the Indian Ocean trade for nearly a century     Western-coast consolidation   Acquired Bassein (1534) and Diu (1535) from Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, securing strategic ports and trade routes   Teacher: [1613: the EIC's Surat factory, after defeating the Portuguese] marks the end of the "nearly a century." 4.6 · Religious intolerance: Inquisition and Francis Xavier  4.6 Religious Intolerance. Most aggressive power: the Portuguese were among the most religiously aggressive of all European powers in India; Jesuit missionary activity generated widespread resistance. Slavery and forced conversions: their administration was marked by the slave trade (including in the Hughli settlement in Bengal) and forced conversions. Goa Inquisition (1560-1812): a brutal colonial church court set up to investigate and punish heresy (beliefs contradicting church doctrine) and violently enforce Portuguese cultural and religious orthodoxy, an era of persecution that caused deep socio-religious backlash. items.t: 5 · How the Dutch and English broke the Portuguese-Spanish monopoly
items.x: By the second half of the 16th century two new naval powers had emerged: Britain and the Dutch Republic (Netherlands). Both wanted to break the strict monopoly held by Spain and Portugal over European international trade and to achieve freedom of navigation in the oceans. 1588: the British Navy defeated the Spanish Armada ("Invincible Armada") in the Atlantic, severely weakening Spanish-Portuguese naval supremacy. By 1580 Portugal had entered a political union with Spain, so defeating Spain also opened trade routes Portugal had controlled. With the Armada defeated, British and Dutch ships could travel safely to Asia via the Cape of Good Hope. First priority for both: Indonesia (the spice trade of the East Indies). India came later, for a commercial reason: the people of the spice islands had little interest in English or Dutch goods but readily accepted Indian cotton textiles. To buy spices in Indonesia you first needed cloth from India. The handout's clarification: the Netherlands, Holland and "the Dutch Republic" all refer to the same country. "Dutch" is the adjective; "Holland" is technically a region within the Netherlands but is often used as a general name. The trilateral (triangle) trade: England → India → Indonesia → England. This is the commercial logic that shifted the EIC's focus from Indonesia to the Indian subcontinent. (Compare the teacher's triangle in section 1.) Teacher: Board, slide 2: why the monopoly had to be broken. "End the rival's monopoly (e.g. 1502, Da Gama in coastal Malabar) -> a multi-player domain -> establish your own monopoly (requires additional resources), i.e. the Battle of Diu 1509 -> Arabian Sea." Two challenges for the British and the Dutch in trading with the East Indies: (1) How to reach India, China, Indonesia: Spain and Portugal dominate the routes and oceans. (2) How to purchase goods from India: the Portuguese dominate the Indian coastline and the Indian international market. In a small table on the right: "1588: end of monopoly over routes" (the second row was left empty). Indonesia at the top, India bottom right, the EIC bottom left. Arrows: the EIC buys goods from India; sells Indian goods to Indonesia; buys Indonesian goods. Teacher: Board, slide 6 (right): CHARTER, State and Company. Charter = founding document, issued by the State (Monarchy or Parliament), granting special powers and rights to a company. State = an organisation with a territorial (circled T) motive (defend, annex), so it has a military and may wage war. A State rules a territory, so coins, currency and taxation are with the State; the circled L, E, J powers are also with the State (my reading: legislative, executive, judicial). Company = an organisation with a profit motive for its shareholders, and it requires property. items.t: 6 · The Dutch VOC
items.x: 1602: the Dutch East India Company (VOC, Vereenigde Oost-Indische Compagnie) was established by a Charter issued by the Dutch Parliament, by merging six smaller Dutch companies that had been competing for eastern trade. Takeaway (handout): the VOC was the world's first multinational company, and the first to issue publicly tradable stocks and shares on a formal exchange: the world's first joint-stock company. An ordinary person could become a part-owner by buying shares, without a say in management: the ancestor of the BSE, NSE, NYSE and the modern shareholder economy. Charter powers: the right to wage war, sign treaties, acquire territory, build forts and mint its own currency: powers that ordinarily belong to a State, showing how European powers saw companies as an extension of State power. The first Dutch expedition (1595) went to the East Indies (Indonesia), not India. Dutch settlements in India: Masulipatnam (Northern Sarkars) 1605 (first factory), Pulicat (Carnatic) 1610, Surat (Gujarat) 1616, Bimilipatam (Golconda) 1641, Karikal (near Pondicherry) 1645, Chinsura (Bengal) 1653, later Kasimbazar, Baranagore, Patna, Balasore, Nagapatnam, Agra, Cochin (where they captured the Portuguese fort in 1663). At its peak in 1669 the VOC was the richest private company in the world: 150 merchant vessels, 40 warships, an army of 10,000 soldiers, 50,000 employees; over its life 5,000 voyages from the Netherlands to the East Indies. 1799: bankrupt and dissolved; possessions taken over by the Dutch government as the Dutch East Indies (Indonesia), a Dutch colony until independence in 1945 after World War II. Prelims 2022 trap: the Gajapati dynasty and the Dutch. The claim that the Dutch received land grants from the Gajapati dynasty of Odisha is INCORRECT. The Gajapatis were a 15th-century dynasty centred in Odisha whose power had declined well before the Dutch arrived. Do not confuse later local rulers of the Odisha coast with the Gajapati dynasty itself. items.t: 7 · The English EIC and the Royal Charter of 1600
items.x: The English East India Company was formed on 31 December 1600: its founding document was a Royal Charter issued by Queen Elizabeth I 58-03. A Royal Charter is essentially a licence granted by the Monarch. If it was not renewed, the company would legally cease to exist. This shaped the EIC's relationship with the British State for the next two and a half centuries: its survival depended on the goodwill of whoever held power in Britain. The EIC was the 4th joint-stock company in England, formed by pooling money from 215 London merchants ("merchant adventurers") who wanted to challenge Dutch dominance in European trade with the East. The stated goal was trade with the East, not empire-building or colonialism. Britain or England? In 1600 it was England (not Britain) that granted the Charter. England and Scotland united in 1707 to create the Kingdom of Great Britain; in 1801 Ireland was added, creating the United Kingdom. Before 1707 "British" technically means English. What the Royal Charter of 1600 gave the EIC A monopoly over England's trade with the East Indies for 15 years. The right to carry gold (foreign exchange) out of England to purchase eastern goods. Management by a body of private people: a Governor, a Deputy Governor and 24 members, which later evolved into the Board or Court of Directors. The handout's forex aside: for a State, forex is the currency that matters in international trade; domestic currency works only within a country's borders (like a household's internal reward system for children, valid only inside the home). Until 1971, Gold was forex, until the Dollar took over. (Same idea as the teacher's board in section 1.) Teacher: Ink on the 1600 Charter slides (slides 12 to 16). Board, slide 12: the EIC = joint-stock company; special rights and powers via a Charter (31 Dec 1600); Dutch competition. Slide 13: he underlined founding document, Royal Charter and Elizabeth I 58-03. Teacher: Board, slide 14: why is the VOC (1602) called the first joint-stock company when the English EIC (1600) was also one? "Answer: in 1600 the EIC was not a proper joint-stock company. It operated on a per-VOYAGE system: before each journey to the East Indies the EIC gathered Rs from the public; brought and sold goods in Europe at a profit and shared all the profits; for the next journey, repeated. It is later that the EIC became a proper joint-stock company, i.e. one with permanent capital." Board, slide 15: a proper joint-stock company "does not usually give back all profits; it gives dividends." A pie of the profit: Retain, Re-invest, assets, Dividends. "WRONG = monopoly over trade with India with the EIC. CORRECT = monopoly over England's (or British) trade with the East Indies, with the EIC." items.t: 8 · Charters until 1793: the EIC's changing legal character
items.x: The EIC's legal existence depended on Charter renewal, and the Charters also tell the shift of power in Britain from the Monarch to Parliament. Year   Event   What it did 1600   Founding Charter (Queen Elizabeth I 58-03, 1558-1603)   15-year monopoly on East Indies trade; carry gold out; Governor, Deputy Governor and 24 members 1601-03   First voyage (James Lancaster)   Sailed not to India but to Indonesia (Java and Sumatra); first EIC factory there; looted the Portuguese ship Sao Tome in the Strait of Malacca 1609   Charter of King James I 03-25   Replaced the 15-year monopoly with a perpetual (indefinite) monopoly 1657   Cromwell 51-60's Charter   Reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company (continuous capital fund) 1661   Charter of King Charles II 60-85   Quasi-State powers: forts, troops, war and peace, civil and criminal jurisdiction (right to mint money came in 1676) 1793 onwards   Parliament takes over   Parliament begins passing Acts to renew the Charter 1601-03, the first voyage (James Lancaster): the fleet sailed not to India but to Indonesia, consistent with the EIC's original priority of the spice trade. They reached Java and Sumatra, where they set up the very first EIC factory. On the way Lancaster's fleet looted a Portuguese ship, the Sao Tome, in the Strait of Malacca (a cargo of textiles and spices). William Dalrymple and others note that the EIC's first major profit came not from trade but from outright piracy. Shareholders got substantial dividends; the fleet returned in 1603. 1609, James I 03-25: the original 15-year monopoly became a perpetual monopoly. 1657, Cromwell 51-60's Charter: Context: Charles I 25-49 tried to levy taxes without Parliament's consent, which triggered the English Civil War (1642-51). The Parliamentarians (largely Protestant) defeated the Royalists; Charles I 25-49 was beheaded in 1649; England became a Republic under Oliver Cromwell 51-60 (the handout writes his years as 51-60). After Cromwell 51-60's death in 1658 his son briefly took over, but the experiment proved autocratic and unpopular. In 1660 the Monarchy was restored under Charles II 60-85. Cromwell 51-60 issued a new Charter in 1657, declaring the previous Royal Charter invalid, and reorganised the EIC into a permanent joint-stock company. Earlier, money was raised voyage by voyage (pool, voyage, profits, fund dissolved); from 1657 one continuous unified capital fund, giving a stable financial foundation. 1661, Charles II 60-85's Charter (after the Restoration) was arguably the most consequential legally: it turned the EIC from a commercial trading body into a quasi-State power. It gave the right to build forts, command troops, make war and peace, and exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over settlements in India. (The right to mint its own money came in 1676.) From 1793 Parliament takes over: the British Parliament begins passing Acts for the renewal of the EIC's Charter, mirroring the democratisation of Britain (power moving from Crown to elected representatives). Indian constitutional history and British political history are inseparable threads. Takeaway (1661): the 1600 EIC was a merchant association with a trade monopoly; the 1661 EIC had the legal powers of a State within its territories. A trading company had, through successive Charters, accumulated the powers of a sovereign. Teacher: Ink on the charter timeline (Lecture 11, slides 17 to 22). So learn 1600, 1661 and 1793 first; 1609, 1657 and 1676 are the lower-priority years. Slide 20, the 1661 Charter: next to "quasi-State power" he wrote "semi" (semi-State). Beside civil and criminal jurisdiction he wrote "[Ruling Power]." Underlined: forts, troops, war and peace, 1676 (mint), and "legal powers of a State." items.t: 9 · The Danish East India Company
items.x: Established 1616, out of envy of Dutch and English profits. Its Charter was issued by King Christian IV 88-48 of Denmark-Norway, granting a 12-year monopoly on trade between Denmark-Norway and the East Indies. The Danes were never in the same league: weaker finance, limited military capacity. The first Danish company ended around 1650; a second Danish EIC was set up in 1670 but wound down gradually, selling all its Indian mainland settlements to the British EIC by 1845. Danish settlements in India 1620: Tranquebar (Tharangambadi), Tamil Nadu: first factory; first fort: Fort Dansborg; official administrative HQ of Danish India from 1620 until 1845. 1624: Pondicherry (brief): under Roland Crappe; a short-lived factory, abandoned for lack of resources, long before the French arrived. 1625: Masulipatnam (Andhra Pradesh); Pipli and Balasore (Odisha). 1755: Serampore (Srirampur / Frederiksnagore), Hooghly district, Bengal: a parwana from Nawab Alivardi Khan 40-56. Tranquebar remained the HQ, but Serampore became the most commercially successful and culturally significant Danish post. Colonial powers in Tranquebar, Serampore and the Nicobar Islands (the Nicobars were sold separately to the British in 1868; today part of India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands UT). 1799-1800: Serampore Mission Press, associated with Baptist missionaries including William Carey: translated the Bible into Indian vernacular languages, ran schools, and made an immense contribution to early printing and education in Bengal. Their architectural legacy at Tranquebar and Serampore and their missionary work (not forced conversions) are the most visible Danish traces. items.t: 10 · How the EIC broke Portuguese dominance: Hawkins, Swally and Surat
items.x: 1608: the EIC decided to set up a factory at Surat, then the most important port on India's west coast and firmly within Portuguese-dominated territory. It sent Captain William Hawkins to the court of Jahangir 05-27. Jahangir 05-27 first gave Hawkins a Mansab (rank of 400) and a Jagir, but Hawkins was ultimately expelled from the Mughal court due to persistent Portuguese pressure. The lesson: Portugal had to be defeated militarily before the EIC could establish itself on the west coast. 1612, Battle of Swally (Suvali): Captain Thomas Best led a small EIC armed trading fleet to a decisive victory over the Portuguese. The Mughal State had its own reason to welcome this: Mughal ships traded in the Arabian Sea but were perpetually vulnerable to Portuguese piracy, a source of humiliation for a great land power. Impressed by English sea capability, Jahangir 05-27 issued a Royal Farman in 1613, giving the EIC the legal right to set up a permanent factory at Surat. 1612 versus 1613: 1612 = the Battle of Swally (military victory) and the local Mughal governor's temporary permission/parwana; 1613 = the legally permanent establishment, when Jahangir 05-27 ratified the local agreement with an imperial farman. 1608: EIC wants a Surat factory; sends Captain William Hawkins to Jahangir 05-27 (bad) Hawkins gets a Mansab (400) and Jagir but is expelled under Portuguese pressure Lesson: defeat Portugal militarily first (good) 1612: Battle of Swally: Captain Thomas Best defeats the Portuguese Mughals welcome it: their ships were vulnerable to Portuguese piracy (good) 1613: Jahangir 05-27's Royal Farman: permanent factory at Surat Teacher: Ink on Hawkins, Swally and Surat (slides 27 to 29). Slide 27: "Jahangir 05-27" at the top; "imp" above the 1612 Battle of Swally; underlined 1612, Captain Thomas Best, Suvali and rank 400. The 1613 Royal Farman heading is circled. If it spent Rupees on an army, it would go against that goal (sad face). If the army came from its own Rupee, it would be small, to meet the core interests of trade." Four points: (1) Britain's trade with the East Indies = the EIC's trade; (2) the EIC has a monopoly over Britain's trade with the East Indies; (3) via the EIC, Britain can dominate WORLD trade. items.t: 11 · The Royal Farman of 1618 and Thomas Roe (1615-19)
items.x: England wanted liberal trading rights across the entire Mughal Empire, so King James I 03-25 sent Thomas Roe as formal ambassador to Jahangir 05-27's court. Roe arrived at Surat in 1615 and stayed until 1619. Jahangir 05-27 refused a formal treaty between equals (a trading company was no sovereign equal). Through sustained diplomacy and personal rapport Roe got a series of privileges and a Royal Farman (1618) allowing the EIC to set up factories throughout the Mughal Empire with liberal trading rights: lower customs duties and ease of doing business. 1616-19: new factories at Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach (Bharuch). With Surat they formed the Surat Presidency (1618): the EIC's first administrative Presidency in India, coordinating English trade on the west coast until the later shift to Bombay (1687). Portuguese enraged; naval conflicts continued. 1631-32: Shahjahan 27-58 ordered his Bengal governor Qasim Khan to defeat the Portuguese and eject them from Hugli, because they were misusing their trade privileges with piracy and the slave trade from their Bengal base. Roe's account, The Embassy of Sir Thomas Roe to the Court of the Great Mogul, is one of the most important primary sources on the Mughal Empire of this period (court administration, wealth, politics, daily life). Teacher: Ink on Roe (slides 30 and 31). Top right: "Ambassador, i.e. British Resident in Jahangir 05-27's court" (starred). Underlined: the title of Roe's memoir, Royal Farman (1618), the right to establish factories across the Empire plus lower duties and ease of business ("= LIBERAL TRADING RIGHTS"), and Surat Presidency (1618). Under Surat Presidency: "HQ (e.g. Cochin 1505-1530, HQ of Portugal; Tranquebar, HQ of the Danes 1620)": a Presidency was the EIC's regional HQ, like those earlier HQs. items.t: 12 · Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1661: dowry diplomacy
items.x: The treaty, signed at Whitehall, London, marked the marriage of King Charles II 60-85 of England and Princess Catherine of Braganza of Portugal. 1. Portugal paid a dowry of 500,000 pounds in cash. 2. England received Bombay and Tangier (Morocco). 3. Trade and military cooperation, with England agreeing to protect Portugal's remaining possessions. Result: a continued Portuguese presence in Goa, Daman and Diu under English protection, lasting until 1961, when independent India took over these territories militarily, after a people's movement. 1668: the British Crown transferred Bombay to the EIC at an annual rent of 10 pounds: the start of Bombay's journey from a Portuguese dowry to the commercial capital of British India. items.t: 13 · The Dutch: rise, dominance and fall in Asia

items.t: 14 · Napoleon's link: the Kew Letters (1795)
items.x: 1795, during the French Revolutionary Wars (1792-1804) leading into the Napoleonic Wars (1804-15): the French army invaded the Netherlands, overthrew the Dutch government and set up a puppet State, the Batavian Republic, controlled by France. Britain declared all Dutch overseas colonies enemy territory. The exiled Dutch leader Prince William V 51-95 had fled to London and issued the "Kew Letters": orders telling Dutch colonial governors to hand over their territories to the British "for safekeeping," so France could not seize them. The British used this as their legal basis to take over the remaining Dutch posts. By 1795 the British occupied the remaining Dutch settlements in South Asia: Cochin (Kerala), Chinsura (Bengal), Pulicat and Tuticorin (Coromandel), and the coastal regions of Ceylon (Trincomalee and Colombo). The teacher marked the Kew Letters "[SYLLABUS X]" (Lecture 11, slide 11): not in the syllabus. Read this section for the story of the Dutch fall, not as an exam topic. Teacher: Ink on slide 6. Under the title: "NOT imp FROM exam - FOR UNDERSTANDING." This is the same call as the Lecture 11 mark "SYLLABUS X" above: read the Kew Letters for the story, do not memorise them. He also inserted "over" so that the line reads "hand over their territories," and wrote "Kew = place near London."

items.t: 15 · Why Ceylon did not become part of British India: the Crown Colony
items.x: 1795-96: the British captured the Dutch areas of Ceylon and gave administration to the EIC, through the Madras Presidency. Treaty of Amiens, 1802: a peace treaty in Europe between Britain and France along with its Dutch ally, the Batavian Republic. The Dutch formally and permanently ceded the coastal regions of Ceylon to Britain. The British government decided Ceylon was too strategically important to be run by a trading company: it removed the EIC's administration entirely and declared Ceylon a British Crown Colony, ruled directly by an appointed British Governor, separate from the EIC's Indian empire. Takeaway: India was a colony ruled by the EIC (a commercial entity with State-like powers); Ceylon was a Crown Colony where the British State itself governed directly. Teacher: Ink on slide 7 (Crown Colony). The words "Crown Colony" in the title are boxed, with "(not imp) BUT concept" and below it "imp: Meaning." So: the Ceylon story is not important for the exam, but the meaning of "Crown Colony" is. Board: British Colonies, RULED BY -> "EIC" = Company's Colony; "Br State" (boxed) = Crown Colony. Under the Amiens panel: "Rule = Doing L, E, J on a T" (L, E, J and T each circled): to rule is to do the Legislative, Executive and Judicial work on a Territory (LEJ as in section 4.1). Underlined in the last panel: "ruled directly" and "by the British State."  Lecture 12 slide 7: why Ceylon became a Crown Colony. items.t: 16 · What were Presidencies?
items.x: A Presidency was a regional headquarters of EIC trade. A settlement got Presidency status when it had grown large enough with significant warehouses, offices, residential buildings and a fort. Initially small coastal towns; as the EIC annexed surrounding territories the towns grew into cities and the Presidencies expanded into provinces of British India (governed directly by the British). The Presidencies were named after the major forts built within them. items.t: 17 · How each of the three Presidencies came to be
items.x: 17.1 · Madras Presidency (from 1652/1653) The EIC's first factory in India was a temporary one at Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in the Northern Sarkars (Andhra Pradesh) in 1611. (Northern Sarkars = the northern coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh, outside Mughal direct control.) 1639: the EIC, led by Francis Day, purchased land at the village of Madraspatanam from Hindu Nayakas (provincial governors of the Vijayanagara Empire, 1336-1646) and built Fort St George (1639-44): the first fort built by the EIC in India and the anchor of the first permanent settlement. 1690: the EIC purchased a fort at Cuddalore (south of Madras) from the Maratha Chhatrapati Rajaram 89-00 and named it Fort Saint David. Its history: partly built by the Dutch from 1608; construction halted due to Portuguese pressure on the Vijayanagara Empire; a Hindu merchant eventually completed it. In 1677 Shivaji 74-80 conquered the nearby Jinji fort and region including Cuddalore before it passed to the EIC. The Madras Presidency was formally established as the Presidency of Fort St George in 1652, on the orders of the Court of Directors in London; because of the ship travel time, it was implemented in India in 1653. (Both dates appear in sources: the London order versus the on-ground implementation.) Teacher: Ink on slide 13 (Madras). Top right: "FACTORY = warehouses + home and office + MAY be a [FORT]" (FORT boxed; "home and office" is hard to read): a factory may or may not have a fort. The shift happened because of the growing power of the Marathas in Gujarat, making Surat increasingly risky. Bombay, a cluster of seven islands, offered a more defensible location. Charles II 60-85 received Bombay in 1661 as part of the Portuguese dowry and transferred it to the EIC in 1668 at 10 pounds per annum. The Bombay Presidency was established in 1687, replacing Surat as the western HQ. Bombay Castle (Casa da Orta) was originally built by the Portuguese and expanded by the EIC through the 18th century. The Calcutta Presidency was formally established in 1699/1700 as the Presidency of Fort William, with its own Governor. Through the 18th century the EIC developed Calcutta Port; Calcutta came to account for 60% of all EIC trade from India. 1800: Fort William College was established by Wellesley 98-05 for training EIC civil servants. 1870: the Calcutta Port Act created the Calcutta Port Commissioners and Port Trust, the first formal legal authority governing the port. Then a line with the word "annexations" and an arrow down: "Presidency = Province"; "Governor = Ruler / CM / Subadar / Nazim." Reason: before annexations the Governor only managed trade in a region; after annexations he ruled a province like a Mughal Subadar or Nazim (or a modern Chief Minister). items.t: 19 · The French in India and the story of Pondicherry
items.x: The French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) was founded in 1664 by Jean-Baptiste Colbert under King Louis XIV 43-15; great-grandfather of Louis XVI, overthrown in the French Revolution of 1789). It started as a private company but was later nationalised, making it in today's terms a Public Sector Undertaking (PSU). Teacher: Ink on slide 19. Beside the title: "# Bengal: Chandernagore" and "# Pondicherry = MAJOR HQ 1674" (Pondicherry, MAJOR HQ and 1674 underlined). So: the French main HQ = Pondicherry (1674); their Bengal base = Chandernagore. Yellow underlines: the 1664 company, King Louis XIV 43-15, "a private company," "later nationalised," Pondicherry (acquired 1674, Sultan of Bijapur, and Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General).  Lecture 12 slide 19: French East India Company and Pondicherry. Teacher's ink: Bengal: Chandernagore; Pondicherry = MAJOR HQ 1674; underlines on 1664, Louis XIV 43-15, private company, later nationalised, Sultan of Bijapur and Francois Martin 01-06. French settlements in India (handout list) 1668, Surat: first factory, on a farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667. 1669, Masulipatnam: farman from the Sultan of Golconda (1518-1687). 1673, Chandarnagar: permission from Shaista Khan 64-88, Mughal governor of Bengal; financial crunch delayed it: a settlement only in 1690-92. 1674, Pondicherry: acquired from Sikandar Adil Shah (1672-86) of Bijapur and his local governor Sher Khan Lodi. Developed as a city by Francois Martin 01-06 (Governor-General 1701-06, earlier Governor), the real founder of French power in India: centralised French administration with Pondicherry as capital (1701) and built Fort Louis. 1723, Yanam: permission from Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48, also called Asaf Jah I. 1724, Mahe (Malabar coast): acquired from the Nair ruler Vazhunnavar in 1721; trade settlement built 1724-25 after overcoming a rebellion; named after Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46, who came with a fleet from Mauritius. 1739, Karaikal: granted by Pratap Singh 39-63, Maratha ruler of Tanjore, as a reward for French help in a succession dispute. (The Thanjavur Maratha dynasty was founded not by Shivaji 74-80 directly but by his half-brother Venkoji (Ekoji) in 1674, defeating the Nayaka rulers of Madurai.) 1721, Mauritius a French colony, but proper control only by 1735 under Mahe de La Bourdonnais 35-46 (Governor 1735-46). He came again with a fleet in 1746 and helped Dupleix 42-54 capture Madras in the 1st Carnatic War (1746-48). 1949: a referendum in Chandernagore merged it into India; the rest stayed under French control until 1954. Teacher: Ink on slide 20 (French acquisitions). Underlined: Surat, "farman given by Aurangzeb 58-07 in 1667," Chandarnagar, Pondicherry, Sultan of Bijapur, "capital 1701," "Fort Louis built," Yanam, "Mahe on the Malabar coast" and Karaikal. A tick stands beside 1674 (Pondicherry is the key row). The 1721/1735 Mauritius row has a cross beside it (no reason is written; treat it as low priority).  Lecture 12 slide 20: French acquisitions in order. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on Surat, Aurangzeb's 1667 farman, Chandarnagar, Pondicherry, capital 1701, Fort Louis, Yanam, Mahe and Karaikal; a tick beside 1674; a cross beside the Mauritius 1721/1735 row. District   Coastline   Surrounded by (State) Puducherry (Capital)   East Coast (Bay of Bengal)   Tamil Nadu Karaikal   East Coast (Bay of Bengal)   Tamil Nadu Yanam   East Coast (Bay of Bengal)   Andhra Pradesh Mahe   West Coast (Arabian Sea)   Kerala Teacher: Ink on slide 21. "East" is underlined in the first three rows (Puducherry, Karaikal, Yanam), and a bracket closes after Mahe. So three districts are on the East coast and Mahe is the odd one out (West coast, Arabian Sea). An empty V-shaped peninsula is drawn under the table; nothing is marked on it. Pondicherry's occupation history (mnemonic PDa-FDu-BFBF to India). Pondicherry is synonymous with the French, but they were not the first there: Portuguese (16th century) → Danes (briefly in 1624) → French (1674) → Dutch (captured briefly in 1693) → British. The English captured Pondicherry in 1761 and restored it to the French via the Treaty of Paris (1763); the British captured it again (for example in 1793) before finally returning it to the French in 1814. It remained French until transferred to India in 1954. items.t: 1 · How did a trading company become a State?
items.x: How Did a Trading Company Become a State? Company purpose: companies exist to make profit for shareholders, the EIC was no different, but in India it became a Company State. By 1857: EIC controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. 1661 Charter gave EIC: (a) right to build forts, (b) command troops, (c) make war and peace, (d) exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India. 1676: right to mint its own money. Teacher's ink: "controlled" struck through and "RULED" written below; "Charles II" under the 1661 row; forts, troops, war, peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction underlined; on the right a fork: INDIA into "Br India: 63% (T), 78% pop" and "565 Princely States: 37% (T), 22% pop". Companies exist to make profit for their shareholders. The EIC was no different. But what the EIC became in India went far beyond a trading enterprise. It became a Company State that, by 1857, controlled 63% of India's territory and 78% of its population. This chapter deals with Empire Building by the EIC. Teacher: On the slide the teacher struck out "controlled" and wrote "RULED": by 1857 the EIC ruled 63% of the territory and 78% of the population. His fork explains the numbers: India = British India (63% of territory, 78% of population) + 565 Princely States (37% of territory, 22% of population). 1.1 The 1661 Charter   Year   What the EIC got    --- ---    1661 Charter (teacher's ink: Charles II 60-85)   The right to build forts       The right to command troops       The right to make war and peace       The right to exercise civil and criminal jurisdiction over its settlements in India     1676   The right to mint its own money   Teacher: The teacher underlined forts, troops, war, peace and civil and criminal jurisdiction: these are State-like powers in the hands of a company. The same charter sits in the EIC charters table of Chapter 8. 1.2 Two kinds of wars: for trade and for territory  Teacher's board (no typed text): why the EIC fought wars. Top line: "EIC formed not for (T), GOAL = TRADE with East Indies (not just India)". Heading "WARS by eic" splitting into two branches. Branch 1 "FOR TRADE": "Defensive: protect present trade", under it "Carnatic Wars" (underlined); "Offensive: to expand trade", under it "Battle of Suvali 1612" (underlined). Branch 2 "FOR (T)": (i) "Whenever empire builder GG or Governors, i.e. for personal ambitions": Clive 57-67 [Governor of Bengal Presidency 1757-60, 1765-67], Wellesley 98-05 [1798-1805], Francis Hastings 13-23 [1813-23], Dalhousie 48-56 [1848-56]; (ii) "because of pressure of EIC army, as armies have vested interest in wars", with a small tree: economic power (Def BD), political power (larger army), social power. The wars the EIC fought in India fall into two broad categories. Wars for trade: fought to protect or expand trade. Wars for territory: fought for empire building. These were different in nature and in motivation. Teacher: The board's tree. The EIC was not formed for territory (T). Its goal was trade with the East Indies (not just India). So its wars were of two kinds. (1) For trade: either defensive, to protect present trade (the Carnatic Wars), or offensive, to expand trade (the Battle of Suvali 1612, from Chapter 8). (2) For territory: only in two situations, given below. Note the point for this chapter: the Carnatic Wars were wars for trade, even though they ended up laying the base for territory. Wars for territory happened under two specific conditions. When the Governor or Governor-General in India was personally ambitious: an empire builder by temperament. Britain was far away. Communication was slow. These men had enough operational freedom to pursue wars that London might not have formally approved. At times the EIC Army put pressure for wars. Any army has a structural interest in war: war brings a bigger defence budget, prestige, promotions and political relevance to the military. The EIC Army was no different.   Empire builder   Post and years    --- ---    Robert Clive 57-67   Governor of Bengal Presidency, in two stints: 1757-60 and 1765-67     Richard Wellesley 98-05   1798-1805     Francis Hastings 13-23   1813-23     Dalhousie 48-56   1848-56   Overhype threats: the army routinely overhyped threats to the borders; war brings budget, prestige, promotions Pressure to expand: overhyped threats create pressure for territorial expansion New borders: expansion always creates new borders (warn) New threats: new borders bring new neighbours, and so new threats, fictional or real (bad) Back to the start: the new threats are overhyped again; a self-reinforcing cycle Teacher: The board gives the army's vested interest in wars as three kinds of power: economic power (a bigger defence budget, written "Def BD"), political power (a larger army) and social power. The handout's present-day parallel: think of how the Pakistan Army today has eaten Pakistan from within by putting its vested interests above the national interest, while the Indian Army has consistently done the opposite.

items.t: 2 · Wars for trade: the Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90)
items.x: Wars for Trade: Anglo-Mughal War (1686-90). Also called Child's War, the 1st significant clash between EIC and an Indian power (Josiah Child: Chairman, Court of Directors, London; John Child: Governor of Bombay and "General" of EIC forces in India). Reason 1: Aurangzeb 58-07's constant warfare disrupted EIC trade (hard to source goods from the hinterland). Reason 2: disputes with the Nawab of Bengal over bribes and heavy customs duties on EIC. Course: EIC seized Hugli and attacked Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea; Aurangzeb 58-07 crushed EIC in Bombay and Bengal; by 1690 the Company surrendered; Feb 1690, Aurangzeb 58-07 pardoned EIC for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation. Why not expel EIC: it was economically useful. Teacher's ink: underlines on economically useful, forex/gold, bankers, merchants, artisans and ryots; a starred yellow box: "1651: 1st EIC factory in Bengal in Hughli"; above it a small unlabelled sketch of a V-shaped line with two circles (a rough river and town sketch). The Anglo-Mughal War of 1686-90 was fought in Bengal and the Arabian Sea. It was the first significant military clash between the EIC and an Indian power. It is also called Child's War, after two men: Josiah Child: Chairman of the Court of Directors of the EIC in London. John Child: Governor of Bombay and the "General" of all EIC forces in India. The reasons were two-fold: Aurangzeb 58-07's constant warfare was disrupting EIC trade (problems in sourcing goods from the hinterland). Ongoing disputes with the Nawab of Bengal over bribes and heavy customs duties levied on the EIC. The EIC seizes Hugli It escalates: attacks Mughal ships in the Arabian Sea (bad) Aurangzeb 58-07's military crushes the EIC in both Bombay and Bengal By 1690 the Company surrenders February 1690: Aurangzeb 58-07 pardons the EIC in return for Rs 1.5 lakh compensation (good) 1691 Farman: old privileges restored and duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year Teacher: The starred box on the slide: "1651: the 1st EIC factory in Bengal, in Hughli." That is why Hugli is the place the EIC seizes in this war. 2.1 Why did Aurangzeb 58-07 not abolish the Company and expel the British? Because the EIC was economically useful. Its trade brought forex/gold into India, and Aurangzeb 58-07 needed them for war. With Aurangzeb 58-07's own constant warfare disrupting domestic trade, the EIC's export business was, ironically, even more valuable to the Indian economy. Indian bankers earned interest by lending money to the Company for the purchase of goods. Indian merchants, artisans and ryots all participated in and benefited from this trade ecosystem. 2.2 The 1691 Farman  Anglo-Mughal War (contd.): the 1691 Farman (technically a Parwana by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman), under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval, restored old privileges and gave duty-free trade in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year. Teacher's ink: underlines on "duty-free trade in Bengal" and "for Rs 3,000/year"; a flow diagram: RYOTS and ARTISANS with arrows to "Indian MERCHANT", then an arrow to "EIC" and onward (exports), with "Indian BANKERS" below sending an up-arrow labelled "Loan" to the EIC; on the right: "Rupees saved by EIC will be used to BUY Indian GOODS, so more exports"; a starred box: "TODAY we don't tax exports". The 1691 Farman was technically a Parwana, because it was issued by the Subahdar of Bengal, not an imperial farman. (For Farman, Parwana and Nishan see Chapter 8.) It was issued under Aurangzeb 58-07's approval. It restored the EIC's old privileges and gave it the right to duty-free trade in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum. The Company had been defeated militarily, yet it got this privilege, because of the benefits of European trade with India. Teacher: Why give duty-free trade to a defeated company? The board's flow answers it. Ryots and artisans sell to the Indian merchant; the Indian merchant sells to the EIC; Indian bankers give loans to the EIC. Everyone in the chain earns. The money the EIC saves on duty will be used to buy more Indian goods, which means more exports. The starred aside: "TODAY we don't tax exports" (the same logic: a State gains more from exports than from taxing them).

items.t: 3 · The Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63): why the French, and why three wars
items.x: Teacher's board (no typed text): the 3 Carnatic Wars. Top: "Who will dominate purchase of goods". "3 Carnatic wars [Reason = international trade of India; main players Br eic vs Fr eic]", with a tree to 1746-48, 1749-54 and 1756-63; from 1756-63 an arrow: "Fr limited to Chandernagore, Pondicherry". Box: "[3 CWs 1746-48, 49-54, 56-63]". "# 1st and 3rd: result or part of some international war, Br vs Fr". "# 2nd: factionalism in Hyd and Carnatic, R vs R", with arrows down to Fr and Br. Right: "# [Br, Fr] ROYAL armies in 3rd CW 1756-63 ONLY" (ONLY underlined). "# Result: 3/2 = 1.5" with a small table: 1st CW and the 1st phase of the 2nd CW marked "French won"; the 2nd phase of the 2nd CW and the 3rd CW marked "British won". To understand why conquest by the EIC began in Bengal, one must first understand what was happening in South India, and why the French were there. Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54 was the Governor-General of the French EIC from 1742-54. Dupleix 42-54 had personal ambitions of empire building and of dominating the international trade of South India. He would become the template for everything that followed. By 1740, French EIC trade was roughly half the value of British EIC trade. Teacher: The board's frame for all three wars. The reason was the international trade of India: "who will dominate the purchase of goods." The main players were the British EIC versus the French EIC. The 1st and 3rd wars were a result or a part of some international war (Britain versus France). The 2nd was caused by factionalism in Hyderabad and Carnatic: "R vs R" (rival against rival), with the French behind one rival and the British behind the other. Royal armies (British and French) took part in the 3rd Carnatic War 1756-63 ONLY. Result: 3 divided by 2 = 1.5 each: the French won the 1st war and the 1st phase of the 2nd; the British won the 2nd phase of the 2nd and the 3rd. After 1756-63 the French were limited to Chandernagore and Pondicherry (the full list of five posts is in section 6.4). 3.1 Reasons for the Carnatic Wars  Reasons for Carnatic Wars. European rivalry: 2 global wars spilled into India, the War of Austrian Succession (1740-48) leading to the 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) and the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) leading to the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63); as nations fought, their companies fought in India. Succession disputes: disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad drove the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54); the strategy was simple, put your chosen candidate in power to gain strategic influence. Dupleix 42-54's ambition: Joseph Francois Dupleix 42-54, Governor-General of French EIC 1742-54, had personal ambitions of empire and of dominating South India's trade, and became the template for all that followed (by 1740 French EIC trade was about half British EIC trade). Teacher's ink: underlines on the two global wars, "Carnatic and Hyderabad", "personal ambitions of empire" and "South India's trade"; under the Dupleix 42-54 row: "42-54", "1742-54" (underlined) and "not in 3CW 1756-63"; on the right: "How a company can build empire: 1st to show, Fr Dupleix 42-54". The EIC-French contest in India had two overlapping reasons. European rivalry. Two global wars spilled into India. As the two nations fought, their respective companies also entered into hostilities in India. Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad contributed to the 2nd Carnatic War (1749-54). The strategy was simple: put your chosen candidates in power to gain strategic influence.   War   Years   Cause   Decisive event   Treaty   Who won (teacher's board)    --- --- --- --- --- ---    1st Carnatic War   1746-48   The War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) spilled into India   Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)   Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748)   French     2nd Carnatic War   1749-54   Succession disputes in Carnatic and Hyderabad (factionalism)   Ambur (1749); Clive 57-67's Arcot (1751)   Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)   Phase 1: French. Phase 2: British     3rd Carnatic War   1756-63   The Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) spilled into India   Battle of Wandiwash (1760)   Treaty of Paris (1763)   British   Teacher: Under the Dupleix 42-54 row the teacher wrote "42-54, 1742-54: not in 3CW 1756-63." Remember it as a check: Dupleix 42-54 was recalled in 1754, so he took no part in the 3rd Carnatic War (he comes back in section 6.2 as "Dupleix 42-54 not here").
