items.t: 4 · The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) and the Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746)
items.x: 4.1 Reason The 1st Carnatic War (1746-48) was the Indian chapter of the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48). In that war Britain and France, along with their respective allies, fought each other across Europe, America and India, each wanting its preferred candidate on the Austrian throne. 4.2 Events during the war  1st Carnatic War (1746-48): Adyar/St Thome. Reason: the Indian chapter of the War of Austrian Succession (1740-48); Britain and France, with their allies, fought across Europe, America and India, each wanting its candidate on the Austrian throne. Events: Dupleix 42-54 captured EIC's Fort St George, Madras; EIC defeated; the Nawab of Carnatic Anwaruddin 44-49 expected the fort handed over as promised; Dupleix 42-54 refused and sent 10,000 cavalry (the slide's wording; it was the Nawab who sent the cavalry). Battle of Adyar/St Thome 1746: on the north bank of the River Adyar about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on the key phrases; "Anwar-ud-din 44-49" written under the name; on the right a small circle "Br" and an oval "Eu"; a box "Turning Point" and under it "Indian kings wanted (EU) help in modernizing military". Dupleix 42-54 captures the EIC's Fort St George in Madras; the EIC is defeated The Nawab of Carnatic, Anwaruddin 44-49, intervenes: he expected the French to hand over the fort to the Nawab as promised (warn) Dupleix 42-54 refuses Anwaruddin 44-49 sends an army of 10,000 cavalry (bad) Battle of Adyar/St Thome (1746): about 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers completely destroy the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry The battle was fought on the north bank of the River Adyar. The French force was roughly 700 French-trained Indian sepoys and 300 French soldiers. It completely destroyed the Nawab's 10,000-strong traditional cavalry. What happened here changed the nature of power in India. Who sent the 10,000 cavalry? The slide's compressed wording ("Dupleix 42-54 refused and sent 10,000 cavalry") can be misread. The handout is clear: Anwaruddin 44-49, the Nawab, sent the army of 10,000 cavalry against the French. The handout's Diagram 1 (section 7) adds one name the text does not give: "La Bourdonnais 35-46 takes Fort St George, Madras." The handout text and the slide credit the capture to Dupleix 42-54 (the Governor-General). La Bourdonnais 35-46 and Madras appear in Chapter 8. 4.3 Why the French won: three advantages of European warfare The French won due to three critical advantages that would define European military superiority in India across all the wars to come.   Advantage   Why it mattered    --- ---    1. Superior artillery   Light, mobile European cannon that could be repositioned rapidly on the battlefield, against which massed cavalry had no answer (link: like the small bronze cannons of Babur 26-30, spelt Babar 26-30 in this handout)     2. Tactical discipline   European-trained infantry fought in coordinated formations, including infantry squares that could hold ground against cavalry charges from any direction     3. Regular cash salaries   Unlike Indian armies, where soldiers were often not paid regularly, European-trained sepoys received regular wages. This created a professional, reliable fighting force with no incentive to desert between campaigns    French-Trained Sepoys: the New Model Force. A black-and-white photograph of a dense body of soldiers in helmets with rifles, kneeling and standing in a tight square (seen from one corner, so it looks like a diamond) on bare rocky ground with hills behind and an officer at the centre. Typed caption: European-trained, regularly-paid Indian sepoys, the disciplined infantry that broke traditional cavalry at Adyar. Teacher's ink: "Infantry Square" written above the picture and two yellow lines tracing the front corner of the square like a roof. Teacher: On the three-advantages slide (Lecture 12, slide 69) the teacher underlined "light, mobile European cannon", "Babur 26-30", "formations", "infantry squares" and "small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery." He labelled the photograph "Infantry Square" and traced its corner: the men face outward on every side, so a cavalry charge from any direction meets a wall of muskets. On the Adyar slide he boxed the words "Turning Point" and wrote under it: "Indian kings wanted European help in modernising their military." Takeaway (Adyar 1746). This was not just a military victory. For the first time it was proven conclusively that a small, disciplined, European-trained infantry with modern artillery could crush a vastly larger traditional Indian army. The psychological impact was enormous: it gave Europeans the confidence to start interfering directly in Indian political disputes, which is exactly what Dupleix 42-54 proceeded to do. The Indian royal elites also wanted to use the military service of the Europeans in their internal and external disputes. Teacher: The Wagner Group analogy (handout). Have you heard of the Wagner Group? It is a company which sells military service to the Russian State. In a way the French were now the Wagner Group of India: a company whose army could be hired by Indian rulers. The teacher develops this on the board in section 5.1. 4.4 Consequence: the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748)  Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748). Ended: the War of the Austrian Succession. Mutual return: both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in America and India. Madras: went back to the EIC. For Dupleix 42-54: deeply frustrating, his victories in India were traded away at a negotiating table in Europe (North America mattered more to France, where Britain had won). Teacher's ink: at the top "Fr won in India BUT Br won in Americas"; "1740-48" beside the Ended row (last digit hard to read); on the right a small table "MAIN INTEREST: Britain = India; France = Americas, especially N and C Am" with a figure-of-8 sketch labelled NAm, CAm and SAm; at the bottom three points: "# No change in (T)", "# (EU) infantry >>> Indian cavalry", "# Dupleix 42-54 KAT Gaya". However, in North America, which was more strategically important to France, Britain had won. So in the Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle (1748), which ended the War of the Austrian Succession, both sides agreed to return each other's possessions in America and India. Madras went back to the EIC. For Dupleix 42-54 this was deeply frustrating: his victories in India were traded away at a negotiating table in Europe. But he was not done. His next opportunity came almost immediately, in the form of succession disputes: one in Hyderabad, one in Carnatic. Teacher: The board's reasoning for the treaty. "The French won in India BUT the British won in the Americas." The two countries valued different places: Britain's main interest = India; France's main interest = the Americas, especially North and Central America. So France gave back Madras to recover what it had lost in America. Three results he lists: (1) no change in territory; (2) European infantry is far greater than Indian cavalry (the lesson of Adyar stays even though Madras is returned); (3) "Dupleix 42-54 KAT gaya" (Hindi: he was cut out, left empty-handed).

Teacher: Learn the map by the board's code "MWP": on the coast from north to south come Madras (HQ of the EIC), Wandiwash (the battle of the 3rd Carnatic War) and Pondicherry (HQ of the French EIC). Arcot, inland, is the capital of Carnatic. Hyderabad lies north of the River Krishna, and the Northern Sarkars run along the coast further up. In the 2nd Carnatic War "all gathered in Carnatic": Nasir Jung 48-50 and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 also arrived in Carnatic. The war has two phases: the French EIC smiles in the 1st phase (till 1751); the English EIC smiles in the 2nd phase. 5.1 Phase 1: French victory (1749-51) Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 is killed (good) Chanda Sahib 49-52 is declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot By December 1750: Nasir Jung 48-50 is also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is declared Nizam Muzaffar Jung 50-51 marches toward Hyderabad, accompanied by Bussy's army (bad) February 1751, Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass: Muzaffar Jung 50-51 is killed by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool; the Nawab of Kurnool is also killed (good) Bussy reaches Hyderabad and installs Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam Battle of Ambur (1749): Nawab Anwaruddin 44-49 was killed. Chanda Sahib 49-52 was declared Nawab of Carnatic at the capital Arcot. (The slide notes: Ambur is 190 km west of Chennai; the teacher added "towards Bengaluru.") By December 1750, Nasir Jung 48-50 was also killed and Muzaffar Jung 50-51 was declared Nizam. Bussy was the junior of Dupleix 42-54. Accompanied by Bussy's army, Muzaffar Jung 50-51 began marching toward Hyderabad. But he was killed in February 1751 at the Battle of Lakkireddipalli Pass by the Afghan Nawab of Kurnool, who felt cheated as he was not given the territory promised to him for his support. The Nawab of Kurnool was also killed. (The slide's aside on the pass: "unlucky lol.") Bussy now reached Hyderabad and installed Salabat Jung 51-62 as Nizam. He was a son of Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 and an uncle of the recently killed Muzaffar Jung 50-51. Teacher: Beside the Hyderabad row the teacher starred: "Asaf Jahi dynasty, by Nizam-ul-Mulk 24-48 [Asaf Jah I]." All the Hyderabad claimants here (Nasir Jung 48-50, Muzaffar Jung 50-51, Salabat Jung 51-62) belong to this one family; see Chapter 3.  Teacher's board (no typed text): the Wagner Group analogy. "# Death of MJ is BLOT on MILITARY reputation of Fr eic", with a line "= Like WAGNER GROUP". In a large bracket: "MJ and C Sahib HIRED Wagner Group / Fr eic TO BE Nawab". On the left: "so BUSSY CREATED TERROR for general msg that Don't mess with Fr eic [on way to Hyd]", with an arrow to "made Salabat Jung 51-62 Nizam". On the right under "WAGNER GROUP": "# a company; # sells service for rupees = MILITARY SERVICE". Teacher: The Wagner Group board. The Wagner Group is a company that sells a service for money, and the service is military service. In the same way Muzaffar Jung 50-51 ("MJ") and Chanda Sahib 49-52 hired the French EIC, like a Wagner Group, to become rulers. So the death of MJ was a blot on the military reputation of the French EIC: a firm that sells protection cannot let its client be killed. That is why Bussy created terror on the way to Hyderabad, as a general message: "don't mess with the French EIC," and then made Salabat Jung 51-62 the Nizam. The gains from Phase 1  Dupleix 42-54's Gains from Phase 1. Hyderabad: Bussy was made French agent/resident at the Nizam's court; a French army stationed for protection of the Nizam; this army was to be paid for by Hyderabad, thus the French EIC was given the Northern Sarkars (present-day Andhra), Bussy administered it and kept its revenues (brutal methods of LR extraction: terror and massacre); 2,00,000 pounds for the French EIC from the Nizam; Bussy got personal jagirs in Masulipatnam and Yanam. Carnatic: Dupleix 42-54 declared himself Nawab of all lands between the River Krishna and Cape Comorin (= Carnatic), with Chanda Sahib 49-52 as Deputy Nawab of Arcot; personal jagir of Rs 1 lakh a year in Villianallur near Pondicherry. (1) Its title dates the 2nd Carnatic War "1750-54"; the handout and every slide give 1749-54. (2) The red bracket is written "x 300%", but Rs 1 lakh becomes Rs 3 crore only when multiplied by 300 times; take the point (a very large income), not the arithmetic.  Teacher's board (no typed text). Left: "THINK: as employee of Fr eic: # SALARY, (BUT) now PERSONAL # JAGIRS + CASH" (BUT circled, jagirs and cash underlined). A vertical divider. Right: "interest of these empire BUILDER (employees)" with employees circled, and lines from it to "Fr eic", "Eng eic" (underlined), "Estado da India" and "Dutch VOC". Teacher: THINK: why do Company men build empires? As an employee of the French EIC a man gets only a salary. BUT empire building now brings him personal jagirs plus cash. So the personal interest of these empire-builder employees drives the wars. And this holds for every company: the French EIC, the English EIC, the Estado da India and the Dutch VOC. (This is condition 1 of section 1.2: the personally ambitious Governor.) Takeaway: Dupleix 42-54 had just invented the model of empire building in India. Put your candidate in power, station your army at his expense, extract territory as payment, and sit in the court as the real power behind the throne. This is exactly the model the British EIC would refine and use with devastating effect for the next century. (The handout's aside: "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54" would be the thoughts of the EIC.) 1. Succession dispute = opportunity: interfere and bring your favourite claimant into power 2. Extract gains, military domination: station your army in the Indian State and make the State pay for this army 3. Extract gains, territory as payment: take land as payment for the army (bad) 4. Puppet State: station your Resident in the Indian King's court, who establishes his indirect rule Teacher: On the model slide (Lecture 13, slide 10) the teacher wrote "FACTIONALISM (R vs R)" above step 1: the opening is always a quarrel between two rivals. Beside step 2 he wrote "Free of cost domination": the Indian State itself pays for the army that dominates it. He underlined "Resident in the Indian King's court" and "Indirect Rule" in step 4.  Teacher's board (no typed text), headed "FYQ-M" (underlined; the first letter is unclear, probably PYQ-M). The question in white ink: "MODEL of empire BUILDING (in India) by TRADING Companies was FOUNDED [by FRENCH] and [implemented by BRITISH]. Analyse". "by French" is boxed with a line below to "CW2" (the 2nd Carnatic War); "implemented by British" is in a larger rounded box with a line below to "future topics". Teacher: The Mains question on the board: "Model of empire building (in India) by trading companies was founded by the French and implemented by the British. Analyse." The teacher split the answer into two parts: "founded by French" = the 2nd Carnatic War (this section: the four steps above, with Hyderabad and Carnatic as the examples); "implemented by British" = future topics (Plassey and Buxar in Chapter 10, the Subsidiary Alliance in Chapter 11).  PYQ 2, Prelims 1996, on Dupleix 42-54: Who among the following were the first European to initiate the policy of taking part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories? (a) Clive 57-67 (b) Dupleix 42-54 (c) Albuquerque 09-15 (d) Warren Hastings 73-85. The typed options carry no years. Teacher's ink: yellow underlines on "first European", "quarrels of Indian princes" and "to acquire territories"; years written in yellow beside the four options in order: "57-60, 65-67 [1700s, Governor Bengal Presidency]"; "42-54 [1742-54]"; "09-15 [1509-1615]" as written; "73-85 [1700s]". Prelims 1996: the first European to take part in the quarrels of Indian princes with a view to acquire territories = (b) Dupleix 42-54. He invented the model: back a candidate, station your army at his expense, take territory as payment, sit in court as the real power. It was first used in the 2nd Carnatic War (backing Muzaffar Jung 50-51 and Chanda Sahib 49-52). Clive 57-67 came later: he used and refined the model in Bengal (Plassey 1757, Buxar 1764) but did not invent it. Albuquerque 09-15 was a 16th-century Portuguese conqueror (took Goa 1510): an earlier era of direct conquest, not the "back-a-claimant" model. Warren Hastings 73-85 was a later EIC Governor-General: a refiner, not the originator. 5.2 Phase 2: the EIC bounces back The EIC decided to fight back by supporting Md Ali 52-95 (Carnatic), who was holding out in Trichinopoly. Dupleix 42-54 got obsessed with eliminating any future challenge to his power. Hence he made the critical mistake of leaving the capital Arcot unguarded and focusing on Trichinopoly. Robert Clive 57-67, operating from Madras with a small force of roughly 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys, took over Arcot (the slide dates it: Arcot 1751). He then defended it against a massive counter-siege for 53 days. The capital was now with the British! Clive 57-67 became a celebrated figure back in Britain. The French government in Paris, anxious to honour the 1748 treaty and preserve its more lucrative American possessions, refused to help Dupleix 42-54. By 1754 the French had lost the 2nd Carnatic War. Md Ali 52-95 holds out in Trichinopoly, backed by the EIC (warn) Dupleix 42-54's critical mistake: he focuses on Trichinopoly and leaves the capital Arcot unguarded Clive 57-67 takes Arcot (1751) from Madras with about 200 Europeans and 300 sepoys He defends it through a 53-day counter-siege (warn) Paris refuses to help Dupleix 42-54: it wants to honour the 1748 treaty and keep its American possessions (bad) By 1754 the French have lost the 2nd Carnatic War Teacher: On the slide the teacher underlined only two phrases: "1748 treaty" and "refused to help Dupleix 42-54." That is the real reason for the defeat: France chose America over India again, exactly as in 1748. 5.3 The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754)  Treaty of Pondicherry (1754). Recall: Dupleix 42-54 recalled to France, replaced by Godeheu, on account of high war expenditure (he died in poverty in France, 1763). 1. Hyderabad: French influence remained in Hyderabad via Bussy as agent; French army in Hyderabad and Northern Sarkars with the French. 2. Factories: French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic were retained. 3. Carnatic: Md Ali 52-95 became Nawab of Carnatic, hence EIC influence in Carnatic. Chanda Sahib 49-52: escaped to Tanjore, beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, Maratha Raja of Thanjavur, an old rival (Maratha rule in Tanjore began 1674 when Venkoji / Ekoji, half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80, conquered the region). Teacher's ink: "42-54" written above the recall row; underlines on high war expenditure, French influence, Bussy as agent, French army, Northern Sarkars and EIC influence in Carnatic, with small numerals 1, 2, 3 over the three French retentions; "[Fr (smiley)]" beside the Hyderabad row and "[Br (smiley)]" beside the Carnatic row; "[Company = ORG with PROFIT MOTIVE]" beside the recall row; "[FACTORY: warehouses + homes + offices + maybe fort]" beside the Factories row. Dupleix 42-54 was recalled to France, replaced by Godeheu, on account of the high war expenditure. He died in poverty in France in 1763, abandoned by the State he had served. The Treaty of Pondicherry (1754) was a middle path:   Clause   Terms   Who smiles (teacher's ink)    --- --- ---    1. Hyderabad   French influence remained in Hyderabad: (1) Bussy as agent, (2) the French army in Hyderabad, (3) the Northern Sarkars with the French   French     2. Factories   French factories in Pondicherry and Carnatic were retained       3. Carnatic   Md Ali 52-95 became Nawab of Carnatic: hence EIC influence in Carnatic   British   Chanda Sahib 49-52, having escaped to Tanjore (present-day Thanjavur in Tamil Nadu), was beheaded by Pratap Singh 39-63, the Maratha Raja of Thanjavur: an old rival. Maratha rule in Tanjore had begun in 1674 when Venkoji (also known as Ekoji), half-brother of Chhatrapati Shivaji 74-80, conquered the region. Teacher: Why was a winning Governor-General recalled? The teacher's bracket: "Company = an organisation with a profit motive." High war expenditure eats profit, so the company removes the man who causes it. Beside the Factories row he repeats the definition from Chapter 8: "Factory = warehouses + homes + offices + maybe a fort." His two smileys read the treaty as a split: the French smile in Hyderabad, the British smile in Carnatic.  Teacher's board (no typed text): how wars end. "# WAR is expensive for BOTH: losing party, victorious party". "# So BOTH want end of war". "# VICTOR would go for end of war if achieved [WAR AIMS] (boxed), i.e. core goal of war". In yellow: a bracket at the top right "1740-48: AWoS; 1st CW 1746-48", and under the war aims line "[EIC = core motive: TRADE]" with two branches "HYD (smiley)" and "CARNATIC (smiley)". "# When TREATY is negotiated, then power differential between both sides and ability (economic, military etc.) = imp factors" (imp factors underlined). Teacher: The board's theory of treaties (marked "imp factors"). War is expensive for both, the losing party and the victorious party, so both want an end to the war. The victor will agree to end the war if it has achieved its war aims, that is, the core goal of the war. For the EIC the core motive was trade, so it could settle once its trade was safe (the two branches read Hyderabad and Carnatic, each with a smiley, matching the treaty slide's split). When a treaty is negotiated, the important factors are the power differential between the two sides and their ability, economic and military. Apply this to all three treaties: 1748 (the bracket recalls the Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 and the 1st Carnatic War 1746-48), 1754 and 1763.

items.t: 6 · The 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)
items.x: 6.1 Reason  Teacher's board (no typed text). "3 CW 1746-63" (the three Carnatic Wars) with a tree: on the left the circled numbers 1 and 3 with a circled "IR" below; on the right a circled 2 with "Factionalism" below. Then "(3): ROYAL MILITARIES (Fr, Br) joined armies of Fr eic, Eng eic". Bottom left: "3rd CW: [EIC + Br] vs [Fr eic + Fr]". The 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) was once again a European conflict brought to Indian shores: the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63), fought across Europe, the Americas, Africa and India. French side: Count de Lally (of the French State, not the French EIC) arrived from France with the Royal military and led the French alongside Bussy of the French EIC. British side: Eyre Coote (of the British State, not the EIC) arrived from Britain with the Royal military and led the British alongside Robert Clive 57-67 of the EIC. Teacher: The board's recap before the 3rd war. Of the three Carnatic Wars (1746-63), wars 1 and 3 come from "IR" (international relations: Britain against France), war 2 from factionalism. What is new in war 3: the Royal militaries (French and British) joined the armies of the French EIC and the English EIC. So the line-up is [EIC + Britain] versus [French EIC + France]. On the typed slide he wrote "had impacts" above "a European conflict on Indian shores" and underlined Count de Lally, Eyre Coote and royal military on both sides. 6.2 Why did France lose the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63)?  Handout map (also Lecture 13, slide 16): a close-up of the Coromandel Coast from an old printed map. Labels from north to south: Masulipatam 175? (year cut off), Coromandel Coast, Madras 1639, Chingleput 1780, Wandiwash 1760, Pondicherry (Fr.), Karikal (Fr.), then Trincomali 1782 and Ceylon (Dutch) at the bottom; "Circars" and "Fr. 1718: Br. 178?" are partly cut off at the top. Caption strip: Ch 9, Carnatic Wars: Madras (Br.) vs Pondicherry (Fr.); Wandiwash 1760. On the slide version the teacher drew three yellow pointer lines from Madras 1639, Wandiwash 1760 and Pondicherry (Fr.). The most decisive battle was the Battle of Wandiwash (1760). (The handout's memory line: "where the French were washed away.") After that the French lost everywhere, including Pondicherry itself, their headquarters officially since 1701, with Fort Louis. The chain slides add: Wandiwash was fought on 22 January 1760, and the Siege of Pondicherry came in 1761. Teacher: The three pointer lines on the map mark the same three coastal places as the board's "MWP": Madras (the British base), Wandiwash (between the two) and Pondicherry (the French base). Wandiwash lies between the two headquarters, which is why the decisive battle was there.  PYQ 1, Prelims 1995, Battle of Wandiwash: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched? (a) Battle of Buxar: Mir Jafar vs. Clive 57-67 (b) Battle of Wandiwash: French vs. East India Company (c) Battle of Chilianwala: Dalhousie 48-56 vs Marathas (d) Battle of Kharda: Nizam vs. East India Company. Teacher's ink: a circled F beside (a); a tick beside (b); in (c) "Marathas" struck through, "SIKH" written beside it, circled F; in (d) "East India Company" struck through, "MARATHAS 1795" written below, circled F. Prelims 1995: UPSC asked "match the battle to who fought it" by jumbling correct pairs. The correct pairs are: Battle of Buxar (1764) = EIC vs Mir Qasim 60-63 (with Awadh and Shah Alam II 60-06); Battle of Chilianwala (1849) = EIC under Dalhousie 48-56 vs the Sikhs (2nd Anglo-Sikh War); Battle of Kharda (1795) = Nizam of Hyderabad vs the Marathas; Battle of Wandiwash (1760) = French vs the East India Company. The answer was (b). The trap in (a): Mir Jafar was the EIC's man at Plassey 1757, not its enemy at Buxar. France lost for four reasons.  Wandiwash (1760): Why France Lost the 3rd War. Battle of Wandiwash 1760: the most decisive battle; after it the French lost everywhere, including Pondicherry, their headquarters since 1701 with Fort Louis. 1. Tactical mistake: Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic; Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Bengal and took the Northern Sarkars in 1759. 2. Poor leadership: Lally, despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, demoralised his army. Teacher's ink: underlines on Fort Louis, Lally and rude conduct; under row 2 "# DUPLEIX 42-54 not HERE"; top right a sketch: a line from "CARNATIC" up to "N. SARKARS" with "Bussy" at its end, a curve marked (1) "LALLY" with an arrow "TO HELP" back to Carnatic, and (2) "BENGAL" with an arrow down into the N. Sarkars.  Why France Lost the 3rd War (contd.). 3. Financial weakness: French soldiers went unpaid for months; the French EIC had spent heavily in earlier wars without gains; Britain had profited from eastern trade since 1600; British capitalism was mature (Industrial Revolution 1750-1850) while French feudalism ended only after the French Revolution of 1789. 4. Superior British navy: Britain dominated the Coromandel coast, decisive in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic. Teacher's ink: "Financial weakness", "soldiers" and "unpaid for months" underlined; on the right, arrows from "earlier wars" to "1740-48 AWoS [1st CW 1746-48]" and "2nd CW 1749-54: Hyd gains BUT STILL higher war expenditure" (BUT and STILL underlined); at the bottom left, written along a diagonal line, "CARNATIC" above and "COROMANDEL COAST" below.   Reason   Detail    --- ---    1. Tactical mistake   Bussy abandoned the Northern Sarkars to reinforce Lally in Carnatic. Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Bengal and took over the Northern Sarkars in 1759     2. Poor leadership   Lally was despised by his own officers and sepoys for his rude conduct, which demoralised the army     3. Financial weakness   French soldiers went unpaid for months. The French EIC had spent heavily in the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-48) and the first two Carnatic Wars without commensurate gains. In contrast, Britain had been profiting from eastern trade since 1600. British capitalism was mature; feudalism in France ended only after the French Revolution of 1789, while the Industrial Revolution had begun in Britain (1750-1850)     4. Superior British navy   This gave Britain decisive advantages in the coastal warfare of the Northern Sarkars and Carnatic. Britain's navy was able to dominate the Coromandel coast   Teacher: The sketch for the tactical mistake. Step (1): Bussy leaves the Northern Sarkars and goes down to Carnatic to help Lally. Step (2): from Bengal, Clive 57-67 comes down into the now unguarded Northern Sarkars (1759). Under "Poor leadership" the teacher wrote "Dupleix 42-54 not here": the one able French leader had been recalled in 1754, so France fought this war with Lally. Teacher: On financial weakness. The "earlier wars" that drained the French EIC are the Austrian War of Succession 1740-48 [the 1st Carnatic War 1746-48] and the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54. His note on the second: "Hyderabad gains, BUT STILL higher war expenditure": even the winning phase cost more than it earned. For the navy point he wrote Carnatic over Coromandel Coast: Carnatic is the land along the Coromandel coast, so whoever commands the sea commands the war there.  Teacher's board (no typed text): "if you want to see [CAPITALISM] in SOCIETY" (Capitalism boxed), with three bullets: "wake up at 4am and sit in BALCONY (facing a main road)"; "[PPL] at mass level have a belief [can be RICH by WORKING HARD]"; "BOMBAY never sleeps [so CITY provides money opportunities 24x7]". On the left: "FR 1789 ended Feudalism, then Capitalism in France" and "[BUT merchants existed PRE 1789]" (BUT underlined). Teacher: What does "British capitalism was mature" mean? The board's picture. If you want to see capitalism in a society: wake up at 4 am and sit in a balcony facing a main road. People are already at work. In a capitalist society people at the mass level have a belief that they can become rich by working hard. Bombay never sleeps, because the city provides opportunities to earn 24x7. The French Revolution of 1789 ended feudalism, and only then did capitalism come to France (but note: merchants existed in France before 1789 too). Britain had this money-making society earlier, so it could pay for its wars. 6.3 Why did the EIC win the Carnatic Wars (1746-48, 49-54, 56-63)?   Factor   Detail    --- ---    1. France starved Dupleix 42-54 of reinforcements   To preserve its gains from the 1748 Treaty (Aix-La-Chapelle)     2. Leadership   French: the recall of Dupleix 42-54 after the 2nd Carnatic War hurt the chances of French victory; Lally displayed poor leadership in the 3rd Carnatic War. British: Robert Clive 57-67 and Eyre Coote displayed good leadership     3. Superior British navy   British naval dominance of the coast     4. Finances   The EIC was a private joint-stock firm with deep capital; it had accumulated wealth, along with huge monetary gains after Plassey 1757. The French EIC was a State PSU with weak finances. The French economy was weak compared to Britain, which was the world's top economy of the time. Past war expenditure without any formidable gains hurt French capabilities, e.g. Lally's troops went unpaid (the slide adds: unpaid for months, so low morale)     5. Tactical mistakes   Leaving Arcot (the capital of Carnatic) unguarded in the 2nd Carnatic War and leaving the Northern Sarkars unguarded in the 3rd Carnatic War   Teacher: Above the slide's title the teacher wrote "all (3)": this table answers "Why the EIC won all 3 Carnatic Wars," while section 6.2 answers only the 3rd war. For a Mains answer, use 6.3 for the whole contest and 6.2 for Wandiwash. The handout numbers these factors 1, 2, 2, 3, 4 (the number 2 is printed twice). There are five factors; they are renumbered 1 to 5 here. 6.4 The Treaty of Paris (1763)  Treaty of Paris (1763). France lost all gains since 1749, under "PM KYC (Yojana)": restricted to its pre-1749 position; France retained only 5 small trading posts: Pondicherry (E), Mahe (west coast), Karaikal (E), Yanam (E), Chandernagore (E). Barred: France was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases. 1769: French EIC abolished by France = the French State gave up ambitions of dominating India's international trade. British monopoly: having countered the Portuguese by 1612, the Dutch by 1650s and the French by 1763, the British EIC now held monopoly over India's international trade. Teacher's ink: at the top "[1748: T of Aix La Chapelle, T of Pondicherry 1754]"; "PM KYC (Yojana)" underlined; "CENTRES" written over "posts", which is struck through; "Malabar" under Mahe (west coast) and "BENGAL" under Chandernagore; underlines on strong army or fortifying its bases, French EIC abolished by France, British EIC, monopoly and India's international trade; a word above "1650s" [unclear: ROYALTY or RIVALRY]; below the last row "NOT (T)"; on the right "Who will BUY INDIAN GOODS; Who will DOMINATE exports from India". Under the Treaty of Paris (1763): France lost all gains made in India since 1749 and was restricted to its pre-1749 position. France retained only five small trading posts: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam and Chandernagore. France was barred from maintaining a strong army or fortifying its bases.   Letter   Post   Where (slide and teacher's ink)    --- --- ---    P   Pondicherry   East coast     M   Mahe   West coast (teacher: Malabar)     K   Karaikal   East coast     Y   Yanam   East coast     C   Chandernagore   East (teacher: Bengal)   Teacher: The slide's mnemonic "PM KYC (Yojana)" is underlined by the teacher: Pondicherry, Mahe, Karaikal, Yanam, Chandernagore. Only Mahe is on the west coast (Malabar); Chandernagore is in Bengal. He replaced "trading posts" with "trading CENTRES." At the top he lined up the three treaties to learn in order: 1748 Treaty of Aix-La-Chapelle, 1754 Treaty of Pondicherry, 1763 Treaty of Paris. In 1769 the French EIC was abolished by France. This signifies that the French government had given up on its ambitions of dominating the international trade of India. The abolition of the French EIC does not mean other French traders could not trade in India, just that the French State was not interested in running a government company for it. After successfully countering the Portuguese by 1612, the Dutch by the 1650s and the French by 1763, the British EIC now had a monopoly over India's international trade. Teacher: Under the British monopoly row the teacher wrote "NOT (T)": in 1763 the EIC has a monopoly over trade, not territory. What was decided was only "who will buy Indian goods, who will dominate exports from India." This fits the board in section 1.2: the Carnatic Wars were wars for trade. A handwritten word above "1650s" on this slide is [unclear: it reads ROYALTY or RIVALRY]. Check your own notebook. 6.5 Link with Plassey, and what came later  Carnatic Wars: Legacy and After. Link with Plassey 1757: the 3rd Carnatic War brought large British royal military to India; that strength and Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy made Plassey possible; without Carnatic, perhaps no Plassey would have happened, which led to empire building by EIC. Treaty of Hyderabad 1766: Hyderabad ceded the Northern Sarkars to EIC for Rs 7 lakh a year and protection against Marathas and Mysore. Domination of South India by EIC: the Carnatic Wars, though fought for India's international trade, laid the foundation of British domination of South India; Subsidiary Alliance: Hyderabad = 1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with EIC (1798); Mysore 1799; Travancore 1805; Carnatic was annexed 1801. Teacher's ink: on the right a flow "7yr GLOBAL WAR, then 3rd CW, then Br ROYAL MILITARY in INDIA, then confidence of CLIVE for accepting Jafar's offer"; under the Domination row "3rd CW + 3.5 Decades"; underlines on Northern Sarkars to EIC, Hyderabad, Subsidiary Alliance, (1798), Mysore 1799, Travancore 1805, Carnatic and annexed 1801. Takeaway: link with the Battle of Plassey (1757). The 3rd Carnatic War brought large numbers of British Royal military troops to India, and it was this military strength, and Clive 57-67's shrewd diplomacy, that made Plassey possible. Without Carnatic there may not have been a Plassey, which led to Empire Building by the EIC. Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) 3rd Carnatic War British Royal military in India (good) Confidence of Clive 57-67 for accepting Jafar's offer: Plassey 1757 Later: In the Treaty of Hyderabad (1766), Hyderabad formally ceded the Northern Sarkars to the EIC in exchange for Rs 7 lakh annually and protection against the Marathas and Mysore. Hyderabad became the 1st Indian state to sign a Subsidiary Alliance with the EIC, in 1798. Mysore signed in 1799 and Travancore in 1805, while Carnatic was annexed in 1801. Thus the Carnatic Wars, though fought for the international trade of India, laid the foundation of British domination of South India. Teacher: Under "Domination of South India" the teacher wrote "3rd CW + 3.5 decades": that is, from the end of the 3rd Carnatic War (1763) it took about three and a half decades to reach the first Subsidiary Alliance (Hyderabad, 1798). He underlined each item of that row: Hyderabad 1798, Mysore 1799, Travancore 1805, Carnatic annexed 1801. "Jafar's offer" in his flow is Mir Jafar's deal with Clive 57-67, the story of Chapter 10.
