items.t: 1 · Plassey marks the beginning of conquest
items.x: Plassey Marks the Beginning of Conquest. Conquest began: conquest (military domination and political supremacy) by the EIC in Bengal. EIC did not establish its Rule: it did not legally take over sovereign functions in Bengal after Plassey 1757; it focused on military control and extracting wealth. Takeaway: Rule did not begin in 1757; Conquest and the Drain of Wealth from India, however, did. Teacher's ink: after "extracting wealth" he writes "= PLUNDER", which splits into ATTACK and LOOT; on the right "PLASSEY PLUNDER [1757-65]" with "illegal" under it; below, "1765: because FM of Bengal and LEGAL RIGHT TO USE Bengal WEALTH, therefore LOOT LEGALIZE". Plassey marks the beginning of the transformation of the EIC into a Company State. Conquest means military domination and political supremacy. It began here, in Bengal. But the EIC did not legally take over sovereign functions in Bengal after the Battle of Plassey 1757. It focused on military control and on extracting wealth. Takeaway: Rule did not begin in 1757. Conquest and the Drain of Wealth from India, however, did. Teacher: Extracting wealth = PLUNDER, and plunder has two parts: ATTACK and LOOT. The Plassey Plunder runs from 1757 to 1765 and it was illegal. In 1765 the EIC became the FM (finance minister, that is the Diwan) of Bengal and so got the LEGAL RIGHT to use Bengal's wealth: the loot was legalised. This is the thread that ties Plassey to Buxar.

items.t: 2 · The Royal Farman of 1717: the seed of conflict
items.x: 2.1 The four Farmans that strengthened the EIC  Farmans that strengthened the EIC. 1613 (Jahangir 05-27): right to establish a factory at Surat, after the EIC beat the Portuguese in the Battle of Suvali 1612. 1618 (Jahangir 05-27): right to factories across the whole Mughal empire plus liberal trading rights, won by Thomas Roe's lobbying (British Resident 1615-19). 1691 (Subahdar of Bengal, under Aurangzeb 58-07): right to Duty-Free Trade (DFT) in Bengal for Rs 3,000 a year; EIC trade was economically beneficial and brought forex into India. 1717 Imperial Farman (Farrukhsiyar 13-19): "Magna Carta of the Company", won by medical diplomacy, the EIC's Dr William Hamilton cured Farrukhsiyar 13-19 of a serious illness. Teacher's ink: a bracketed note beside the title (reads like "FYI") and an arrow under it reading "Eco [one unclear sign] of EIC"; from "liberal trading rights" three lines fan out: Lower export duties, Less paper work, use More ports.   Farman   Issued by   What it gave the EIC    --- --- ---    1613   Jahangir 05-27   The right to establish a factory in Surat, after the EIC defeated the Portuguese in the Battle of Suvali 1612     1618   Jahangir 05-27   The right to establish factories in the whole of the Mughal empire and liberal trading rights, due to lobbying by Thomas Roe (British Resident 1615-19)     1691   The Subahdar of Bengal, with Aurangzeb 58-07's approval   The right to Duty-Free Trade (DFT) in Bengal in exchange for Rs 3,000 per annum. The EIC's trade was economically beneficial and brought forex into India     1717 Imperial (Royal) Farman   Farrukhsiyar 13-19   Often called the "Magna Carta of the Company". It was the result of medical diplomacy: Dr William Hamilton, an English surgeon with the EIC, successfully treated Farrukhsiyar 13-19 for a serious illness   Teacher: "Liberal trading rights" (1618) meant three things: lower export duties, less paperwork, and the use of more ports. Beside the title the teacher wrote a short bracketed note (it reads like "FYI") and under it "Eco ... of EIC" (the Farmans as the economic strengthening of the EIC). Unclear handwriting on slide 29. The bracketed note beside the title and the middle sign in "Eco [unclear] of EIC" cannot be read with confidence. Check your notebook for what the teacher said here. 2.2 What the 1717 Farman gave, and what the Nawab refused  1717 Imperial Farman: source of conflict between the EIC and the Nawab of Bengal. The 1717 Farman gave the EIC (a) DFT in Deccan, Gujarat and Bengal (a Royal Farman reiterating the 1691 provincial privilege or Parwana), (b) the right to use the Royal Mint, to mint Indian coins (sikkas) and save the cost of converting gold, (c) the right to rent 38 villages around Calcutta to expand the settlement. Nawab MQK 17-27 (Murshid Quli Khan) allowed DFT but refused to let EIC officials misuse Dastaks for private trade; refused use of the Royal Mint (it diluted sovereign authority and led to loss of the commission earned on gold to sikka); allowed renting villages but NOT purchase. Teacher's ink: "MAGNA CARTA of EIC" under the title; "[Presidency 1699]" and "[1690]" under the settlement clause; on the right "Within Indian territory one can use only Indian SIKKAS", "EIC sends GOLD/SILVER to the ROYAL MINT" with a curved arrow "SIKKAS" coming back, and "Here the ROYAL MINT earned commission". The 1717 Imperial (Royal) Farman gave the EIC three rights: The right to Duty-Free Trade (DFT) in Deccan, Gujarat and Bengal. For Bengal this was a Royal Farman reiterating a pre-existing privilege, granted under the sign and seal of the Subahdar in 1691 (the slide calls the 1691 grant a provincial privilege or Parwana). The right to use the Royal Mint. The EIC could mint Indian coins and so save the cost of converting gold into Indian currency (sikkas) for purchasing Indian goods. The right to rent 38 villages around Calcutta for expanding its trading settlement. Teacher: Why the mint mattered. Within Indian territory one can use only Indian sikkas. So the EIC took its gold and silver to the Royal Mint and got sikkas back, and here the Royal Mint earned a commission. The right to mint its own coins would save the EIC that cost and take that commission away from the government. Under the settlement clause the teacher noted two years: [1690] (under "expand the settlement") and [Presidency 1699] (they read as the year of the Calcutta settlement and the year it became a Presidency; the story is in Chapter 8). The 1717 Farman became a source of conflict between the EIC and the Nawab of Bengal. Bengal by 1717 was a successor State. Recall: successor means uttaradhikari, one who comes from within the family. Here the family is the political family of the Mughal State (the Mughal Emperor and his Mansabdars). So certain powerful Mansabdars established their rule in certain provinces and took away the real powers of the Emperor, making him a symbolic authority. They were MQK 17-27, Sadat Khan 22-39 and Nizam 24-48 in Bengal, Awadh and Hyderabad respectively (Chapter 3). Nawab Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27) dealt with the three rights like this:   Right in the 1717 Farman   What MQK 17-27 did   Why    --- --- ---    Duty-free trade   Allowed duty-free trade by the EIC, but refused to let EIC officials misuse Dastaks for their own private trade   The privilege was for the Company's goods, not for the officials' personal goods     Use of the Royal Mint   Refused   It hurt sovereign authority and government revenue (the government earned commission on the conversion of gold into Indian sikkas)     38 villages around Calcutta   Allowed renting but NOT purchase   The teacher underlined "NOT purchase"   The slide table for the Nawabs (Lecture 13, slide 41) says MQK 17-27 "won the 1717 Farman"; the handout's own figure says he "accepted the 1717 Farman, resisted Dastak abuse". The Farman was issued to the EIC by Farrukhsiyar 13-19; MQK 17-27 is the Nawab who accepted it in part and resisted the rest. Read the slide's phrase in that sense.

items.t: 3 · The Dastak problem
items.x: 3.1 Private trade and what a Dastak was  Teacher's board on private trade and the Dastak. Top: "PVT TRADE: when EIC officers purchase Indian goods for trade in their personal capacity, apart from purchasing goods on behalf of the EIC. [Reason = GREED; = CORRUPTION; STAB in the BACK of the EIC by its employees]". It "VIOLATES the ROYAL CHARTER which gave monopoly over British trade in the East Indies to the EIC", and "an employee should not become a competitor to his own company". Bottom: "DASTAK = Document by EIC officers, therefore it operationalized DFT. Misuse = using a Dastak for PVT TRADE by MISDECLARING that the goods are of the EIC. Led to loss of DUTY [TAX Revenue] for the Indian State." In the middle a drawn sample Dastak with a signature: "It is certified that these 100 goods are of the EIC. Please allow DFT exit from port." It goes "To the Indian Custom officers", and "he allows the Container to leave India without Duty Payment". Teacher: Private trade (PVT TRADE) is when EIC officers purchase Indian goods for trade in their personal capacity, apart from purchasing goods on behalf of the EIC. The reason is greed; it is corruption; it is a "stab in the back" of the EIC by its own employees. It violates the Royal Charter, which gave the monopoly over British trade in the East Indies to the EIC: an employee should not become a competitor to his own company. Teacher: A Dastak is a document issued by EIC officers; it is what "operationalised" duty-free trade. The teacher drew one: "It is certified that these 100 goods are of the EIC. Please allow DFT exit from port. (Signed)". It is shown to the Indian customs officer, who then allows the container to leave India without duty payment. Misuse = using a Dastak for private trade by MISDECLARING that the goods are the EIC's. It led to a loss of duty [tax revenue] for the Indian State.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    What a Dastak is   A permit issued by EIC officials certifying that goods belonged to the EIC, and hence exempt from export duty     Misuse   In practice EIC officials also used these permits for their own private trade, claiming goods bought in a personal capacity as company goods. They also sold Dastaks to other exporters     Scale (by 1750)   Private trade by EIC officials was worth 1,00,000 pounds per annum, roughly fifty times their annual salaries     Why the EIC could not control it   Even its own top officials in India engaged in private trade     Effect   Tax (duty) evasion and loss of revenue for the Bengal Suba     Who curbed it later   Cornwallis 86-93 curbed private trade: an honest Governor General of that era   Teacher: On the Dastak slide (Lecture 13, slide 32) the teacher wrote: "therefore primary motive is not salary BUT PVT TRADE". Because private trade was worth 50 times the salary, an EIC officer came to India for the private trade, not for the salary. Beside the underlined Cornwallis 86-93 he wrote [increased salary]: that is how private trade was curbed. 3.2 Who was violating whose law?  Who was violating whose law? The Royal Charter: trade in the East Indies by any British entity other than the EIC broke the Royal Charter of the British Crown, British law. Interlopers: non-EIC British merchants who traded with India and so broke the Charter, which led to court cases back in Britain. Free merchants: non-EIC British merchants in India who agreed to sell Indian goods to the EIC inside India, making their trade artificially legal under British law. Dastak misuse (EIC officials): broke NOT British law but Indian law, customs-duty evasion under Bengal's framework. Teacher's ink: beside Interlopers "[BRITISHERS]", with "TRADERS" and "OTHER companies" under it; under Free merchants "ex-interloper"; on the right "gave monopoly over British TRADE with the East Indies to the EIC". It is worth understanding exactly what was illegal, and for whom. Trade in the East Indies by any British entity other than the EIC violated the Royal Charter issued by the British Crown: that was British law.   Category   Who they were   Whose law was broken    --- --- ---    Interlopers   Non-EIC British merchants who traded with India (the teacher: Britishers, either traders or other companies)   They violated the Royal Charter (British law), leading to court cases back in Britain     Free merchants   Non-EIC British merchants stationed in India who agreed to sell Indian goods to the EIC in India itself rather than exporting independently (the teacher: an "ex-interloper")   None: their trade became artificially legal in the eyes of British law     Dastak misuse by EIC officials   EIC officials passing private goods as Company goods   NOT British law but Indian law: specifically customs duty evasion (the slide adds: under Bengal's framework)    Teacher's board: interlopers against free merchants. Row 1 "Earlier": Ryots and Artisans sell to the Indian merchant, who sells to the EIC, which carries the goods across the line (out of India). Row 2: Ryots and Artisans sell to Indian merchants, who sell to interlopers, who carry the goods out of India themselves, "e.g. PROFIT = Rs 100"; on the right "EIC UNABLE TO STOP IT" and "LOSS = Rs 100 to EIC". Row 3 (below a line): Ryots and Artisans, Indian merchants, then the Free merchant, who sells to the EIC, which exports; the free merchant's own arrow across the India line is crossed out with x marks; under Free merchant and EIC a bracket "SHARE Rs 100". On the right: "therefore no CHARTER BROKEN"; "Benefits": EIC = earns some SHARE; No court case in Britain = GAIN for the free merchant. Earlier: ryots and artisans sell to the Indian merchant, who sells to the EIC, which exports (bad) Interloper: buys from Indian merchants and exports on his own; say his profit is Rs 100, which is a loss of Rs 100 to the EIC (warn) The EIC is unable to stop it: the Charter is broken, and there are court cases in Britain (good) Free merchant: the same man now sells to the EIC inside India and does not export himself; the Rs 100 is shared (good) No Charter is broken: the EIC earns some share, and the free merchant gains because there is no court case in Britain

items.t: 4 · Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 and the road to Plassey (1757)
items.x: Siraj-ud-daula and the road to Plassey (1757). Alivardi Khan 40-56 tolerated the EIC: from 1755 the EIC fortified Fort William, Calcutta without his permission (afraid of the French), but Alivardi 40-56 chose diplomacy, as EIC trade helped Bengal (and the Battle of Adyar 1746 proved the superiority of European infantry). Siraj 56-57: grandson of Alivardi 40-56 (through his daughter; no sons, only grandson); disliked at court, he disrespected senior Mansabdars and once jailed the banker Jagat Seth for extortion; young, impulsive, surrounded by enemies. Trigger: Siraj 56-57 stopped all Dastak misuse, hurting EIC officials' private fortunes; when the British sheltered the fugitive Krishna Ballabh (for money) and added new fortifications, Siraj 56-57 seized the EIC factory at Kasimbazar, then captured Calcutta and renamed it Alinagar. Teacher's ink: "1756 7 YEAR GLOBAL WAR, so an Anxious EIC" above the table; beside the Alivardi row a bracket to "CW 1746-63" and "BoADYAR 1746"; "60% of EIC TRADE = Bengal"; from "afraid of the French" a line to a partly unclear note about gains made in the Carnatic Wars after the first phase and to "we need to be ATMANIRBHAR because ADYAR 1746 tells us that the Nawab won't be able to help us"; top right "FORT = MILITARY STRUCTURE" and "Fortification: FORT build; FORT fill gaps in walls, increase HEIGHT, increase THICKNESS". 4.1 Why Alivardi Khan 40-56 tolerated the EIC's provocations Afraid of the French, the EIC began adding fortifications in Calcutta, that is strengthening Fort William (thickening walls, filling gaps, raising the height), from 1755, without the permission of Alivardi Khan 40-56. A fort is a military structure. Building or expanding one on another sovereign's territory without permission is a challenge to that sovereign's authority. However, Alivardi Khan 40-56 was pragmatic and followed the path of diplomacy rather than military confrontation, since the EIC's trade was economically beneficial to Bengal. He must also have noticed the Battle of Adyar 1746, which proved the military capabilities of European infantry. Teacher: Why the EIC was fortifying. 1756: the Seven Years' Global War made the EIC anxious. 60% of the EIC's trade was Bengal, so Bengal had to be protected. The EIC's reasoning, in the teacher's words: "We need to be ATMANIRBHAR (self-reliant), because Adyar 1746 tells us that the Nawab won't be able to help us" against the French. Fort = military structure. Fortification means either building a fort or strengthening one: filling gaps in the walls, increasing the height, increasing the thickness. The same Battle of Adyar 1746 (in the Carnatic Wars, which the teacher dates 1746-63) explains both sides: it made Alivardi Khan 40-56 cautious and it made the EIC rely on itself (Chapter 9). Unclear handwriting on slide 35. One line reads roughly "because of gains made in [unclear] CW after 1st phase" (the unclear word looks like "2nd"); it is attached to "afraid of the French". Check your notebook for the exact wording. 4.2 Why Siraj 56-57 did not tolerate them Siraj 56-57 was the precious grandson of Alivardi Khan 40-56 through his daughter, as Alivardi Khan 40-56 had no sons and Siraj 56-57 was the only grandson. Siraj 56-57 was disliked in the Bengal court. He had disrespected senior Mansabdars and had at one point imprisoned Jagat Seth, the powerful banker, for extortion. He was young, impulsive, surrounded by enemies. When he came to power he stopped all Dastak misuse, hurting the private trade fortunes of EIC officials. The British then gave asylum to Krishna Ballabh (for money), a fugitive from Siraj 56-57's court, charged with fraud, and added new fortifications to Calcutta. Siraj 56-57 first seized the EIC factory at Kasimbazar and then captured Calcutta. He renamed Calcutta Alinagar. 1717 Farman: duty-free trade; Dastaks misused for private trade; the Bengal Suba loses revenue From 1755: the EIC fortifies Fort William without permission; Alivardi Khan 40-56 chooses diplomacy (warn) Siraj 56-57 becomes Nawab: he stops all Dastak misuse; EIC officials' private fortunes are hurt (warn) The British shelter Krishna Ballabh (for money) and add new fortifications (bad) Siraj 56-57 seizes Kasimbazar and captures Calcutta (Alinagar): the Black Hole Tragedy Clive 57-67 arrives from Madras, recaptures Calcutta; Treaty of Alinagar; the French are neutralised (bad) Conspiracy with Mir Jafar 57-60: Plassey, 23 June 1757 4.3 The Black Hole Tragedy (1756): fact versus propaganda  Handout illustration of the Black Hole of Calcutta (the same picture is slide 37 of Lecture 13): a grey period drawing of a turbaned guard standing beside a heavy bolted door and looking at a small barred window, where a prisoner's hands grip the bars; more guards stand at the right edge. The slide's caption: a period illustration of the Black Hole, the incident colonial writers inflated into propaganda against Siraj 56-57. A second slide (38) shows a painting of crowded prisoners in a yellow-lit cell. There is no ink on these slides.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    What happened   During the capture of Calcutta, British prisoners were locked overnight in a small, airless guardroom in Fort William     The colonial account   Written by J.Z. Holwell, a survivor and briefly Governor of Bengal. It claimed that 146 were locked in and 123 died of suffocation     Modern historians   The actual number of dead was approximately 30 to 40     Why it mattered   It became a powerful propaganda tool to justify the EIC's military response against Siraj 56-57 and to demonise Indian rulers in the British public imagination     Year   What happened    --- ---    1760   Holwell built a monument in memory of the Black Hole Tragedy     1821   It had fallen into ruin and was demolished     1901   Viceroy Curzon 99-05 (1899-1905) built a marble replica at the same spot     1940   Netaji Bose led a big agitation to remove it, calling it colonial propaganda to tarnish Siraj 56-57's image, and used the campaign to build Hindu-Muslim unity     Result   The monument was not demolished but shifted from the public square to the graveyard of St. John's Church, Calcutta, where it stands today   The slide puts the 1940 result a little more sharply than the handout: Netaji Bose's agitation for demolition "forced the British to shift it" to the graveyard of St. John's Church. Both agree that it was shifted, not demolished.

items.t: 5 · Robert Clive 57-67, the conspiracy and the battle
items.x: Was the Battle of Plassey (23rd June 1757) really a battle? 5.1 Clive 57-67 recaptures Calcutta and neutralises the French  Robert Clive recaptures Calcutta; the French are neutralised. Clive arrives: Robert Clive 57-67 came from Madras with the Royal military and recaptured Calcutta. Treaty of Alinagar: restored all EIC privileges. French threat ended: Clive 57-67 destroyed the French-used Hugli port and beat the French at Chandarnagar (a French settlement since 1690); reason: the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63) was on. Teacher's ink: Hugli port and Chandarnagar underlined; on the right a sketch of Plassey: a curved hill with a row of stick figures labelled "Bengal Army" and a taller figure labelled SIRAJ, yellow dashed lines falling on them labelled "rain", and below the hill an arrow pointing up from "Clive + EIC ARMY + British ROYAL MILITARY". Robert Clive 57-67 arrived from Madras with Royal military forces and recaptured Calcutta. The Treaty of Alinagar (Alinagar was the name Siraj 56-57 had given to Calcutta) restored all EIC privileges. Clive 57-67 destroyed Hugli port, which was being used by the French, and defeated the French at Chandarnagar (the slide adds: a French settlement since 1690). The reason: the Anglo-French conflict was live as part of the Seven Years' Global War (1756-63). The French threat in Bengal was neutralised. Teacher: The teacher's sketch of the field: the Bengal Army with Siraj 56-57 standing on the higher ground, rain falling on it, and below it, advancing upward, Clive 57-67 + the EIC army + the British Royal military. Note the three separate forces on the British side: the Company's own army and the Royal (King's) military are different things (this matters again for the plunder figures in section 6). In his margin note (Lecture 14, slide 4) the teacher expands the code: Clive 57-67 was Governor of the Bengal Presidency of the EIC in two terms, 1757-60 and 1765-67. 5.2 Plassey, 23 June 1757: conspiracy, not a battle What happened next was not war: it was conspiracy. Mir Jafar 57-60 was the commander of Bengal's army. That is what the books say. Technically the Subahdar was the commander of the army. Mir Jafar 57-60 was the Bakshi (Bakhshi) at the province level, that is the war paymaster and head of military intelligence. Since Siraj 56-57 was young and inexperienced, in practice Mir Jafar 57-60 was the real commander. He approached Clive 57-67 and made a deal with the EIC to remove Siraj 56-57. At the Battle of Plassey (1757), Mir Jafar 57-60 ensured that the bulk of the Bengal army did not fight and turned back. Siraj 56-57 was easily defeated and fled. He was later captured and beheaded on the orders of Miran, Mir Jafar 57-60's son. Mir Jafar 57-60 became Subahdar (he was again Subahdar from 1763 to 1765). But he was now the EIC's puppet, as the EIC did not withdraw from the military domination established after the defeat of Siraj 56-57. The political supremacy of the EIC in India had begun. Takeaway: Plassey was no real battle. The EIC's victory in Bengal came from court conspiracy. The first real military victory for the EIC comes seven years later, at Buxar (1764). Teacher: On the Plassey slide (Lecture 13, slide 40) the teacher underlined five phrases, which are the exam points: "made a deal with EIC", "Bengal army did not fight", "Mir Jafar 57-60", "EIC's puppet", "EIC's political supremacy in India had begun". This is exactly statement 3 of Prelims 2004.  PYQ 1, Prelims 2004: Mir Jafar's conspiracy. Consider the following statements: 1. In the Third Battle of Panipat, Ahmed Shah Abdali defeated Ibrahim Lodi. 2. Tipu Sultan was killed in the Third Anglo-Mysore War. 3. Mir Jafar entered into conspiracy with the English for the defeat of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula in the Battle of Plassey. Which of the statement(s) given above is/are correct? (a) 1, 2 and 3 (b) Only 3 (c) 2 and 3 (d) None of these. Teacher's ink: beside statement 1 "[1st BoP 1526]" and a circled F; beside statement 2 "[4th 1799]" and a circled F; beside statement 3 a circled T; option (b) Only 3 is circled. Prelims 2004: answer (b) Only 3. The traps are the two battle mix-ups. Statement 1: Ibrahim Lodi belongs to the First Battle of Panipat (1526), which he lost to Babur 26-30; in the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) Abdali defeated the Marathas. Statement 2: Tipu 82-99 Sultan was killed in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1798-99) at Srirangapatna, not the Third (1789-92); the teacher wrote [4th 1799]. Statement 3 is correct: Mir Jafar 57-60, the Bakhshi and de facto commander since Siraj 56-57 was young, conspired with Clive 57-67 and ensured that the bulk of the Bengal army did not fight at Plassey (1757).

items.t: 6 · The Plassey Plunder (1757-65)
items.x: What did the EIC extract from Bengal after Plassey? Remember that companies are organisations with a profit motive, and the EIC was a company even if it had started behaving as a State. The immediate financial settlement after Plassey was staggering. 6.1 The cash   To whom   Amount   When    --- --- ---    The Royal British military   2,75,000 pounds, for distribution to soldiers (not the EIC army, which was different)   Immediately after the Battle of Plassey 1757     Clive 57-67 personally   2,34,000 pounds, plus a personal jagir of 35,000 pounds per annum   Immediately after the Battle of Plassey 1757     The EIC   Rs 2.25 crore   Immediately after the Battle of Plassey 1757     The EIC, as "political gifts" from Bengal   A further 2.5 million pounds   Between 1757 and 1765   Teacher: On the slide (Lecture 13, slide 43) the teacher bracketed the first three rows as "immediately after BoPlassey 1757" and the last row as "1757-65". He underlined "personal jagir" and "2.5 million pounds extracted as political gifts". To understand the scale of 2.5 million pounds (the handout's note): multiply by 250 for inflation alone, as per the Retail Price Index. Alternatively: in 1760 the GDP of Britain was 70 million pounds, so 2.5 million pounds is 3.5% of GDP. In 2026 the UK GDP is 2.27 trillion pounds; 3.5% of that equals 80 billion pounds, or 108.5 billion USD. The multiplier is approximately x32,000. 6.2 Beyond the cash: Bengal's economy and polity, the EIC's trade structure and the EIC army  Teacher's board, in two halves. Left: "PVT DOMESTIC TRADE of EIC officers": Ryots and Artisans used to sell to the Indian merchant (now crossed out), who sold to EIC officers or the EIC; two curved arrows now go round the merchant, both labelled "via GOMASTAS [Indian Agents of EIC]". Right: "EIC TOOK money from the Bengal TREASURY", which branches into BOUGHT Indian GOODS (then Exported), BOUGHT Chinese GOODS (then SOLD in Europe), TOOK GOLD to Britain, and a yellow arrow to BUILT Large ARMY. Bottom: "Earlier: GOLD inflow TO India. Now: GOLD OUTFLOW from India = DRAIN" (DRAIN in a box). 1. Private trade, international and now domestic too After Plassey there was rampant misuse of Dastaks. EIC officials made large fortunes not just from private international trade but also from private domestic trade. This domestic trade was conducted through Indian agents called Gomastas, who procured goods directly from peasants and artisans, cutting out Indian merchants and traders. They also did not pay domestic taxes on this trade, which hurt further the Indian merchants competing against them. Teacher: The board: ryots and artisans used to sell to the Indian merchant, who sold to the EIC. Now the Indian merchant is crossed out, and the goods go "via Gomastas [Indian agents of the EIC]" straight to the EIC's officers. The teacher ticked "Private trade" and "Domestic trade" on the slide (Lecture 13, slide 44) and underlined "paid no domestic tax". 2. The structure of the EIC's international trade changed: the Drain of Wealth begins Before Plassey, gold had to be shipped from Britain to buy Indian goods. After Plassey, Bengal's own Diwani revenues funded the purchase of not just Indian but also Chinese goods: tea, silk, porcelain. Further, gold from the Bengal treasury was also shipped to Britain. Thus, from gold inflow before 1757, there was now gold outflow from India. Hence began the Drain of Wealth. Teacher: "The EIC took money from the Bengal treasury" and did four things with it: bought Indian goods and exported them; bought Chinese goods and sold them in Europe; took gold to Britain; and built a large army. Earlier: gold INFLOW to India. Now: gold OUTFLOW from India = DRAIN (the teacher put DRAIN in a box). A wording point. The handout and slide 44 say that after Plassey "Bengal's own Diwani revenues" funded the purchases, but the Diwani was legally received only in 1765 (section 8.2). The teacher's board uses the safer phrase "money from the Bengal treasury", and his slide 28 note calls the 1757-65 extraction illegal plunder that was legalised in 1765. In an answer, write "Bengal's revenues" or "the Bengal treasury" for 1757-65 and "Diwani revenues" from 1765. 3. A large standing army The EIC also used the Plassey Plunder to build its own large standing army. For a trading company, maintaining a large army made no economic sense (it hurt dividends to shareholders). But now it could be funded from Bengal's extracted wealth rather than from company profits. Thus Robert Clive 57-67 laid the foundation of the real military strength of the EIC and of Empire Building by the EIC. 4. A change of puppet When Mir Jafar 57-60 could no longer meet the EIC's growing financial demands, the EIC replaced him with his son-in-law, Mir Qasim 60-63, an efficient administrator (the slide says "a brilliant administrator"). Hence the EIC was the real political power in Bengal after 1757. Before 1757: gold is shipped from Britain to buy Indian goods: gold inflow to India Plassey 1757: military domination; a puppet Subahdar (warn) Bengal's own revenue now pays for Indian goods (exported) and Chinese goods (tea, silk, porcelain, sold in Europe) (warn) Gold from the Bengal treasury is shipped to Britain, and the plunder pays for a large standing army (bad) After 1757: gold outflow from India = the Drain of Wealth 6.3 The Nawabs of Bengal: the succession  Handout flow chart of the Nawabs of Bengal: Murshid Quli Khan 17-27 (1717-27), accepted the 1717 Farman, resisted Dastak abuse; then Shuja-ud-din (1727-39), continuity Nawab, low-drama interim; then Alivardi Khan 40-56 (1740-56), pragmatic tolerance of the EIC, warned Siraj on his deathbed; then a box on Siraj: precious grandson of Alivardi via his daughter, disliked in court, Jagat Seth, Mansabdars and the EIC all antagonised; then Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57 (1756-57), stopped Dastak abuse, Black Hole, Plassey 23 Jun 1757, defeated and beheaded; then Mir Jafar 57-65 (1757-60, restored 1763-65), EIC puppet after Plassey, conspired with Clive against Siraj; then Mir Qasim 60-63 (1760-63), son-in-law of Jafar, shifted capital to Patna, militarised, ended Dastak abuse; then Najm-ud-Daula (1765 onwards), Nizamat reduced to a puppet role under the Dual Government (1765-72).   Nawab   What to remember    --- ---    Murshid Quli Khan (MQK 17-27)   The Nawab of the 1717 Farman: accepted it in part, resisted Dastak abuse and the Royal Mint     Shuja-ud-din 27-39   Continuity Nawab: a low-drama interim     Sarfaraz Khan (1739-40)   Added by the teacher in ink beside Shuja-ud-din 27-39 (the gap between 1739 and 1740)     Alivardi Khan 40-56   Pragmatic; tolerated the EIC's provocations and warned Siraj 56-57 on his deathbed     Siraj-ud-Daula 56-57   Precious grandson; stopped Dastak abuse; Black Hole; defeated at Plassey on 23 June 1757, then beheaded     Mir Jafar 57-60   The EIC's puppet after Plassey (ruled 1757-60, then 1763-65)     Mir Qasim 60-63   Son-in-law of Mir Jafar 57-60; shifted the capital to Patna (Bihar); militarised; ended Dastak abuse; then rebelled     Najm-ud-Daula (1765)   The Nizamat reduced to a puppet role: the Dual Government (1765-72) begins   Reign-year code for Mir Jafar. The handout text writes Mir Jafar 57-60 and adds "again Subahdar from 1763-65"; the slide table (Lecture 13, slide 42) and the handout's own flow chart write Mir Jafar 57-65; the teacher's board (Lecture 14, slide 2) writes "Jafar 57-60, 63-65". All mean the same two terms: 1757-60 and 1763-65, with Mir Qasim 60-63 in between. This notebook keeps the handout's 57-60.

items.t: 7 · Battle of Buxar (1764): the EIC gets the right to rule
items.x: 7.1 Why did Mir Qasim 60-63 rebel?  Battle of Buxar (1764): why Mir Qasim rebelled. Qasim 60-63: did not want to be a puppet, so he shifted his HQ from Murshidabad to Bihar to gather resources and build an army quietly; punished zamindars who underreported revenue and, to get the support of Indian merchants, abolished all internal duties on domestic trade (think 0 GST), giving Indian merchants a level field against EIC officials' untaxed domestic trade via Gomastas. Qasim 60-63 builds a coalition: the streak of independence was intolerable to the EIC; Qasim 60-63 was defeated in Bihar; he escaped to Awadh with money and allied with Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 of Awadh and Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06; Shuja 54-75 joined on a promise of 3 crore rupees plus Bihar and its treasury after victory; the EIC brought Mir Jafar 57-60 back as puppet Nawab (1763-65). Teacher's ink: beside the first row a curved arrow from MURSHIDABAD to BIHAR; on the right a vertical line with AWADH on its left and "Bi Be" (Bihar, Bengal) on its right, and an arrow crossing the line westward into Awadh; several phrases underlined. Mir Qasim 60-63 was an able man and had no intention of remaining a puppet. To escape the EIC's constant supervision, he shifted his base from the capital Murshidabad to Bihar, where he could gather resources and build an army quietly. (The slide table and the handout's flow chart say he shifted the capital to Patna, which is in Bihar.) To gather money for the army he punished zamindars who underreported their land revenue. For the support of Indian merchants he abolished all internal duties on domestic trade (like GST today; the slide says "think 0 GST"). This brought a level playing field between Indian merchants and the EIC officials who had been doing untaxed domestic trade via their Gomastas since 1757. This autonomous behaviour was intolerable to the EIC. A battle was fought in Bihar; Mir Qasim 60-63 was defeated, and the EIC brought back Mir Jafar 57-60 as puppet Nawab of Bengal (1763-65). Mir Qasim 60-63 escaped westward to Awadh (the slide: with money) and forged an alliance with Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 of Awadh and Emperor Shah Alam II 60-06. Shuja 54-75 agreed on the promise of 3 crore rupees, the territory of Bihar and its treasury, after victory. Teacher: Two small sketches. Murshidabad to Bihar (a curved arrow): Mir Qasim 60-63 moves west, away from the EIC's eyes. Awadh, then a line, then "Bi Be" (Bihar and Bengal), with an arrow pointing west across the line: after his defeat Mir Qasim 60-63 crosses out of the Bengal Suba into Awadh. The teacher underlined "Punished zamindars", "support of Indian merchants", "Shah Alam II 60-06", "Shuja 54-75 joined", "3 crore rupees + Bihar and its treasury", and the whole line "EIC brought Mir Jafar 57-60 back as puppet Nawab (1763-65)". 7.2 Why Shah Alam II 60-06 was in Awadh   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    Danger at Delhi   Shah Alam II 60-06 had left Delhi, frustrated with court factionalism and fearing for his life after the murders and brutalities inflicted on his predecessors by Wazir Imad-ul-Mulk (also known as Gaddar-ul-Mulk)     Two Emperors destroyed by their own Wazir   Imad-ul-Mulk blinded Emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur 48-54 in 1754 and murdered Emperor Alamgir II 54-59 in 1759     His own kingdom   So Shah Alam II 60-06 left Delhi to establish his own kingdom in Bengal, which had stopped paying tribute since 1751     1761   He attacked Bengal in 1761 but was defeated by the EIC. The EIC still respected him, since he was Emperor of Hindustan     In Awadh   Since then he was in Awadh and had chosen Shuja 54-75 as his Wazir   7.3 The battle and after  Teacher's board: "Bo BUXAR 1764". On the Indian side (the word Indian is circled): AWADH in a yellow box, and under it "Mughal emperor [practically as individual]" and "Mir Qasim 60-63 [as individual]". Then a circled "vs". On the other side, in a yellow box: EIC + Bengal, with the bracket "[Jafar 57-60, 63-65]". Bottom: "very closely fought battle, therefore we can judge that in 1764 (circled), AT BEST, EIC military power = one of the multiple Indian kingdoms / states". The Battle of Buxar (1764) was fought in Bihar. All preparations had been made for a defensive strategy: laying siege to the fort where the EIC army was stationed. But Shuja 54-75 lost patience. Against the explicit advice of Mir Qasim 60-63, he switched to an offensive strategy and ordered a direct attack on the fort, handing the advantage to the EIC. The battle was closely fought, and at one point the Indian side appeared to be winning. Then the EIC commander Hector Munroe launched a final charge and turned the tables. Clive 57-67 was in London at the time.   Person   What happened after Buxar    --- ---    Mir Qasim 60-63   Escaped and died somewhere later     Shuja 54-75   Was surprised to find himself not beheaded     Shah Alam II 60-06   Was treated with respect, as in him resided the symbolic sovereignty of the Mughal State. With him as an ally, the foreigner EIC's legal right as a political power in India would be stronger   Teacher: Who really fought at Buxar. On the Indian side the only State was Awadh. The Mughal Emperor was there "practically as an individual", and Mir Qasim 60-63 "as an individual" (neither had a State behind him any more). On the other side was the EIC + Bengal (Bengal under the puppet Mir Jafar 57-60, in his 1763-65 term). And it was a very closely fought battle. So the teacher's judgement: in 1764, AT BEST, the EIC's military power was equal to that of one of the multiple Indian kingdoms. It was not yet a superpower. 7.4 The teacher's question: why was the EIC able to build an empire?  Teacher's board: "WHY EIC able to build empire?" "imp Reason (underlined): Indian territory had multiple States and not one State ruling the whole of India." In a bracket: "These multiple States were NOT united; each State had a territory motive; each Kingdom wanted to be an empire", which is "very natural" [Rivalry], "and please DON'T use it to BASH India, bash Indians and lament Indian unity". To the left: "therefore Resources are not united: economic, military". In yellow at the bottom: "[Indian kings, not Indians, were not united]". Top right in yellow, with an asterisk: "WHY CHINA not politically conquered? weak but one State; Manchu dynasty till 1911". Teacher: Why was the EIC able to build an empire? imp Reason: the Indian territory had multiple States and not one State ruling the whole of India. These multiple States were not united: each State had a territory motive; each kingdom wanted to be an empire. That is rivalry, and it "is very natural". Therefore resources were not united: neither the economic nor the military resources. So a power that was "at best one of the multiple Indian kingdoms" in 1764 could defeat or ally with them one at a time. Teacher: A warning from the teacher, in his own words: "Please don't use it to bash India, bash Indians and lament Indian unity." The correct statement is: Indian KINGS were not united, not "Indians were not united". And the comparison he starred: Why was China not politically conquered? It was weak, but it was ONE State: the Manchu dynasty, till 1911.

items.t: 8 · Treaty of Allahabad 1765 (ToA 1765)
items.x: Why is the Treaty of Allahabad of 1765 so important, and what exactly did it decide?  Handout diagram: Treaty of Allahabad 1765, "The Architecture of Empire: three signatories, three sets of clauses". Signatories across the top: Robert Clive 57-67 (for the EIC), Shah Alam II 60-06 (Mughal Emperor), Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 (Nawab of Awadh). Column 1, @ THE EMPEROR: annual tribute Rs 26 lakh (paper only, never paid); EIC to militarily recapture Delhi from the Rohillas (held since 1761), never delivered; Allahabad + Kora granted as seat (taken from Awadh); so EIC = MANSABDAR of the Mughal State and Bengal becomes the EIC's Jagir; why pay tribute to a defeated Emperor? to absorb itself into the existing Mughal legal-political structure (technically Mughal till 1858). Column 2, @ BENGAL (the Diwani): Diwani granted to the EIC over Bengal Suba = Bengal + Bihar + Orissa; Diwani = revenue admin + treasury + Civil Courts (NOT health or education); the Nawab keeps the NIZAMAT (law and order + domestic governance); so DUAL GOVERNMENT (1765-72), Md Reza Khan = Naib Nazim; 1770 Great Bengal Famine, 1 crore dead; 1772 Dual Government ENDS, Direct Rule installed (W. Hastings 73-85). Column 3, @ AWADH (mini Subsidiary Alliance): compensation Rs 50 lakh paid by Shuja 54-75 to the EIC; Benaras separated from Awadh (formally annexed by the EIC in 1775); duty-free trade for the EIC in Awadh (Dastak misuse spreads to Awadh); so RING FENCE + MINI SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE, EIC army stationed, Awadh pays subsidy; architecture drawn here in 1765, formal Subsidiary Alliance signed with Awadh in 1801 by Wellesley 98-05. Bottom bar: three policies installed in ONE treaty: INDIRECT RULE + RING FENCE + mini SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE; Clive 57-67 wrote the empire-builder's playbook, Wellesley 98-05 only refined it. Clive 57-67 was sent back to India from London after the Buxar victory to negotiate the settlement. The Treaty of Allahabad (ToA 1765) was signed by Clive 57-67 on behalf of the EIC, and by Shah Alam II 60-06 and Shuja 54-75 on the Indian side. It is one of the most consequential treaties in Indian history, because it laid the legal and structural foundation of the British Empire (the Company State) in India. Clive 57-67 did insider trading on EIC shares. He asked his broker in London to buy EIC shares before the terms of ToA 1765 became public. This made Clive 57-67 one of the wealthiest men in Europe. ToA 1765 can be understood by breaking it into three components: @ Emperor, @ Bengal, @ Awadh.   Signatory   Side    --- ---    Robert Clive 57-67   Signed for the EIC     Shah Alam II 60-06   Mughal Emperor: the Indian side     Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75   Nawab of Awadh: the Indian side   Teacher: On the signatories slide (Lecture 14, slide 4) the teacher underlined "after Buxar" and wrote in the margin: Clive 57-67 = Governor of the Bengal Presidency of the EIC, 1757-60 and 1765-67. So the treaty belongs to his second term. On slide 8 he repeats the insider-trading story: Clive 57-67 bought shares of the EIC before ToA 1765 became public, and became the "richest man of Europe". 8.1 @ The Emperor  Treaty of Allahabad: @ The Emperor (the teacher boxed "@ The Emperor" in yellow). Annual tribute: the EIC promised Shah Alam II 60-06 an annual tribute of Rs 26 lakh (paper only, never paid in practice). Recapture Delhi: the EIC promised to militarily help him recapture Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans (who had held it since 1761), never delivered. Allahabad and Kora: given to him (taken from Awadh) as his seat, so the Emperor keeps his status. Design: the EIC absorbed itself into the Mughal legal-political structure, posing as a Mansabdar (who keeps an army for the Emperor and pays tribute); Bengal became, in law, the EIC's Watan Jagir; in practice it was all legal formality. Teacher's ink: a yellow box round "annual tribute of Rs 26 lakh"; on the right "EIC TRYING TO BECOME PART OF the Indian POLITICAL LEGAL STRUCTURE i.e. a MANSABDAR", then four points: mansab = post = Finance ministership [Diwani] of Bengal; maintain army for the king = helping the king militarily; Promise of help; Vatan Jagir, so tribute to the emperor; bottom: "Bengal is LIKE (circled) a Vatan Jagir of the EIC = FM".   Clause   Terms   In practice    --- --- ---    Annual tribute   The EIC promised to pay Shah Alam II 60-06 an annual tribute of 26 lakh rupees   Not paid     Recapture Delhi   The EIC promised to militarily help him recapture Delhi from the Rohilla Afghans (who had held it since 1761)   No army was supplied     Allahabad and Kora   Given to him (taken from Awadh) so that the Emperor maintains his status   His seat   This was deliberate and clever. The EIC was absorbing itself into the existing legal-political structure of the Mughal State, positioning itself as a Mansabdar (who maintains an army for the Emperor and pays tribute), and Bengal became, in legal terms, the EIC's Watan Jagir. Recall: this is exactly how Rebel States got absorbed into the Mughal Empire instead of declaring independence (Chapter 3). In practice the EIC paid neither the Rs 26 lakh nor did it supply an army to recapture Delhi. It was all legal formality. Teacher: The EIC is trying to become part of the Indian political-legal structure, that is, a Mansabdar. The teacher matches each clause to a Mansabdar's features: (1) mansab = a post: here the finance ministership [Diwani] of Bengal; (2) a Mansabdar maintains an army for the king = helping the king militarily: here the promise of help to recapture Delhi; (3) a Vatan Jagir holder pays tribute to the Emperor: here the Rs 26 lakh (which he boxed). So "Bengal is LIKE a Vatan Jagir of the EIC", and the EIC is the FM (finance minister) of Bengal. The word LIKE is circled: it is a legal dress, not a real one. The handout spells it Watan Jagir; the teacher's board (and Chapter 7) writes Vatan Jagir. Same term. The handout's diagram adds one more line: the country stayed "technically Mughal till 1858". 8.2 @ Bengal 8.2.1 Dual Government (1765-72) First, the background the teacher drew: who did what in a Mughal Suba.  Teacher's board: the Suba system of Akbar 56-05 (name boxed). At the top: King, with the Wazir and the Mir Bakshi (and one more line) reporting up to him. "@ SUBA": three columns. Nazim / Subadar = Military commander + Law and Order. Diwan = CM + FM, that is Civil Admin and Finance of the Suba. Bakshi = Military intelligence + War paymaster. Curved arrows labelled REPORTING run from the Diwan and from the Bakshi towards the Nazim and are marked with x marks (they did not report to him); each line instead goes up to the centre. Below: Naib Nazims, Naib Diwans, Naib Bakshis. Under a horizontal line, an arrow down to "1717 Bengal": "Above system DILUTED, Checks and Balances ended, so Subadar / Nawab = like a King, and all report to him at the Suba level".   Officer in the Suba   Functions   Reported to    --- --- ---    Nazim / Subadar   Military commander + law and order   The centre (the King)     Diwan   "CM + FM": civil administration and the finance of the Suba   The centre (the Wazir's line), not the Nazim     Bakshi   Military intelligence + war paymaster   The centre (the Mir Bakshi's line), not the Nazim     Deputies   Naib Nazims, Naib Diwans, Naib Bakshis   Their own heads   Teacher: Under Akbar 56-05 the three provincial officers did not report to each other (the crossed "reporting" arrows): that was the system of checks and balances. By 1717 in Bengal this system was diluted and the checks and balances ended: the Subadar / Nawab became "like a King", and all reported to him at the Suba level. This is also why Mir Jafar 57-60, the Bakshi (war paymaster and head of military intelligence), was the man who mattered at Plassey.  Teacher's board: the chain of reporting in 1717 and in 1765. Left, "1717" (circled): Delhi at the top with two X marks on the line down to the Subadar (the link with Delhi is cut); arrows pointing up to the Subadar from Bakshi, Diwan and Other mansabdars. Right, "1765" (circled): Delhi at the top; lower left "Subadar [Nizamat] minus military", lower right "Diwan [EIC] [Diwani]"; an arrow from each up to Delhi, one with a + mark beside it and one with an X beside it; and an arrow from the Diwan to the Subadar marked with an X. Teacher: 1717: the line between Delhi and the Subadar is crossed out, and the Bakshi, the Diwan and the other Mansabdars all report to the Subadar. 1765: there are again two separate heads under Delhi: the Subadar, holding the Nizamat "minus military", and the Diwan, who is now the EIC, holding the Diwani. The arrow from the Diwan to the Subadar is crossed: the EIC as Diwan does not report to the Nawab. Unclear marks on slide 7. In the 1765 sketch the two arrows going up to Delhi carry a "+" mark (beside the Subadar's arrow) and an "X" (beside the Diwan's arrow). What exactly the + and the X stand for is not written. Check your notebook for the teacher's explanation; the safe reading from the handout is that both links to the Emperor were legal formality.  Dual Government (1765-72): the structure. Top box: sovereign functions of Bengal split into 2, run by 1 Indian bureaucracy. Left box: DIWANI to the EIC: revenue admin + treasury + civil justice (Civil Courts) over Bengal + Bihar + Orissa. Right box: NIZAMAT to the Nawab: law and order + police + criminal justice (military in practice with the EIC). Bottom box: Md Reza Khan = Naib Nazim (Deputy Nawab) and ALSO the EIC's Diwan; Indian civil servants run it on the ground, reporting Diwani to the EIC and Nizamat to the Nawab. Teacher's ink: "2 TOP AUTHORITIES" under the title; "Two Bosses BUT" above the top box; "STAYED WITH" above "NIZAMAT to Nawab"; "military in practice with EIC" underlined with "since 1757" written below; "Admin" written under the word "it" in the bottom box.  Handout diagram: DUAL GOVERNMENT (1765-72): sovereign functions of Bengal Suba split into TWO, administered by ONE Indian bureaucracy. Left box: EIC controls DIWANI = Revenue Administration + Treasury + Civil Justice over Bengal + Bihar + Orissa. Right box: NAWAB controls NIZAMAT = Law and Order + Police + Criminal Justice. Both arrows meet at: Md Reza Khan (Naib Nazim = Deputy Nawab), ALSO appointed as the EIC's Diwan. Below: Indian Civil Servants run the administration on the ground; they report DIWANI matters to the EIC and NIZAMAT matters to the Nawab. Diwani meant revenue administration, control of the revenue (treasury), civil administration and civil justice. The EIC received the Diwani of Bengal Suba, that is Bengal, Orissa and Bihar. This was the first time the EIC formally received a sovereign function, for example the power to tax. Before Buxar the EIC had only trade income (since 31st December 1600). From 1765 it had two incomes: trade income and tax revenue from the richest province of India. The Nizamat remained with the Nawab legally: law and order and criminal justice. The military, in practice, was with the EIC. This arrangement was the Dual Government (1765-72).   Function   Legally with   What it covered    --- --- ---    Diwani   The EIC   Revenue administration, the treasury, civil administration and civil justice (Civil Courts) over Bengal, Bihar and Orissa     Nizamat   The Nawab   Law and order, police, criminal justice (the military was in practice with the EIC, the teacher adds "since 1757")   In practice the EIC appointed a Deputy Nawab (Naib Nazim), Md Reza Khan, as its Diwan. Indian civil servants continued to run the administration, reporting to the EIC on Diwani matters and to the Nawab on Nizamat matters. The Dual Government meant, in effect, that sovereign functions had been split into two and two separate top authorities installed over each. Teacher: Dual Government = "2 TOP AUTHORITIES": two bosses, BUT one administration. The Nizamat "stayed with" the Nawab, except the military, which had been with the EIC since 1757. On the next board (Lecture 14, slide 10) he draws it as a Y: the Nawab [Nizamat] and the EIC [Diwani] at the top, both lines meeting at the Deputy Nawab (Naib Nazim), and below him one long line of officials: "Admin = Indians". So the men on the ground were the same Indian officials; only the top was split. Teacher: Notes on the Diwani slide (Lecture 14, slide 8): under the first row, "PLUNDER (1757-65) now LEGAL"; under "Two incomes now", "OLD = TRADE, NEW = revenue of Bengal". Small differences in how the functions are listed. The handout text defines the Diwani as revenue administration, treasury, civil administration and civil justice; the handout's Treaty diagram adds "(NOT health/education)" and describes the Nizamat as "law and order + domestic governance"; the slide lists the Nizamat as law and order + police + criminal justice. For the exam: Diwani = revenue + civil justice; Nizamat = law and order (police) + criminal justice. Why did the EIC not annex Bengal outright?  Treaty of Allahabad: @ Bengal: what the Diwani meant. 1st sovereign function: the EIC received the Diwani of Bengal Suba (Bengal, Orissa and Bihar), the first time it formally held a sovereign function, e.g. the power to tax. Two incomes now: before Buxar the EIC had only trade income (since 31 Dec 1600); from 1765 it had two, trade income and tax revenue from the richest province of India. Why not annex Bengal: a company works for profit, not to rule; outright annexation would bring administrative cost and responsibility; after Plassey it was safe militarily; after Buxar it held the legal right over Bengal's finances, so draining Bengal's wealth was now a legal right, not illegal plunder. Teacher's ink: "PLUNDER (1757-65) Now LEGAL"; "OLD = TRADE, New = Rev of Bengal"; beside the third row "RULING is a Tension OR Responsibility" and "Lack of experience of Ruling"; on the right "Clive DID insider trading: bought shares of EIC before ToA 1765 became public, so Richest man of Europe". The EIC was a company, and companies work for profit, not for ruling. When the opportunity existed to annex Bengal outright, it chose not to, because annexation would bring administrative costs and responsibilities. Military domination after Plassey 1757 meant the company was not threatened militarily. After Buxar 1764 it secured only the legal right over the finances of Bengal. So now the drain of Bengal's wealth was not illegal plunder but a legal right of the EIC. Teacher: Two more reasons in ink: "RULING is a tension OR a responsibility", and the EIC had a "lack of experience of ruling". So it took the money (Diwani) and left the headache (Nizamat) with the Nawab. 8.2.2 Policy of Indirect Rule, the 1770 famine and Direct Rule  Teacher's board: "PoIR concept" (Policy of Indirect Rule). "3 step PROCESS" (PROCESS circled, with the note "can take years"): (a) Nawab = puppet; (b) British Resident stationed in court [to play the Nawab as a puppet]; and a curved arrow from (b) back to (a) labelled "(c) controls". The Policy of Indirect Rule was now formally installed in Bengal's Nizamat. The three elements of Indirect Rule are: 1. The King or Nawab is a puppet. 2. A British Resident is stationed in court. 3. The Resident controls the puppet and thus governs indirectly. All three were now in place. The EIC also obtained the legal right to appoint the Deputy Nawab. This meant that if the Deputy Subahdar refused to follow informal EIC instructions in Nizamat matters, he could be removed by the EIC. By 1772 the British Resident had established complete indirect control over the Nizamat. Teacher: PoIR is a "3 step PROCESS", and a process "can take years". (a) The Nawab is a puppet; (b) a British Resident is stationed in the court, "to play the Nawab as a puppet"; (c) the Resident controls him. On the slide (Lecture 14, slide 15) he writes "Policy implementation takes time" and, under the row label, "Began in Bengal, ToA 1765". That is why the handout says it was "installed" in 1765 but "complete" only by 1772. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (GBF 1770) and the end of the Dual Government  Indirect Rule, the 1770 Famine and Direct Rule (the teacher wrote "ToA 1765: @ Bengal" above the title). Policy of Indirect Rule: now formally installed in Bengal's Nizamat, 3 elements: (a) the Nawab is a puppet, (b) a British Resident sits in court, (c) the Resident controls the puppet and so governs indirectly; the EIC also won the legal right to appoint (and remove) the Deputy Nawab. Great Bengal Famine 1770: killed about 1 crore, about one-third of Bengal's population; high revenue demand and harsh collection continued as crops failed; hoarding went unchecked as neither the EIC nor the Nawab took charge of relief. Dual Government ends 1772: by 1772 the Resident had complete indirect control; the famine collapsed revenue and order, forcing the EIC to take the Nizamat legally and replace Indian officers with its own: Direct Rule under W. Hastings 73-85; the Company State was now properly established (the Nawab now as powerless as the Maratha Chhatrapati after the 1750 Treaty of Sangola). Teacher's ink: "Policy implementation takes time"; "Began in Bengal ToA 1765"; "efforts" added after relief; "Law and" added above "order"; on the left "GBF 1770, then L and O sad face (Nizamat), then LR sad face (Diwani)"; on the right a circled "PYQ (M)": "WHY THERE WERE Recurrent famines in British RULED India: one para from this topic". In 1772 the Dual Government was formally ended. The Nizamat was taken over legally from the Nawab, and the EIC replaced Indian administrators with its own officers, establishing Direct Rule. Thus the Company State was properly established in Bengal. The reason was the Great Bengal Famine of 1770 (GBF 1770). The famine killed one crore people, an estimated one-third of Bengal's population. High land revenue demand and harsh tax collection methods continued even as crops failed and people starved. Grain hoarding by speculators went unchecked, because neither the EIC nor the Nawab took responsibility for famine relief. The EIC claimed that famine relief was the Nawab's domain, and the Nawab lacked the resources for it. Due to the famine, land revenue collection and law and order collapsed, forcing the EIC to establish its own Direct Rule. From 1772 the Nawab of Bengal became as powerless a figurehead as the Chhatrapati of the Marathas had become after the Treaty of Sangola 1750 (Chapter 4). Teacher: The teacher's chain beside the slide: GBF 1770 led to the collapse of L and O (law and order), which is the Nizamat side, and of LR (land revenue), which is the Diwani side. Both halves of the Dual Government failed together. The slide names who brought Direct Rule: W. Hastings 73-85. And the exam mark: PYQ (Mains): "Why were there recurrent famines in British-ruled India?" One paragraph of that answer comes from this topic.  Teacher's board: "Concept of Famine". "Famine = fn [Nature factor AND Human factor]" (the word AND is written large). Under Nature factor: Drought, Floods, which lead to Supply of Food falling (three down arrows), which leads to Prices of Food rising (three up arrows, circled). Under Human factor: "if people are PROSPEROUS and have good savings, then (smiley) imports"; "a Caring / Welfare State: maintains a Buffer, and imports". Teacher: Concept of famine: Famine = a function of [a NATURE factor AND a HUMAN factor]. Nature factor: drought or floods reduce the supply of food, so the price of food shoots up. That alone is not yet a famine. Human factor: if the people are prosperous and have good savings, they can still buy (food can be imported); and a caring, welfare State maintains a buffer stock and imports food. A famine happens when nature fails and the human side fails too. In Bengal in 1770 the human side failed completely: revenue demand stayed high, hoarding went unchecked, and neither authority took charge of relief. This is the paragraph for the Mains question.  Teacher's board: "Concept of Bankrupt": one is unable to meet liabilities, that is loan repayment, employees' salary, and the price of purchased G and S (goods, services). "In Capitalism": a table: a 1 crore company will take a 0.4 crore loan; a 10 crore company a 4 crore loan; 100, 40; 1000, 400; 10000, and a last figure written unclearly; the word LEVERAGE is written down the side. On the right: "Bank gives a loan when it has confidence of you paying the EMI, BUT income SHOCK, then EMI (crossed out), then Bank-RUPT".  Teacher's board: "EIC went BANKRUPT (1772)". "2 incomes: TRADE and LR." "Since 1757, EIC not BRINGING GOLD FROM Britain TO BUY GOODS"; instead it "used Indian (Bengal) money" (boxed) to buy goods, which is "money in the Bengal TREASURY", which comes from "LR PAID BY the PEOPLE" (LR circled). Left: "LR income (two sad faces) because of GBF 1770", with an arrow down to "TRADE income (two sad faces)". Teacher: Concept of bankruptcy: one is unable to meet one's liabilities (loan repayment, employees' salaries, the price of goods and services purchased). In capitalism companies run on LEVERAGE: the teacher's table shows a company of 1 crore taking a loan of 0.4 crore, a company of 10 crore taking 4 crore, 100 crore taking 40, 1,000 crore taking 400, and so on. A bank gives a loan when it is confident that you will pay the EMI. BUT an income shock means the EMI cannot be paid, and the company goes bankrupt. Teacher: "The EIC went BANKRUPT (1772)." The reasoning: the EIC had two incomes: trade and LR (land revenue). Since 1757 it was not bringing gold from Britain to buy goods; it used Indian (Bengal) money, that is the money in the Bengal treasury, which was the LR paid by the people. So when GBF 1770 hit the LR income, the trade income fell with it (no revenue, no purchases). Both incomes collapsed together: that is the income shock. This is the money side of why the Dual Government had to end in 1772. Unclear figure on slide 13. The last row of the loan table (the 10,000 crore company) is written unclearly; by the pattern it should be 4,000. Check your notebook. 1765: Diwani to the EIC, Nizamat with the Nawab: power without responsibility at the top, one Indian bureaucracy below High revenue demand and harsh collection continue (bad) 1770 Great Bengal Famine: about 1 crore dead (one-third of Bengal); hoarding unchecked; neither the EIC nor the Nawab takes charge of relief (bad) Land revenue (Diwani side) and law and order (Nizamat side) collapse; the EIC's two incomes fall; the teacher: the EIC went bankrupt (1772) (warn) 1772: the EIC takes the Nizamat legally, replaces Indian administrators with its own officers Direct Rule (W. Hastings 73-85): the Company State is properly established in Bengal 8.3 @ Awadh  Treaty of Allahabad: @ Awadh. Compensation and Benaras: Shuja-ud-Daula 54-75 was made to pay Rs 50 lakh compensation to the EIC; Benaras was separated from Awadh (the EIC formally annexed it in 1775); Kora and Allahabad went to the Emperor. Duty-free trade: the EIC was granted duty-free trade in Awadh, and Dastak misuse began there too. Policy of Ring Fence: initiated with Awadh, a military buffer around the EIC's core, built by alliances with neighbours: if anyone attacked the EIC in Bengal, Awadh was treaty-bound to help (mainly linked to W. Hastings 73-85 later, but Clive 57-67 planted the seed). Teacher's ink: underlines on "Rs 50 lakh compensation to EIC", "Benaras was separated from Awadh", "Kora and Allahabad" and "Dastak misuse began there too"; beside the Ring Fence row "[Concept: NEXT PAGE]"; below the table "In PRELIMS: MATCH THE FOLLOWING. CORRECT: PoRF = W. Hastings 73-85".   Clause   Terms    --- ---    Compensation   Shuja 54-75 was made to pay 50 lakh rupees to the EIC as compensation     Benaras   Benaras was separated from Awadh (the EIC formally annexed it in 1775)     Kora and Allahabad   Went to the Emperor     Duty-free trade   The EIC was granted duty-free trade in Awadh, and Dastak misuse began there too     Policy of Ring Fence   Initiated with Awadh (see below)     Mini Subsidiary Alliance   Awadh partially outsourced its military to the EIC (see below)   The Policy of Ring Fence (PoRF) The Policy of Ring Fence was initiated with Awadh. It is mainly associated with Warren Hastings 73-85, but Clive 57-67 planted its seed here. It meant creating a military buffer around the EIC's core territory by signing military alliances with neighbouring States. Under this military alliance with Awadh, if anyone attacked the EIC in Bengal, Awadh was treaty-bound to help. Think of it like the US using NATO during the Cold War: a buffer of allied Western Europe protected the core, that is the USA, from the USSR. Prelims match-the-following (the teacher's forecast). If "Policy of Ring Fence" is to be matched with a name, the correct pair is PoRF = Warren Hastings 73-85, even though Clive 57-67 planted the seed with Awadh in 1765. Do not pick Clive 57-67 in a matching question.  Teacher's board: "PoRF: concept". Urban home, of two kinds: Lower middle class, where BROKEN GLASS fixed on top of the Wall of the Home = Ring Fence (drawn as small triangles on a wall), and Rich, where BARBED WIRE coiled on top of the Wall of the Home = Ring Fence; in both the wall or home is the "core interest". Rural: a FIELD inside a thorny hedge drawn as a scalloped ring = Ring Fence, so that "CATTLE does not DESTROY CROP"; the field is the "CORE interest". Yellow dotted lines join all three fences to the big words: "Common: BUILD BUFFER AROUND CORE".  Teacher's board: "PoRF @ Bengal" (Bengal circled: core interest of the EIC). AWADH (white oval) sits to the west of Bengal (yellow oval); a dotted arrow from "enemy of EIC" on the left has to pass through Awadh to reach Bengal, and a second dotted arrow comes up from another "Enemy of EIC" below; under Awadh: "= BUFFER" and "Ring Fence via MILITARY alliance". Right: "Simple: PoRF = MILITARY alliance WITH NEIGHBOURS", and a small target diagram: "Br India" in the inner circle, a yellow outer ring of neighbours, and dotted lines from four enemies outside pointing at the centre. Teacher: The Ring Fence analogy. Urban home: a lower-middle-class house fixes broken glass on top of its boundary wall; a rich house puts coils of barbed wire there. Rural: a farmer rings his field with a thorny hedge so that cattle do not destroy the crop. In each case the home or the field is the CORE interest, and the glass, wire or hedge is the Ring Fence. The common idea: BUILD A BUFFER AROUND THE CORE. Teacher: Applied to 1765: Bengal is the core interest of the EIC, and Awadh is the buffer. An enemy of the EIC coming from the west must first pass through Awadh. The fence is made not of wire but "via military alliance". Simple definition: PoRF = military alliance with neighbours. In the small target diagram, British India is the inner circle, the allied neighbours are the ring, and the enemies are outside it. The mini Subsidiary Alliance A mini Subsidiary Alliance was signed. Awadh was forced to partially outsource a core sovereign function, its own military, to the EIC. The size of the Awadh army was reduced, and an EIC army was permanently stationed in Awadh and paid for by Awadh via an annual subsidy. (The handout's joke: the EIC saying "haha, thank you Dupleix 42-54 for the 1751 idea at Hyderabad".) Thus the EIC now partially controlled the military resources of Awadh. Combined with the military alliance, it meant that these resources could be used directly by the EIC itself (under its command) for protecting Bengal. The clauses relating to Awadh are a prelude to the full Subsidiary Alliance that Wellesley 98-05 would formalise three decades later (Chapter 11). A formal and proper Subsidiary Alliance was signed with Awadh in 1801, when Awadh's own army was disbanded and its foreign policy was also taken over by the EIC. But the architecture was drawn here in 1765.  Teacher's board: mini SA against the formal SA of 1801. Left: "mini (circled) SA": point 1 is left blank and point 2 reads "Legally, external sovereign functions not taken". Centre: "AWADH ARMY: (1) size reduced BUT not DISBANDED". Under "FORMAL SA in 1801" a checklist: British Resident (tick), military alliance (tick), EIC ARMY stationed (tick), SUBSIDY (tick), AWADH ARMY DISBANDED (cross), "D, L, FA taken" (cross); to the right of a vertical line the last two rows get ticks with "1801" written beside them.   Feature   Awadh in 1765 (mini SA)   Awadh in 1801 (formal SA)    --- --- ---    British Resident   Yes (tick)   Yes     Military alliance   Yes (tick)   Yes     EIC army stationed   Yes (tick)   Yes     Subsidy paid by Awadh   Yes (tick)   Yes     Awadh's own army   Size reduced BUT not disbanded (cross)   Disbanded (tick, 1801)     External sovereign functions ("D, L, FA taken")   Legally not taken (cross)   Taken (tick, 1801): the handout says its foreign policy was also taken over   Two traps here. (1) "Awadh was the first to sign a Subsidiary Alliance" is FALSE. The handout: when any source says so, it is false, as it was Hyderabad in 1798. Awadh's 1765 arrangement was only a mini Subsidiary Alliance, and its formal one came in 1801. (2) On slide 20 the teacher's last row reads "D, L, FA taken" as written. FA matches the handout's "foreign policy"; the other two letters are not expanded on the board ([unclear]). Check your notebook. 8.4 Clive 57-67's empire toolkit: born in one treaty   Instrument   What Clive 57-67 invented or operationalised in ToA 1765    --- ---    Policy of Indirect Rule (ticked)   Puppet Nawab + British Resident + control through the Resident: installed in Bengal's Nizamat     Policy of Ring Fence (ticked)   A buffer of allied neighbouring States around the EIC's core: seeded with Awadh     Mini Subsidiary Alliance (ticked)   Outsourcing a State's military to the EIC, stationed and subsidised: drawn with Awadh   Takeaway: Clive 57-67 was the father of the strategic policy toolkit that the EIC used for empire building. The Policy of Indirect Rule, the Policy of Ring Fence and the mini Subsidiary Alliance were all either invented or operationalised by Clive 57-67 in this single treaty. Thus the foundations of Empire were laid by Clive 57-67 in ToA 1765, and men like Wellesley 98-05 later built upon it. Teacher: On the toolkit slide (Lecture 14, slide 21) the teacher wrote "ToA 1765" above the table and put a tick after each of the three instruments. Learn the three as a set, each with its place: Indirect Rule in Bengal's Nizamat; Ring Fence and the mini Subsidiary Alliance with Awadh.
