items.t: 1 · Who were the Wellesleys?
items.x: Who Were the Wellesleys? Table of two rows. Richard Wellesley 98-05: Governor General of Bengal 1798–1805; empire builder who saw that expanding the empire raised his profile with a nationalistic British public; founded Fort William College, Calcutta 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs before posting them to districts. Henry Wellesley: handled administration and diplomacy of the EIC. Teacher's yellow underlines: "empire builder", "Fort William College, Calcutta 1800", "train British civil servants", "Indian languages, laws". No handwriting.   Brother   Role    --- ---    Richard Wellesley 98-05   Governor General of Bengal from 1798 to 1805. He was joined in India by both his brothers, Arthur and Henry Wellesley 98-05. An empire builder     Henry Wellesley 98-05   Handled the administration and diplomacy of the EIC     Arthur Wellesley 98-05   A military commander, but NOT an EIC officer: a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army   Wellesley 98-05 was an empire builder. He understood that expanding the empire raised his profile among a nationalistic British public, which was useful for his political ambitions back home. He established Fort William College in Calcutta in 1800 to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs before posting them to the districts. Teacher: The yellow underlines on this slide are "empire builder", "Fort William College, Calcutta 1800", "train British civil servants" and "Indian languages, laws". These are exactly the words UPSC has used: the founder pair and the purpose. Fort William College has been tested in UPSC Prelims three times. Prelims 2018: the institution and founder pair (alongside Sanskrit College Banaras and Calcutta Madarsa). Prelims 2020 and Prelims 2021: the purpose of establishment. Learn: Wellesley 98-05, Calcutta, 1800, to train British civil servants in Indian languages, laws and customs. 1.1 Arthur Wellesley 98-05: a Royal Army officer, not an EIC officer  Who Were the Wellesleys? (contd.) Arthur Wellesley: military commander but NOT an EIC officer; a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (infantry); led his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99) including the Siege of Seringapatam (1799), and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) including the Battle of Assaye (1803); also fought Napoleon's army 1808–15. Yellow underlines: "NOT an EIC officer", "Royal Army", "4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99)", "2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) incl. Battle of Assaye (1803)", "fought", "Napoleon's army 1808–15". Teacher's handwriting on the right: "Br State helped eic in INDIA, e.g. 3rd CW 1756-63, therefore eic GOT HELP of Br State in Empire BUILDING in INDIA". Arthur Wellesley 98-05 was a military commander, but he was NOT an EIC officer. He was a commissioned officer in the British Royal Army, commanding the 33rd Regiment of Foot (that is, infantry). He led his Royal regiment alongside EIC forces in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99), including the Siege of Seringapatam (1799), and in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05), including the Battle of Assaye (1803). He also fought Napoleon's army between 1808 and 1815. Teacher: Written beside the Arthur row: "Br State helped EIC in India, e.g. 3rd CW 1756-63; therefore the EIC GOT HELP of the Br State in Empire BUILDING in India." The reasoning: Arthur is proof that the British State's own army fought the EIC's wars. This was not new in 1798: Royal help goes back to the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63). So the empire was built by the Company and the British State together, not by a private company alone. 1.2 Two European armies in India (3rd Carnatic War 1756–63 till 1858)  Two European Armies in India (3rd Carnatic War 1756–63 till 1858). Company's Army: the EIC's own private military, paid for by the EIC; majorly Indian sepoys but also European sepoys; senior officers always European i.e. British. King's Army (Royal Military): official British State's regiments sent to India to support the EIC; the EIC had to reimburse the British State for the cost of Royal troops deployed in India. Legally distinct: both forces fought together but were legally and institutionally distinct; the Company State received direct military support from the British Crown, hence the British State cannot escape responsibility for empire building in India. Teacher's yellow underline: "EIC had to reimburse the British State". No handwriting. From the 3rd Carnatic War (1756-63) till 1858, two separate European military forces operated in India side by side:   Force   What it was   Who paid    --- --- ---    Company's Army   The EIC's own private military. Majorly Indian sepoys, but it also had European sepoys. Senior officers were always European, that is, British   Paid for by the EIC     King's Army (Royal Military)   The official British State's regiments sent to India to support the EIC   The EIC had to reimburse the British State for the cost of Royal troops deployed in India   Both forces fought together, but they were legally and institutionally distinct. The handout's note: the Company State in India received direct military support from the British Crown. Hence the British State cannot escape responsibility for empire building in India. (The teacher underlined "EIC had to reimburse the British State" in yellow: the Crown lent its regiments, and the Company paid the bill.) 1.3 Arthur's own verdict on the Marathas  Two European Armies in India (contd.). Arthur's own verdict: on record, the Marathas were the most formidable enemy he ever faced, and the Battle of Assaye (1803) the toughest fight of his career. Had India been one State ruling the whole, not a fragmented polity, it would not have been colonised. No handwriting on this slide. Arthur Wellesley 98-05 on record stated that the Marathas were the most formidable enemy he ever faced, and that the Battle of Assaye (1803) against them was the toughest fight of his entire military career. The Marathas were harder to defeat militarily. The handout's conclusion: had India not been a fragmented polity, that is, had there been one State ruling the whole of India, India would not have been colonised. This is a ready Mains line on why the EIC won.

items.t: 2 · Pitt's India Act 1784 banned conquest: how Wellesley 98-05 re-initiated it
items.x: 2.1 Context of Pitt's India Act 1784 (the teacher's board)  Teacher's board: "Context of PIA 1784 [passed by Br (P), William PITT = PM]". A left-to-right chain: GBF 1770, then by 1772 eic bankrupt, then sought help of Br State, then Br State gave money or a loan to eic BUT (circled) brought eic under Br State's supervision via the boxed "Regulating Act 1773". Under the box: "CORE GOAL: Eic shall NOT waste Br taxpayer money on WARS and again go bankrupt". Right column: "1st A-Ma war 1775-8[last digit unclear]" plus (circled +) "2nd A-My war 1780-84" equals "HIGH WAR expenditure", "therefore Br State anxious", "therefore passed PIA 1784 which banned conquest i.e. eic can DEFEND but Cannot START WARS on its own" (the last phrase underlined in yellow). GBF 1770 (as written on the board) (warn) By 1772 the EIC is bankrupt; it seeks the help of the British State The British State gives money (a loan) to the EIC, BUT brings the EIC under its supervision via the Regulating Act 1773 Core goal of 1773: the EIC shall not waste British taxpayers' money on wars and go bankrupt again (warn) 1st Anglo-Maratha War plus 2nd Anglo-Mysore War (1780-84): high war expenditure; the British State is anxious (bad) Pitt's India Act 1784 bans conquest: the EIC can defend but cannot start wars on its own Teacher: The heading reads "Context of PIA 1784 [passed by Br (P), William PITT = PM]": the Act was passed by the British Parliament (the circled P) when William Pitt was Prime Minister. The logic of the chain is money: the British State had already rescued a bankrupt Company once (the loan, with supervision through the Regulating Act 1773). Its core goal was that the EIC should not waste British taxpayers' money on wars and go bankrupt again. When two more wars again produced high war expenditure, the State grew anxious and wrote the ban into law. The teacher underlined in yellow: "Cannot START WARS." Unclear handwriting on slide 34. The years of the "1st A-Ma war" on the board read "1775-8[unclear]": the last digit is not legible. The handout and slide 35 print 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82). Use 1775–82, and check your class notebook. The board's abbreviation "GBF 1770" is not expanded on this slide; it is from the Chapter 10 boards of the same lecture, see Chapter 10. 2.2 The ban and the reason for it  Pitt's India Act 1784 Banned Conquest: How Wellesley 98-05 Re-initiated It. Ban: the Governor-General could not start an offensive war without express command of the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State; he had the right to enter war only on grounds of defence. Reason: high war expenditure; the Three Carnatic Wars (1746–63), Battle of Buxar (1764), two Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–69 and 1780–84) and the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82) had drained company finances; Parliament mandated diplomacy over war: Policy of Indirect Rule plus a balance of power among Indian States instead of direct conquest. Teacher's yellow underlines: "could not start an offensive war", "High war expenditure", "drained company finances". No handwriting.   Aspect   Detail    --- ---    The ban   Pitt's India Act of 1784 had banned conquest. The Governor-General (GG) could not start an offensive war without the express command and authority of either the Court of Directors of the EIC or the Board of Control of the British State (discussed in a later chapter)     The exception   The GG had the right to enter war on grounds of defence     The reason   High war expenditure     The wars that drained Company finances   The Three Carnatic Wars (1746–63), the Battle of Buxar (1764), two Anglo-Mysore Wars (1767–69 and 1780–84) and the 1st Anglo-Maratha War (1775–82)     What Parliament mandated instead   Diplomacy rather than war, in the form of the Policy of Indirect Rule (PoIR) and maintaining a balance of power among Indian States, instead of pursuing direct conquest   The handout's recall: the pacifist policy of the Mughals after 1707 was also for the same reason (the cost of war). And the handout's note: Wellesley 98-05 could not legally start an offensive war without prior authorisation. 2.3 The Napoleon threat: there, but not real  Teacher's board headed "WORLD HISTORY" (underlined in yellow). A rough map in yellow outline: "France" at top left; a yellow dotted line from France through "1798" to "Egypt"; "M. east" with another dotted line; a pink dotted line running on from France towards the V-shaped sea on the right; three yellow arrows pointing down to "Br TRADE of ARABIAN Sea"; a curved line from the right-hand V to "DIPLOMATIC CONTACT WITH TIPU 82-99". A pink arrow leads to "THREAT of Napoleon-Mysore alliance / Napoleon ATTACKING Br India". Below, "PRELIMS" (pink underline), then "# THREAT Was THERE BUT not Real", with a tree: "Real [High Chance]" and "un Real [Less Chance]", and the reason "because Br NAVY = SUPERIOR [Wont have been able to Reach India]". 1798: France (Napoleon) attacks Egypt; the dotted line on the board runs France to Egypt, marked 1798 Aim: the Middle East; to hurt the British trade of the Arabian Sea (three arrows on the board) Diplomatic contact with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore (warn) Threat: a Napoleon and Mysore alliance, or Napoleon attacking British India (good) But the threat was "there, not real"; the British Navy was superior, so the French would not have been able to reach India Teacher: This is the board marked PRELIMS. The teacher splits the word "threat" into two kinds: Real = high chance; Unreal = less chance. His verdict: "THREAT was THERE BUT not Real", that is, a threat existed, but with a low chance. The reason he writes beside it: "because Br NAVY = SUPERIOR [would not have been able to reach India]." So in an exam statement, "Napoleonic danger" is a correct feature of the Subsidiary Alliance (the danger was there), even though the danger was not a real, high-chance one.  Pitt's India Act 1784 Banned Conquest: How Wellesley 98-05 Re-initiated It (contd.). Wellesley's trick: re-initiated conquest by overhyping a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance; Napoleon attacked Egypt in 1798 to control the Middle East and hurt British trade, and was in contact with Tipu 82-99; a threat existed but not a real one, as Britain's superior navy would have destroyed a French fleet in the Arabian Sea before it arrived. Middle path: the British State agreed anyway, since protecting India from European rivals was the primary goal of British foreign policy; Wellesley 98-05 offered the Subsidiary Alliance: political domination without the cost, administrative burden and symbolism of full annexation. Teacher's ink: beside "Middle path" he wrote "= SA = CONTROL w/o annexation"; a handwritten "w/o" after "administrative burden &". Yellow underline: "Re-initiated conquest". Pink underlines: "overhyping", "A threat existed but not a real one", and the whole Subsidiary Alliance phrase. Wellesley 98-05 re-initiated conquest by overhyping the threat of a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance. Napoleon had attacked Egypt in 1798 with the goal of controlling the Middle East and hurting British trade, and he was in communication with Tipu 82-99 of Mysore. A threat existed, but not a real one. Britain's navy was superior to France's, and a French fleet heading for India through the Arabian Sea would have been destroyed before arriving. The handout's note: the British had already burnt French ships in the Mediterranean once Napoleon landed in Egypt, leaving his army stranded with no way home. But the British State agreed anyway, because protecting India from European rivals was the primary goal of British foreign policy and it did not want to take any risks. Wellesley 98-05 also offered a middle path: the Subsidiary Alliance. It gave political domination without the cost, the administrative burden and the symbolism of full annexation. Teacher: Beside "Middle path" the teacher wrote "= SA = CONTROL w/o annexation." He also added a handwritten "w/o" before "symbolism", so the phrase reads: without the cost, without the administrative burden and without the symbolism of full annexation. This is the one-line definition to carry: the Subsidiary Alliance is control without annexation. It suited a State that had banned conquest because conquest was costly: the SA promised the gains of conquest without its bill. Pitt's India Act 1784: no offensive war without the Court of Directors or the Board of Control; war only in defence 1798: Napoleon attacks Egypt and is in communication with Tipu 82-99 (warn) Wellesley 98-05 overhypes the threat of a Napoleon and Tipu 82-99 alliance The British State agrees anyway: protecting India from European rivals is its primary foreign-policy goal; it will not take risks (good) Middle path: the Subsidiary Alliance; control without annexation Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: option (b) was a TRUE statement: "Napoleonic danger was a feature of the SA." The danger was not real (less chance of a Napoleonic attack on India), but the danger was there (a chance existed). Do not mark it false. Prelims 1999: "At a time when empires in Europe were crumbling before the might of Napoleon, which one of the following Governors General kept the British flag flying high in India?" Options: (a) Warren Hastings 73-85, (b) Lord Cornwallis, (c) Lord Wellesley 98-05 (correct), (d) Lord Hastings. The trap: two different Governors General share the surname Hastings. Warren Hastings 73-85 is the pre-Napoleon era: wrong. Francis Hastings 13-23 (also called Lord Hastings) is the post-Napoleon era: wrong. Why (c): the tenure of Wellesley 98-05 (1798–1805) overlaps with Napoleon's offensive phase (1796–1812). Students sometimes pick (d) Lord Hastings because the name sounds Napoleon-era. It is NOT.

items.t: 3 · Two roots of the SA: Dupleix 42-54 and ToA 1765
items.x: The Policy of Subsidiary Alliance did not appear from nowhere. It has two roots: one French and one British.  Two Roots of SA: Dupleix 42-54 (French) plus ToA 1765 (British). French root, Dupleix 42-54 at Hyderabad, 1751: as GG of French Establishments in India he installed the first proto-form of SA; when Salabat Jung 51-62 became Nizam of Hyderabad with French backing, a French force under Bussy was permanently stationed, paid via Northern Sarkars revenues; the template: an external army at the Indian State's cost plus a foreign adviser at court who established indirect rule. British root, Clive 57-67's ToA 1765: Robert Clive 57-67 planted a mini SA at Awadh via the Treaty of Allahabad (1765): EIC army in Awadh paid by subsidy from Awadh, the Nawab's own army reduced, a British Resident stationed; very close to the French template. No handwriting on this slide.   Feature   French root: Dupleix 42-54 at Hyderabad, 1751   British root: Clive 57-67's ToA 1765 at Awadh    --- --- ---    Who   Dupleix 42-54, as Governor General of French Establishments in India (GG of the French EIC)   Robert Clive 57-67     What he set up   The first mini or proto-form of the Subsidiary Alliance, at Hyderabad in 1751   The mini Subsidiary Alliance planted at Awadh via the Treaty of Allahabad (1765)     The occasion   Salabat Jung 51-62 became Nizam of Hyderabad with French backing   The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) with Awadh     The army   A French force under Bussy was permanently stationed   An EIC army in Awadh     Who paid   Paid out in the form of Northern Sarkars revenues (and control)   Paid by subsidy from Awadh     The ruler's own army   Not stated in the handout   Size of the Nawab's controlled army reduced (not disbanded)     The man at court   A foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule   A British Resident stationed   Dupleix 42-54 had discovered the template: an external army at the Indian State's cost, with a foreign adviser at court who would not just advise but establish indirect rule. Clive 57-67's mini SA at Awadh was the British version, very close to the French template that Dupleix 42-54 had pioneered. 3.1 Wellesley 98-05's step: from a device to a policy  Two Roots of SA (contd.). Wellesley's step: formalised the relationship in a written treaty, took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy explicitly, and disbanded its army. The SA was NOT his invention, but he initiated it as a policy: a pre-meditated formalised plan implemented State by State across India. No handwriting on this slide. Wellesley 98-05 took the next step. He formalised the relationship in a written treaty, took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy explicitly, and disbanded its army. The Subsidiary Alliance was NOT a Wellesley 98-05 invention. BUT the Policy of Subsidiary Alliance was initiated by him. Why "policy": a policy means a pre-meditated, formalised plan of action with a pre-decided intent, which is reflected in a series of events executed in line with that policy. Wellesley 98-05 formalised the SA into a policy, added the takeover of Foreign Policy and the disbanding of the Indian State's army, and implemented this policy State by State across India. Invention versus policy. The idea is older: Dupleix 42-54 (Hyderabad, 1751) and Clive 57-67 (Awadh, ToA 1765). The policy is Wellesley 98-05's: a written treaty, Foreign Policy taken over, the army disbanded, applied State by State. If a statement says "Wellesley 98-05 invented the Subsidiary Alliance", it is wrong; if it says he "initiated the Policy of Subsidiary Alliance", it is right. 1751, Hyderabad (Dupleix 42-54): French force under Bussy stationed, paid from the Northern Sarkars; a foreign adviser at court 1765, Awadh (Clive 57-67, ToA 1765); EIC army paid by Awadh's subsidy, Nawab's army reduced, British Resident stationed (warn) Wellesley 98-05: written treaty, Foreign Policy taken over explicitly, the State's army disbanded (bad) A policy, not a one-off: implemented State by State across India

items.t: 4 · The model treaty of the Subsidiary Alliance and its legal logic
items.x: The standard terms of any Subsidiary Alliance fell into two groups, though the actual terms varied a little from State to State, depending on context. 4.0 The teacher's board: how the SA splits sovereignty  Teacher's board headed "SA" (circled, underlined in yellow). "Sovereignty:" on the left; in the centre "Symbolic Sovereignty (Indian king)". Below, underlined in yellow: "Power to Do" and the circled letters L, E, J. Left half, tagged "[Taken By eic]": "External Sovereign Fns" with three branches marked "D, C, FA": Def, Communications, Foreign Affairs. Under Def: "eic will maintain Army BUT (circled) TAKES money (circled rupee sign)" and "= SUBSIDY: Def BD [Decided By eic]". Right half, tagged "[Indian king]": "Domestic Sovereign Functions" with branches Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.   Part of sovereignty   What it contains   Who holds it under the SA    --- --- ---    Symbolic Sovereignty   The throne and the title   The Indian king     External Sovereign Functions: D, C, FA   Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs   Taken by the EIC     Domestic Sovereign Functions   Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.   The Indian king   Teacher: The teacher starts from the word Sovereignty and separates Symbolic Sovereignty (who is called king) from the "power to do" (the three circled letters L, E, J; the board does not expand them here). The power to do is then cut in two. External Sovereign Functions (D, C, FA: Defence, Communications, Foreign Affairs) are "[Taken by EIC]". Domestic Sovereign Functions (Home, Finance, Transport, Agri, Health etc.) stay with the "[Indian king]". Under Def he writes the heart of the SA: "EIC will maintain the Army BUT TAKES money = SUBSIDY: Def BD [Decided by EIC]." That is: the subsidy is simply the Indian State's defence budget (Def BD), but the size of that budget is decided by the EIC, not by the ruler who pays it.  Teacher's board: "Symbolic Sovereignty" with a line splitting into two branches. Left branch: "Nizamat [minus Domestic L&O]" in a bracket. Right branch: "Nizamat (minus MILITARY) + Diwani (civil admin + Finance)", with "= Criminal Jurisdiction" written beside "Nizamat (minus MILITARY)". Bottom line: "# simple: MILITARY, Foreign Policy with eic; Rest of Nizamat and Diwani and Symbolic Sovereignty with Indian King". Teacher: The same split, now in the Mughal vocabulary of Nizamat and Diwani. Diwani = civil administration plus Finance. Nizamat (minus Military) = Criminal Jurisdiction. The teacher's own summary line: "Simple: MILITARY and Foreign Policy with the EIC; the rest of Nizamat, and Diwani, and Symbolic Sovereignty with the Indian King." This is why the handout writes the ruler's promise as non-interference in "succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military)". Unclear on slide 41. The left branch of the diagram reads "Nizamat [minus Domestic L&O]" and the board does not label whose share it is. Going by the summary line at the bottom, it appears to be the part of Nizamat that went to the EIC (Nizamat without domestic law and order, that is, the military), set against the right branch that stayed with the king. Treat this reading as [unclear] and check your class notebook. 4.1 What the EIC got (5 terms)  Model Treaty: What the EIC Got (5 terms). 1: British Resident permanently in the Indian ruler's court, with the ruler as a puppet (elements 1 and 2 of PoIR). 2: Formal military alliance between EIC and Indian State. 3: Indian State's army DISBANDED, replaced by an EIC army stationed in the State. 4: Indian State pays ANNUAL SUBSIDY to fund that EIC army. 5: EIC takes over FOREIGN POLICY: war and peace, diplomacy, defence budget, foreign trade; the GG's consent needed before any European could be stationed at the court, and the ruler had to consult the GG before negotiating with any other Indian State or foreign power. Note: the subsidy was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. Teacher's ink: term 1 joined to "(1) Puppet Nawab (2) Br Resident", two arrows meeting in a V at a circled 3 "CONTROL" crossed by yellow dotted lines, "= promise in SA TREATY"; beside term 2: "So MILITARY maintained for Indian State, can be used FOR Br India as well"; beside term 4: "= Def BD"; from term 5 a curved arrow to "money will GO TO Indian State BUT Decisions of eic". Yellow underlines on the key words of each term.   #   Term   Fine print from the handout    --- --- ---    1   A British Resident stationed permanently in the Indian ruler's court, with the ruler as a puppet   Elements 1 and 2 of PoIR, but not yet element 3: the British promised non-interference in internal affairs by the British Resident. This promise was seldom kept, and the British breached the treaty in many cases     2   A formal military alliance between the EIC and the Indian State       3   The Indian State's own army was disbanded and replaced by an EIC-maintained army permanently stationed in the State       4   The Indian State paid an annual subsidy to fund this EIC army   So technically this army is owned by the Indian State; the EIC only maintains it. But because of the 5th point, this ownership of the Indian State was lost     5   The EIC took over the Indian State's Foreign Policy   Decisions on war and peace, diplomacy, the defence budget and foreign trade. The GG's consent was needed before any European could be stationed at the court. The ruler had to consult the GG before negotiating with any other Indian State or foreign power. The subsidy, that is, the defence budget of the Indian State, was decided by the EIC   Teacher: Ink on the five terms (slide 42), with the reasoning. Term 1: the teacher writes "(1) Puppet Nawab (2) Br Resident" and draws both into a circled "(3) CONTROL", which he crosses with dotted lines and labels "= promise in SA TREATY". Meaning: the three elements of indirect rule are a puppet ruler, a Resident, and control through the Resident. The SA treaty openly had the first two; the third (control) was promised away on paper by the non-interference clause. Term 2: "So the MILITARY maintained for the Indian State can be used FOR Br India as well." An alliance cuts both ways: the army paid for by the ruler is now also the EIC's army for British India's needs. Term 4: "= Def BD". The annual subsidy is nothing but the State's defence budget. Term 5: "The money will GO TO the Indian State BUT the Decisions are the EIC's." The State keeps earning and paying; the EIC decides. The handout's note: the annual subsidy money was NOT surplus income that the EIC could use for anything. The subsidy was to be spent only for maintaining the army. The slide adds: the subsidy was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. 4.2 What the Indian ruler got (2 terms)  Model Treaty: What the Indian Ruler Got (2 terms). 1: EIC protection against neighbours and domestic threats. 2: Formal promise of NON-INTERFERENCE in internal affairs: succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military). Imbalance: the ruler gets 2 promises, the EIC takes 5 operational levers; the non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident: creeping PoIR through the back door. Teacher's ink: "Indian" written above "Ruler gets 2 promises"; under "Imbalance" a dot marked eic joined by a thick sloping line down to a dot marked Indian state; on the right "[Compare with DUAL GOVT (1765-72) in Bengal]" and "From 1772 everything in Bengal with eic [symbolically Nawabs contd into 19th c]". Yellow underlines: "Indian Ruler Got", "EIC protection", "neighbours", "domestic threats", "NON-INTERFERENCE in internal affairs", "succession", "Diwani", "Nizamat", "non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident".   #   Term    --- ---    1   EIC protection against neighbours and domestic threats     2   A formal promise of non-interference in internal affairs: succession, Diwani, Nizamat (minus military)   Teacher: The imbalance. The slide's own line: the ruler gets 2 promises; the EIC takes 5 operational levers. The non-interference promise was routinely broken via the Resident: "creeping PoIR through the back door". Under the word Imbalance the teacher redraws the sloping line: EIC on top, Indian State below (the same picture as on slide 29). His comparison: "[Compare with DUAL GOVT (1765-72) in Bengal]". Then: "From 1772 everything in Bengal with the EIC [symbolically the Nawabs continued into the 19th century]." The point of the comparison: in both cases an Indian ruler keeps the name and the responsibility while the Company holds real power. In Bengal the split ended in 1772 with everything going to the EIC; the SA sets up a similar split in State after State. 4.3 Why the EIC took Foreign Policy: the legal logic  Model Treaty: Why the EIC Took Foreign Policy (Legal Logic). Legal logic of Term 5: the EIC's army was paid by the Indian State's subsidy, so legally the right to deploy it could still rest with the ruler; taking over Foreign Policy closed that loophole: war and peace (and thus the right to deploy the army) now legally rested with the EIC. Note: ToA 1765 was a mini SA: EIC army stationed at Awadh's expense, BUT Awadh's own army was NOT disbanded and Foreign Policy NOT taken over; the full package came only in 1801. Formula: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC military replacing the Indian State's military + Annual Subsidy + Loss of Foreign Policy. No handwriting on this slide. The EIC maintains the army using the Indian State's own subsidy money (warn) Loophole: one could argue that legal ownership, and the right to deploy that army, still belong to the Indian ruler The EIC takes Foreign Policy: the decision of war and peace (bad) Loophole closed: the right to deploy the army now legally rests with the EIC There is a legal logic to why the EIC specifically demanded Foreign Policy. The EIC maintained the army using the Indian State's own subsidy money. One could therefore argue that legal ownership, and the right to deploy that army, still belonged to the Indian ruler. The EIC closed this loophole by taking Foreign Policy. The decision of war and peace, and therefore the right to deploy the army, now legally rested with the EIC. Why ToA 1765 was only a "mini" Subsidiary Alliance: an EIC army was stationed there at Awadh's expense, BUT Awadh's own army was not disbanded and Foreign Policy was not taken over. The proper SA (the full package) came only in 1801. The formula: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC Military replacing the Indian State's Military + annual subsidy + loss of Foreign Policy. (PoSA = Policy of Subsidiary Alliance; PoIR = Policy of Indirect Rule; PoRF = Policy of Ring Fence, from Chapter 10. "Informally" because the treaty itself promised non-interference.)  Handout diagram: MODEL TREATY OF SUBSIDIARY ALLIANCE, "What each side gave and got, plus the legal logic of why EIC demanded Foreign Policy". Left column, What the EIC GOT (5 terms): 1. British Resident permanently in the Indian ruler's court (elements 1 and 2 of PoIR); 2. formal military alliance between EIC and Indian State; 3. Indian State's army DISBANDED, replaced by an EIC army stationed in the State; 4. Indian State pays ANNUAL SUBSIDY to fund this EIC army; 5. EIC takes over FOREIGN POLICY (war and peace, diplomacy, defence, foreign trade); note: the annual subsidy was NOT surplus income for the EIC, it was earmarked for that army, but the EIC commanded it, so operational control was fully with the EIC. Right column, What the INDIAN RULER GOT (2 terms): 1. EIC PROTECTION against neighbours and domestic threats; 2. formal promise of NON-INTERFERENCE in internal affairs (succession, Diwani, Nizamat); Imbalance: the ruler gets 2 promises, the EIC takes 5 operational levers; the non-interference promise was ROUTINELY broken via the British Resident's interference (creeping PoIR through the back door). Red box: LEGAL LOGIC of Term 5: the EIC's army was paid for by the Indian State's subsidy, so legally the right to deploy it could still belong to the ruler; taking over Foreign Policy CLOSED this loophole. Note: the Treaty of Allahabad 1765 with Awadh was a mini SA (Awadh's own army NOT disbanded, Foreign Policy NOT taken over; the full package came only in 1801). Bottom line: PoSA = PoIR (informally) + PoRF + EIC Military replacing Indian State's Military + Annual Subsidy + Loss of Foreign Policy. 4.4 The PYQ on SA features (Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021) UPSC asked the same question in both Prelims 2018 and Prelims 2021: "Which statement does NOT apply to the Subsidiary Alliance?" The four options tested the features of the SA. The false option was (c) "Secure a fixed income for the Company." The SA's annual subsidy was earmarked for maintaining the EIC army stationed in the host State. It was NOT surplus income for the EIC. The other three options were true: to maintain a large standing army, to defend against Napoleonic danger, and to establish British paramountcy.

items.t: 5 · The vicious chain: consequences of the Subsidiary Alliance for Indian States
items.x: Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance. Link 1, disbanded armies to mass unemployment: disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men: Mansabdars lost their positions, sepoys lost their livelihoods (the EIC also recruited sepoys from outside the host State to cut any loyalty to the Nawab: a classic Divide and Rule). Link 2, EIC's compounded military power: since the EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, operational control was entirely with the EIC; having taken Foreign Policy it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere, so the EIC now maintained a large army at the expense of Indian States. Teacher's ink: "positions" struck through and "MILITARY ROLE" written above it; a yellow line to a circled "DnR: Eic will NOT (Less) keep sepoys FROM Bengal in Bengal ARMY"; lower left "WHO PAYS for eic ARMY in Indian State (SA)? Indian State / King, therefore Free of ARMY" (underlined); at the bottom a bracket: "every SA LEADS (Free of Cost, circled) EIC ARMY increases".   #   Link   How it worked    --- --- ---    1   Disbanded armies, so mass unemployment   Disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men: Mansabdars lost their positions (the teacher corrects this to "military role"), sepoys lost their livelihoods     2   The EIC's compounded military power at the host State's expense   The EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, so operational control was entirely with the EIC. Having taken over Foreign Policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. The EIC could now maintain a large army at the expense of Indian States     3   High and rising subsidy, so Drain of Wealth   Subsidy payments were high to begin with and the EIC gradually increased its demands. The same money could have been used by the ruler for his own State's development. Instead there was Drain of Wealth     4   Tax hikes, so unrest   To pay the ever-rising subsidy, rulers had to raise taxes. High taxes made rulers unpopular, fuelled peasant resentment and created conditions for unrest     5   Maladministration accusations, so grounds for annexation   The EIC then accused Indian rulers of maladministration. In reality the ruler had no real power left     6   Territory in lieu of cash   When the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment     7   Permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity   By losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC   5.1 Links 1 and 2: unemployment and the EIC's free army Link 1. Disbanding Indian State armies caused mass unemployment for military men. Mansabdars lost their positions; sepoys lost their livelihoods. The handout's note: the EIC also recruited sepoys from outside the host State, to reduce any chance of loyalty to the Nawab in case he revolted: a classic Divide and Rule strategy. Link 2. Since the EIC maintained and commanded the army in the Indian State, operational control was entirely with the EIC. Since it had also taken over Foreign Policy, it could deploy these armies for its own wars elsewhere. Hence the EIC could now maintain a large army at the expense of Indian States. The handout's note: EIC Armies = the army of the Indian State maintained by the EIC using the Indian State's subsidy + the EIC's own army maintained from its own money. Both were available to the EIC for its own wars. Teacher's correction on slide 45. In the line "Mansabdars lost their positions", the teacher struck out "positions" and wrote "MILITARY ROLE" above it. The handout prints "positions". Use the teacher's wording: Mansabdars lost their military role. Teacher: Divide and Rule (the circled "DnR"). Beside the note on recruiting outsiders the teacher wrote: "DnR: the EIC will NOT keep sepoys from Bengal in the Bengal Army", with "(Less)" written above "NOT". So read it as: the EIC would keep few or no local men in the army of their own region. The reasoning is in the handout's note: a sepoy from outside has no loyalty to the local Nawab if he revolts. Who pays? The teacher asks: "WHO PAYS for the EIC army in an Indian State (SA)?" Answer: "the Indian State / King", therefore a "FREE army" for the Company (his written phrase is "Free of ARMY"). The boxed conclusion: "[Every SA leads to a free-of-cost increase in the EIC army]". Each new treaty adds a paid-for army to the Company's strength without adding a rupee to its costs.  Teacher's board, the analogy: "SA Concept LIKE BALI of Ramayana" (the word LIKE underlined, BALI inside a large circle, "Concept" written small under SA). Below: "SA (circled) LED TO MILITARY Power SHIFT". Teacher: The Bali analogy. The board reads: "SA concept LIKE BALI of Ramayana" (BALI in a big circle), and under it "SA LED TO MILITARY POWER SHIFT." Read it together with the previous board: under every SA the Indian State's military strength moves across to the EIC. The State pays, its own army is disbanded, and the army it pays for fights for the Company. So with each alliance the ally grows weaker and the EIC grows stronger: a shift of military power. High and rising subsidy to Drain of Wealth: subsidy payments were high to begin with and the EIC gradually raised its demands; the same money could have funded the Indian ruler's own State development; instead there was Drain of Wealth. Maladministration accusations to annexation grounds: the EIC then accused rulers of maladministration; in reality the ruler had no real power left: the Resident had in many cases established Indirect Rule illegally, breaching the treaty's own non-interference promise; the ruler had no power but all the responsibility (starkest: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh, State annexed 1856). The EIC then accused Indian rulers of maladministration. In reality the ruler had no real power left. The British Resident had in many cases established Indirect Rule illegally, in direct breach of the treaty's own promise of non-interference. The ruler had no power, but all the responsibility. The most stark example was Nawab Wajid Ali Shah of Awadh: accused of maladministration, his State annexed in 1856. Link 6. When the subsidy could not be paid in cash, the EIC simply took territory as payment. In 1801, half of Awadh was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. In 1853, Hyderabad was made to give Berar. The handout's aside: the EIC can say "Thanks, Dupleix 42-54". He gave this idea when he took the Northern Sarkars from Hyderabad in 1751. Teacher: Under "Territory in lieu of cash" the teacher wrote: "Subsidy = TOOL of empire building." The subsidy was not only a payment. It was set high, it kept rising, and when the ruler defaulted the EIC took land. So the subsidy itself was the instrument that turned an "alliance" into annexation. He underlined the two examples to memorise: 1801, half of Awadh; 1853, Berar from Hyderabad. 5.4 Link 7 and the takeaway  Vicious-Chain Consequences of Subsidiary Alliance (contd.). Permanent loss of alliance-forming capacity: by losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC; so the SA was, in effect, a sophisticated Divide and Rule instrument at the level of an entire subcontinent. Takeaway: the EIC via SA got all military and diplomatic powers with no responsibility of ruling and no burden of finances; the seven links explain why every single SA signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent. No handwriting on this slide. Link 7. By losing Foreign Policy and military control, Indian States permanently lost the ability to form alliances against the EIC. Hence the Subsidiary Alliance was, in effect, a sophisticated Divide and Rule instrument at the level of an entire subcontinent. Takeaway: the EIC via the SA got all military and diplomatic powers, with no responsibility of ruling and no burden of finances. The seven vicious-chain links explain why every single SA signatory ended up either annexed or permanently dependent. The State's army is disbanded: Mansabdars lose their military role, sepoys their livelihood The EIC's army grows free of cost and can be used for the EIC's own wars (warn) Subsidy high and rising: Drain of Wealth (warn) Taxes raised: rulers unpopular, peasant resentment, peasant revolts (bad) "Maladministration": the ruler has no power but all the responsibility (Awadh annexed 1856) (bad) Territory in lieu of cash: half of Awadh 1801, Berar 1853 (bad) No alliances possible against the EIC: annexed or permanently dependent

items.t: 6 · Which States signed, and under what circumstances
items.x: Sections 6 and 7 are from the handout only. The Chapter 11 slides of Lecture 14 stop at the vicious chain (slide 49), so there is no teacher's ink for the signatories, the annexations or the recall. 6.1 Why some rulers walked in willingly The SA was not forced on every signatory at sword-point. In several cases the Indian ruler walked in willingly, persuaded by five arguments:   #   Argument   What it meant    --- --- ---    1   Protection against internal revolts   A guaranteed EIC army inside the palace walls was attractive insurance against rival claimants or mutinous nobles     2   Protection against external threats   Small States feared Maratha Chauth raids, Mysorean expansion or Rohilla incursions far more than the distant British     3   Better than annexation   The subsidy was, on paper, cheaper than annexation or a losing war against the EIC     4   Preservation of royal dignity   The ruler's title, court and ceremonial status were formally preserved. The flag of sovereignty flew, even after its substance had been handed over     5   For winning succession disputes and for protection from neighbours   In many cases rulers sought EIC help in succession disputes and for protection from other Indian States. The EIC used this as an opportunity by making military help conditional upon the Indian ruler signing the SA   6.2 The nine signatories (1798–1818)   #   Year   State (treaty)   Circumstances   Governor General    --- --- --- --- ---    1   1798   Hyderabad   The Nizam signed first, to get EIC protection against the Marathas and Mysore   Wellesley 98-05     2   1799   Mysore (Wodeyar dynasty)   Forced to sign after defeat in the 4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99). Tipu 82-99 was killed at the Battle of Seringapatam (1799); the Wodeyars were restored as a subsidiary throne   Wellesley 98-05     3   1801   Awadh   Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted on the subsidy; Henry Wellesley 98-05 imposed a full Subsidiary Alliance; half of Awadh annexed (details below)   Wellesley 98-05     4   June 1802   Gaikwad of Baroda (Treaty of Cambay)   Signed in exchange for EIC help in a Gaikwad succession dispute   Wellesley 98-05     5   December 1802   Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18 (Treaty of Bassein / Vasai)   Defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar, he fled and signed to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support   Wellesley 98-05     6   1803   Scindia of Gwalior   Forced to sign during the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05)   Wellesley 98-05     -   1803-05   Jats, Rajputs, Bundelas   During the war the EIC forced them to sign Subsidiary Alliances. They had earlier paid Chauth and Sardeshmukhi to the Marathas; now they paid subsidy to the new regional power, the EIC   Wellesley 98-05     7   1805   Travancore   Signed in exchange for EIC help in crushing a mutiny by Nair troops, who had revolted over non-payment of salary. The last SA signed under Wellesley 98-05 before his recall   Wellesley 98-05     8   1816   Bhonsle of Nagpur (Treaty of Nagpur)   Appa Sahib finally signed, using EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent   Francis Hastings 13-23     9   1818   Holkar of Indore (Treaty of Mandsaur)   Forced to sign after decisive defeat in the 3rd Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19)   Francis Hastings 13-23   Takeaway: 9 SAs in 20 years, 1798 to 1818. The first seven were signed under Wellesley 98-05; the last two under Francis Hastings 13-23. First: Hyderabad (1798). Last under Wellesley 98-05: Travancore (1805). Last of all: Holkar (1818). On the count of nine. The handout's list has ten bullets, because it also lists the Jats, Rajputs and Bundelas (1803-05) as a group. The count of nine (seven plus two) works only if that group entry is not counted. The table above therefore numbers the nine named signatories and leaves the group row unnumbered. Awadh, 1798 to 1801, step by step: 1798: Sadat Ali Khan II offers the EIC Rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy; in exchange John Shore 93-98 is to remove his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98) from the Nawabship Shore 93-98 obliges (warn) By 1801 Sadat Ali Khan II defaults Wellesley 98-05 sends his brother Henry Wellesley 98-05 to impose a full Subsidiary Alliance (bad) Half of Awadh annexed as permanent subsidy payment: the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand 1801, Awadh. In 1798, Sadat Ali Khan II had offered the EIC Rs 76 lakh as annual subsidy in exchange for John Shore 93-98 removing his nephew Wazir Ali (1797-98) from the Nawabship. Shore 93-98 obliged. By 1801, Sadat Ali Khan II defaulted. Wellesley 98-05 sent his brother Henry Wellesley 98-05 to impose a full Subsidiary Alliance. Half of Awadh (the Doab, Gorakhpur and Rohilkhand) was annexed as permanent subsidy payment. The handout's note: this was unfair. The revenue from this territory was twice the Rs 76 lakh annual subsidy it was meant to cover. These territories became the Ceded Districts, and in 1836 were given full province status as the North-West Provinces (NWP 1836) of British India. Recall on Rohilkhand: most of Rohilkhand was annexed by Awadh with EIC help in 1774. The EIC had helped because of the ToA 1765 military alliance. The remaining small part of Rohilkhand became the autonomous State of Rampur, but under Awadh legally, and from 1801 under the EIC legally. The Peshwa and the Treaty of Bassein, 1802: Yashwantrao Holkar defeats Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18; he was avenging his brother's death Bajirao II 96-18 flees (warn) December 1802, Treaty of Bassein (Vasai): he signs the SA to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support Scindia and Bhonsle read this as a Peshwa selling the Confederacy to the British (bad) The 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) follows December 1802, Peshwa Bajirao II 96-18. He had been defeated by Yashwantrao Holkar (avenging his brother's death). He fled, and signed the Treaty of Bassein (1802) to regain the Peshwaship with EIC support. The handout's note: Scindia and Bhonsle read this as a Peshwa selling the Confederacy to the British, and the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803–05) followed. The full treatment of Bassein 1802 and the war is in the Anglo-Maratha Wars chapter (Chapter 13). Recall: the Marathas captured Bassein from the Portuguese via the Treaty of Bassein (1739), and brought it under Peshwa control along with Salsette. So there are two Treaties of Bassein: 1739 (Marathas and the Portuguese) and 1802 (Peshwa and the EIC). 1816, Bhonsle of Nagpur. After defeat in the 2nd Anglo-Maratha War (1803-05) the Bhonsles had resisted signing a full Subsidiary Alliance for over a decade. In 1816 Appa Sahib finally signed, using EIC backing to win the faction fight over who would be regent of the Bhonsle of Nagpur. (The story belongs to the Anglo-Maratha Wars chapter, Chapter 13.) Two wordings to notice in the handout. (1) The date of the 4th Anglo-Mysore War: Section 1, Section 6 and slide 31 print "4th Anglo-Mysore War (1798–99)", while Section 7 and the index of the next chapter print "4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799" (as does Chapter 7). The fall of Seringapatam and the death of Tipu 82-99 are 1799 in every version. (2) Seringapatam: Section 1 and slide 31 call it the "Siege of Seringapatam (1799)"; Section 6 calls it the "Battle of Seringapatam (1799)". It is the same event.

items.t: 7 · Direct annexations and the recall of Wellesley 98-05
items.x: What territory did Wellesley 98-05 directly annex, and why was he eventually recalled? Beyond Subsidiary Alliances, Wellesley 98-05 also directly annexed territory:   When   Territory   Detail    --- --- ---    1799   Mysore territory   Significant territory taken from Mysore after the 4th Anglo-Mysore War 1799     Early 1801   Half of Awadh (the Ceded Districts)   Annexed as permanent subsidy payment (the NWP 1836 territories, covered in section 6)     1801   Carnatic   Annexed on grounds of maladministration, six years after the death of Md Ali 52-95 (1752–1795), who had been the EIC's loyal ally since the 2nd Carnatic War 1749-54     1803–05   2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Bhonsle   Bhonsle of Nagpur lost significant territory, including Orissa (which Bhonsle had himself taken from Bengal in 1751)     1803–05   2nd Anglo-Maratha War: Scindia   Scindia lost territory in Gujarat and all territory north of the River Yamuna, including Delhi   Wellesley 98-05 was eventually recalled to London due to high war expenditure. Empire building was profitable only if wars were short and cheap. His were neither. The chapter comes full circle on money. High war expenditure produced the ban on conquest in Pitt's India Act 1784. Wellesley 98-05 got round the ban with the Napoleon threat and the Subsidiary Alliance. And high war expenditure is what finally got Wellesley 98-05 recalled. The handout page for this chapter ends with an index of the next chapter (Mysore's four wars, Dhondia Wagh, Tipu 82-99's religious policy, the Carnatic annexed in 1801, Travancore and Velu Thampi Dalawa). That material belongs to Chapter 12, not here.
